This is the structure of a typical [Django] project (Example 01): a configuration package ([config]), a [manage.py] file, and code packages. Only two of these are [Django] applications, declared in [INSTALLED_APPS]: [models], because it contains templates from ORM (which [Django] searches for only in applications), and [web], because it contains a tag library ([templatetags], example 16). The others ([dao], [business], [security], [domain]) are simply [Python] packages that the others import: they have nothing to report to [Django]. [Django] does not enforce any of these folders, and a typical project would instead have one application per domain (calendars, accounts, etc.), each with its own models, views, and templates; we preferred, as in the other versions of the case study, a layer-based organization, as shown in Example 28. [Bootstrap] is part of the application this time (folder [static/lib/bootstrap]): the case study is self-contained.

docs.title: 11.5. The Database
docs.text:
The [dbrdvmedecins2] database has five tables:

  • [users]: users authorized to log in;
  • [doctors] and [clients]: doctors and patients, each linked to their user account;
  • [slots]: each doctor’s available time slots;
  • [appointments]: appointments, one client per time slot on a given day.

docs.title: 11.5.1. database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql
docs.text:
-- =========================================================================
-- Database [dbrdvmedecins2] - MySQL 8
--
-- Evolution of [dbrdvmedecins]:
--   1. the [doctors] and [clients] tables get a [user] column,
--      foreign key to users(id): every doctor and every client is
--      now also a user able to log in;
--   2. a third role appears: DOCTOR (in addition to ADMIN and USER);
--   3. the script creates a [users] row for each doctor (role DOCTOR)
--      and for each client (role USER):
--        - login        = last name in lower case
--        - password     = last name in lower case, hashed with bcrypt (10 rounds)
--        - display name = first name + last name
--
--   4. uniqueness constraints, all NAMED (the application recognizes
--      the name of the violated constraint in the MySQL error message):
--        - unq_users_login                   : a login belongs to one account only;
--        - unq_doctors_first_name_last_name  : two doctors cannot have the
--                                              same first and last names;
--        - unq_clients_first_name_last_name  : same for the clients.
--      Beware: the utf8mb4_unicode_ci collation compares regardless of
--      case and accents - "Hélène DUPONT" and "helene dupont"
--      are therefore considered identical.
--
-- The [users] table must now be created BEFORE [doctors] and [clients]
-- (they reference it), and dropped AFTER them.
-- =========================================================================

-- the script is written in UTF-8
SET NAMES utf8mb4;

-- we start again from an empty database on each run of the script (handy in development)
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS dbrdvmedecins2 CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE dbrdvmedecins2;

-- drop order: from the "child" tables to the "parent" tables
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS appointments;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS slots;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS clients;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS doctors;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users;

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [users]: the users allowed to log in to the application
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE users (
  id       INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version  INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  login    VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,                 -- login identifier
  password VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,                -- HASHED password (bcrypt) - never in clear
  name     VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,                 -- name displayed once logged in
  role     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,                 -- 'ADMIN', 'DOCTOR' or 'USER'
  -- a login can belong to one account only
  CONSTRAINT unq_users_login UNIQUE (login)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [doctors]: the doctors of the practice
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE doctors (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,   -- primary key (technical identifier)
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,            -- row version number (optimistic lock)
  title      VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,              -- Melle, Mme, Mr
  last_name  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  first_name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  `user`     INT NOT NULL,                      -- foreign key -> users(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_doctors_user FOREIGN KEY (`user`) REFERENCES users(id),
  -- one account per doctor, and one doctor per account
  CONSTRAINT unq_doctors_user UNIQUE (`user`),
  -- two doctors cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_doctors_first_name_last_name UNIQUE (first_name, last_name)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [clients]: the doctors' patients
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE clients (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  title      VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,
  last_name  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  first_name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  `user`     INT NOT NULL,                      -- foreign key -> users(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_clients_user FOREIGN KEY (`user`) REFERENCES users(id),
  -- one account per client, and one client per account
  CONSTRAINT unq_clients_user UNIQUE (`user`),
  -- two clients cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_clients_first_name_last_name UNIQUE (first_name, last_name)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [slots]: the time slots of each doctor
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE slots (
  id           INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version      INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  doctor_id    INT NOT NULL,                     -- foreign key -> doctors(id)
  start_hour   INT NOT NULL,                     -- start hour of the slot
  start_minute INT NOT NULL,                     -- start minute of the slot
  end_hour     INT NOT NULL,                     -- end hour of the slot
  end_minute   INT NOT NULL,                     -- end minute of the slot
  CONSTRAINT fk_slots_doctor FOREIGN KEY (doctor_id) REFERENCES doctors(id)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [appointments]: the appointments booked by the clients
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE appointments (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  day        DATE NOT NULL,                      -- day of the appointment
  slot_id    INT NOT NULL,                       -- foreign key -> slots(id)
  client_id  INT NOT NULL,                       -- foreign key -> clients(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_appointments_slot   FOREIGN KEY (slot_id)   REFERENCES slots(id),
  CONSTRAINT fk_appointments_client FOREIGN KEY (client_id) REFERENCES clients(id),
  -- the same slot, on the same day, can be booked only once
  CONSTRAINT unq1_appointments UNIQUE (day, slot_id)
);

-- =========================================================================
-- Demo data
-- =========================================================================

-- the users: passwords hashed with bcrypt (10 salt rounds)
--   admin/admin (ADMIN)
--   one DOCTOR account per doctor, one USER account per client
--   (the user/user demo account is gone: a USER account is
--   now ALWAYS a client's account, who can book and manage the account)
--   (login = password = last name in lower case)
INSERT INTO users (login, password, name, role) VALUES
  ('admin',     '$2b$10$YSNBJXXHX9mp13nPZb6YGu8M1jR6uvPwO1s2X73z0QAqBR7TOQjoq', 'Administrator',    'ADMIN'),
  -- doctors
  ('pelissier', '$2b$10$DnSDOK5ONrdMxTTr1NKCHOphR3WSp5QAyG9S9ueruw9HwlxI.16ba', 'Marie PELISSIER',  'DOCTOR'),
  ('tatou',     '$2b$10$PeovBO.gmJUKP4PglI/fwu4xtWOYSxoM5VTWjTj7uQ4wcd9P9.htS', 'Paul TATOU',       'DOCTOR'),
  ('dupont',    '$2b$10$az7wvPKC1h0EiAxXwu/PU.vYjzmB04rd5B7QnK0mvxp4niYIHVoc.', 'Sophie DUPONT',    'DOCTOR'),
  -- clients
  ('martin',    '$2b$10$GT6S5pp.WdGapFw/UmocXesbC6LEjJfZzgatCUyG9Sf4o1iBNlqZW', 'Jean MARTIN',      'USER'),
  ('durand',    '$2b$10$l2gl/zCder8E7Nh4VxGRX.0.SsO3FDiXt6YwqYq3v9nFzgC/jQCy6', 'Alice DURAND',     'USER'),
  ('bistrou',   '$2b$10$naeRp2YUU6c.QDl5itJMAum3Y5aHdUV6jwIcsbp0D.64jPG4F6E9m', 'Brigitte BISTROU', 'USER'),
  ('german',    '$2b$10$tTWxh3ROWF7NjhZOMnWDMOsZcnSWUiwwfy5C3G0.xhccTXALKyLeW', 'Luc GERMAN',       'USER');

-- the doctors: the [user] column is looked up from the login,
-- rather than assuming the values of the primary keys of [users]
INSERT INTO doctors (title, last_name, first_name, `user`) VALUES
  ('Mme',  'PELISSIER', 'Marie',  (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'pelissier')),
  ('Mr',   'TATOU',     'Paul',   (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'tatou')),
  ('Melle','DUPONT',    'Sophie', (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'dupont'));

INSERT INTO clients (title, last_name, first_name, `user`) VALUES
  ('Mr',   'MARTIN',  'Jean',     (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'martin')),
  ('Mme',  'DURAND',  'Alice',    (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'durand')),
  ('Melle','BISTROU', 'Brigitte', (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'bistrou')),
  ('Mr',   'GERMAN',  'Luc',      (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'german'));

-- slots of doctor PELISSIER (doctor_id = 1): from 8:00 to 12:00 in 20-minute steps
INSERT INTO slots (doctor_id, start_hour, start_minute, end_hour, end_minute) VALUES
  (1, 8, 0, 8, 20), (1, 8, 20, 8, 40), (1, 8, 40, 9, 0),
  (1, 9, 0, 9, 20), (1, 9, 20, 9, 40), (1, 9, 40, 10, 0),
  (1, 10, 0, 10, 20), (1, 10, 20, 10, 40), (1, 10, 40, 11, 0),
  (1, 11, 0, 11, 20), (1, 11, 20, 11, 40), (1, 11, 40, 12, 0);

-- slots of doctor TATOU (doctor_id = 2): from 14:00 to 18:00 in 20-minute steps
INSERT INTO slots (doctor_id, start_hour, start_minute, end_hour, end_minute) VALUES
  (2, 14, 0, 14, 20), (2, 14, 20, 14, 40), (2, 14, 40, 15, 0),
  (2, 15, 0, 15, 20), (2, 15, 20, 15, 40), (2, 15, 40, 16, 0),
  (2, 16, 0, 16, 20), (2, 16, 20, 16, 40), (2, 16, 40, 17, 0),
  (2, 17, 0, 17, 20), (2, 17, 20, 17, 40), (2, 17, 40, 18, 0);

-- an appointment already booked, to see an occupied slot right away in the schedule
INSERT INTO appointments (day, slot_id, client_id) VALUES
  (CURDATE(), 2, 3);
  • line 33: the database is created if it does not exist, with the character set [utf8mb4] and the collation [utf8mb4_unicode_ci], which compares strings without regard to uppercase letters or accents (example 28);
  • lines 37–41: The tables are dropped and then recreated; the script restores the database to its initial state. The order matters: a table cannot be dropped as long as another table references it via a foreign key;
  • lines 46–55: users: a login, a password hashed by [bcrypt] (example 25), the display name once logged in, and the role ([ADMIN], [DOCTOR], or [USER]). The constraint [unq_users_login] ensures that a username belongs to only one account;
  • Lines 60–72: Each table has a primary key [id], generated by the database, and a column [version], which is the optimistic lock (Example 28). The column [user] is a foreign key to [users(id)]: the database rejects any value that is not the ID of an existing user. Since [user] is a word in the SQL language, it is surrounded by grave accents. Three constraints: [fk_doctors_user] (the foreign key), [unq_doctors_user] (one account per doctor, and one doctor per account), and [unq_doctors_first_name_last_name] (no homonyms). All constraints are named: the application recognizes a violated constraint by its name;
  • lines 77–89: the [clients] table has exactly the same columns;
  • lines 94–103: a time slot belongs to a doctor; its start and end times are stored in hours and minutes;
  • lines 108–118: an appointment consists of a day (type [DATE], without a time), a time slot, and a client. The constraint [unq1_appointments] prevents the same time slot from being booked twice on the same day: the database enforces this rule, even if two users attempt to book it at the same time;
  • Lines 130–140: Demo users, whose password is their login. The hashes begin with [$2b$10$]: the algorithm ([bcrypt], variant [2b]) and the cost (10: 2^10 computation rounds). Next come the salt (22 characters) and the hash. These hashes were calculated by the [Flask] version of the application, using the [bcrypt] library from [Python], which is also used by this version;
  • lines 144–147: the [user] column for each doctor is retrieved via a subquery based on the login, rather than by assuming the values of the primary keys;
  • lines 170–171: an appointment already scheduled for today ([CURDATE()]) in Dr. PELISSIER’s second time slot for Ms. BISTROU: the calendar thus immediately shows that the time slot is booked.

Unlike in the case of [Django], the database is not created by the migrations for [Django] (Example 28): it is shared with the other versions of the application, and the script SQL is common to all of them. The templates are therefore declared as [managed = False], and the [python manage.py makemigrations] command has no action to perform. The [python manage.py inspectdb] command is used to compare the database to the templates.

docs.text:
# the libraries of the application: pip install -r requirements.txt
Django==6.1.1

PyJWT==2.15.0

The four libraries required by the application, with their exact versions (see introduction): [Django], the driver [MySQL] ([mysqlclient], Example 28), the tokens JWT ([PyJWT], Example 25), and [bcrypt], for the database passwords (see below). [pip] also installs the libraries on which they depend ([asgiref] and [sqlparse], for [Django]). The command [pip freeze] outputs the exact list of what is installed in the environment, including dependencies: this is the way to obtain a file that locks in all versions. A larger project would use a project management tool, such as [uv] or [Poetry], which separates the requested libraries (file [pyproject.toml]) from the exact versions installed (a lock file, such as [composer.lock] for [PHP]).

docs.text:

# of the process; a real environment variable of the system
# takes precedence over this file.

# 1: development (detailed error pages); 0: production (see README.md)

The file containing settings specific to this installation (example 25): these vary from one machine to another (the database, its credentials) or are secrets (the keys). In a real-world project, this file is never released with the code: each installation has its own, and production secrets are often provided via actual environment variables. [Django] does not read a [.env] file on its own: the [config/settings.py] file reads it (as described later). The [python-dotenv] library would do the same, and [django-environ] would add value conversion to it.

  • Line 9: debug mode (example 01): 1 during development (detailed error pages, SQL commands in the console), 0 in production;
  • line 12: the secret key for [Django], which is used for anti-CSRF tokens (example 18) and all signatures (signed cookies, flash messages, examples 20 and 23);
  • line 14: accepted hostnames (example 01);
  • lines 19–23: the database connection (example 28);
  • lines 25–43: application-specific settings: the JWT tokens (example 25), setting cookies to [Secure] mode (discussed later), and protection against bots (example 27).

docs.title: 11.6.3. config/settings.py
docs.text:
The settings file contains the entire configuration, written in [Python] (example 01):

# =========================================================================
# config/settings.py: the configuration of the RdvMedecins application.
#
# The settings specific to an installation (passwords, secret keys, thresholds)
# are read from environment variables, which the .env file provides in
# development (see read_env). Everything else is written here.
# =========================================================================

import os
from pathlib import Path

# the project folder (the one that contains manage.py)
BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# reads the .env file: each NAME=value line becomes an environment
# variable, EXCEPT if it already exists (setdefault): a real environment
# variable of the system takes precedence over the file. Empty lines and
# comments (#) are ignored; quotes around the value are removed
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
def read_env(file: Path) -> None:
    if not file.exists():
        return
    for line in file.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
        line = line.strip()
        if line and not line.startswith("#") and "=" in line:
            name, value = line.split("=", 1)
            os.environ.setdefault(name.strip(), value.strip().strip('"'))


read_env(BASE_DIR / ".env")


# an environment variable: a text, an integer, a boolean (1/0)
def env(name: str, default: str = "") -> str:
    return os.environ.get(name, default)


def env_int(name: str, default: int) -> int:
    return int(env(name, str(default)))


def env_bool(name: str, default: bool) -> bool:
    return env(name, "1" if default else "0") == "1"


# ---- debug mode and security
DEBUG = env_bool("DJANGO_DEBUG", False)
SECRET_KEY = env("DJANGO_SECRET_KEY")
ALLOWED_HOSTS = [h.strip() for h in env("DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS", "localhost").split(",")]

# ---- the applications: Django itself (static files, flash messages,
# forms), and our two applications: models (the tables) and web (the
# template tags). The other folders (dao, business, security...) are
# plain Python packages: they have neither models nor templates
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    "django.contrib.staticfiles",
    "django.contrib.messages",
    "django.forms",
    "models",
    "web",
]

# ---- the middlewares, in order (see example 24):
#   - SetLanguage: the language of the request (cookie rdvmedecins_language);
#   - CsrfViewMiddleware: the anti-CSRF token of every POST request;
#   - MessageMiddleware: the flash messages;
#   - Authentication: the user, from the JWT token of their cookie;
#   - AccessControl: the access rule of each URL (after routing);
#   - ErrorPage: errors become pages of the application
MIDDLEWARE = [
    "web.middleware.SetLanguage",
    "django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware",
    "django.contrib.messages.middleware.MessageMiddleware",
    "security.middleware.Authentication",
    "security.middleware.AccessControl",
    "web.middleware.ErrorPage",
]

ROOT_URLCONF = "config.urls"
WSGI_APPLICATION = "config.wsgi.application"

# ---- the database: MySQL (or MariaDB), the dbrdvmedecins2 database
DATABASES = {
    "default": {
        "ENGINE": "django.db.backends.mysql",
        "HOST": env("DB_HOST", "127.0.0.1"),
        "PORT": env("DB_PORT", "3306"),
        "NAME": env("DB_NAME", "dbrdvmedecins2"),
        "USER": env("DB_USER", "root"),
        "PASSWORD": env("DB_PASSWORD"),
        "OPTIONS": {"charset": "utf8mb4"},
    },
}

# ---- the CACHE: files of the var/cache folder, SHARED by all the
# processes of the server (captchas, failure counters, passes, lists of
# doctors and clients). An in-memory cache (LocMemCache) would be specific to
# each process: a production server starts several of them
CACHES = {
    "default": {
        "BACKEND": "django.core.cache.backends.filebased.FileBasedCache",
        "LOCATION": BASE_DIR / "var" / "cache",
    },
}

# ---- the templates (templates folder) and their context processors
TEMPLATES = [
    {
        "BACKEND": "django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates",
        "DIRS": [BASE_DIR / "templates"],
        "APP_DIRS": True,
        "OPTIONS": {
            "context_processors": [
                "django.template.context_processors.request",
                "django.template.context_processors.i18n",
                "django.contrib.messages.context_processors.messages",
                # the logged-in user, in all the templates (see web/contexts.py)
                "web.contexts.user",
            ],
        },
    },
]

# the form fields are drawn with the Bootstrap 5 classes (see
# example 18 and templates/forms/field.html)
FORM_RENDERER = "web.rendering.BootstrapRenderer"

# ---- the languages (see example 22): English by default, French; the
# dictionaries are in the locale folder
LANGUAGE_CODE = "en"
LANGUAGES = [("fr", "Français"), ("en", "English")]
LOCALE_PATHS = [BASE_DIR / "locale"]
# the cookie that remembers the chosen language (see web/views/language.py)
LANGUAGE_COOKIE_NAME = "rdvmedecins_language"

# ---- the time zone: that of the medical practice. It sets today's date (no
# appointment in the past, see business/dates.py)
TIME_ZONE = "Europe/Paris"
USE_TZ = True

# ---- the static files (static folder): Bootstrap, the style sheet, the script
STATIC_URL = "static/"
STATICFILES_DIRS = [BASE_DIR / "static"]
# in production, collectstatic gathers all the static files there (see README.md)
STATIC_ROOT = BASE_DIR / "var" / "static"

# ---- the flash messages: in a signed cookie (see example 20)
MESSAGE_STORAGE = "django.contrib.messages.storage.cookie.CookieStorage"

# ---- the cookies: never readable by the JavaScript of the page (HttpOnly, even the
# anti-CSRF cookie, which Django leaves readable by default), never sent with a
# POST request coming from another site (Lax), never unencrypted in production (Secure)
COOKIE_SECURE = env_bool("COOKIE_SECURE", False)
CSRF_COOKIE_NAME = "rdvmedecins_csrf"
CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = COOKIE_SECURE
CSRF_COOKIE_HTTPONLY = True
CSRF_COOKIE_SAMESITE = "Lax"
# a missing or wrong anti-CSRF token: our 419 error page (see web/views/errors.py)
CSRF_FAILURE_VIEW = "web.views.errors.csrf_rejected"

# ---- our own settings: authentication (see security/auth.py)...
JWT_SECRET = env("JWT_SECRET")
JWT_DURATION_MINUTES = env_int("JWT_DURATION_MINUTES", 120)
# ... and protection against robots (see security/limiter.py)
LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES = env_int("LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES", 5)
LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES_IP = env_int("LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES_IP", 25)
LOGIN_BLOCK_MINUTES = env_int("LOGIN_BLOCK_MINUTES", 15)
REGISTRATION_MAX_PER_HOUR = env_int("REGISTRATION_MAX_PER_HOUR", 10)

# ---- logging: in debug mode, the SQL statements sent to the database are written to
# the console (see example 28)
LOGGING = {
    "version": 1,
    "disable_existing_loggers": False,
    "handlers": {"console": {"class": "logging.StreamHandler"}},
    "loggers": {
        "django.db.backends": {"handlers": ["console"], "level": "DEBUG"},
    },
}
  • Lines 22–32: Reading the file [.env]. [read_text] reads the entire file, while [splitlines] splits it into lines. Each line of [NAME=value], excluding comments, becomes an environment variable for the process ([split("=", 1)]: split only at the first occurrence of [=], as a value may contain it). [setdefault] does not overwrite an existing variable: a real environment variable takes precedence over the file (example 25);
  • lines 36–45: three small functions that read an environment variable—with a default value—and convert it (to an integer or a Boolean value of 1 or 0);
  • lines 49–51: debug mode, the secret key, and the hostnames, read from the environment. If [.env] is not present, debug mode is disabled: this is the safe choice. [ALLOWED_HOSTS] is a list, constructed from a string of names separated by commas;
  • lines 57–63: the applications (see the architecture): three applications from [Django] (static files, Example 15; flash messages, Example 20; form templates, Example 18) and our two;
  • lines 72–79: the six middleware components, in the order in which the request passes through them (example 24). The order matters: the language is set first, so that all pages—even error pages—are in the correct language; anti-CSRF protection comes before authentication; authentication (which identifies the user) comes before access control (which evaluates the user); and [ErrorPage], the last one, is the first to handle exceptions thrown by the views ([process_exception] is called in the reverse order, Example 24);
  • lines 85–95: the database (Example 28), whose parameters come from the environment;
  • lines 101–106: the application cache (Example 27). It is stored in files ([FileBasedCache]) within the [var/cache] folder, which [Django] creates itself: unlike the in-memory cache in Example 27, it survives server restarts (on a development server, after every code change), and it is shared by all processes on a production server (see the chapter on scopes). The application stores lists of doctors and clients, CAPTCHAs, attempt counters, and passes in this cache. With multiple servers, one would choose a shared cache, such as [Redis];
  • lines 109–124: the templates (Example 13), along with the application templates ([APP_DIRS], for those in [django.forms], Example 18), and four context processors: the request, the language (Example 22), flash messages (Example 20), and ours, which makes the logged-in user available to all templates (see below);
  • line 128: the form rendering engine, with the classes from [Bootstrap] (example 18);
  • lines 132–136: the languages and the dictionary (Example 22). The language cookie has a name specific to the application;
  • lines 140–141: the firm’s time zone. [USE_TZ = True] (the default value) causes [Django] to operate in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) and convert times to this time zone for display; [timezone.localdate()] returns the current date in this time zone. The current date is used for a business rule (no appointments in the past): in Paris, between midnight and 2:00 a.m. during daylight saving time, the date in Coordinated Universal Time is still the previous day; therefore, the firm’s time zone takes precedence;
  • lines 144–147: static files (example 15): the application’s [static] folder, and the folder where [collectstatic] collects them for production;
  • line 150: flash messages, in a signed cookie (example 20);
  • lines 155–161: the cookies from [Django]. [COOKIE_SECURE], read from [.env], will also be used for our own cookies (the token, language, etc.) : In production, on HTTPS, no cookies are transmitted in plain text. The anti-CSRF token cookie is given a name specific to the application; it is rendered as [HttpOnly] (the [JavaScript] on the page does not need it: it does not send any requests itself) and [SameSite=Lax]. A missing or invalid anti-CSRF token will display a page from the application (see below), rather than the 403 page for [Django] (Example 18);
  • lines 164–170: application-specific settings, read from the environment: the tokens JWT (Example 25) and bot protection (Example 27);
  • lines 174–181: the SQL command log, in debug mode (example 28).

The [python manage.py diffsettings] command displays all settings that differ from the default values of [Django].

from django.urls import include, path

urlpatterns = [
    path("", include("web.urls")),

The four views of the error pages that [Django] generates itself (Example 24) are designated here by strings (the full path to the function): [Django] will import them itself.

docs.title: 11.7.1. manage.py and config/wsgi.py
docs.text:
The files [manage.py] and [config/wsgi.py] are from Example 01: the command-line tool, and the application WSGI, which is launched by the development server and the production servers. Upon startup, [Django] reads the settings (the [config/settings.py] file then reads the [.env] file), loads the applications from [INSTALLED_APPS] (their models, their configuration, example 24), creates an object for each middleware component (example 03), and then waits for requests. Everything built at startup is shared by all requests as long as the process is running: this applies to unique application objects (the business layer, the [ApplicationModel] facade), which are created by their providers when first used (example 06).

Two things are checked at startup, and an error shuts down the server before any requests are processed: the JWT token key (if it is too short, it is rejected; see [security/auth.py]) and, with [MySQL], the database connection (see “Common Problems”).

docs.title: 11.8. The Templates
docs.text: The templates for ORM (Example 28): one class per table, in the [models/models.py] file of the [models] application.

docs.title: 11.8.1. models/apps.py
docs.text:
# models/apps.py: the configuration of the models application

from django.apps import AppConfig


class ModelsConfig(AppConfig):
    name = "models"

The application configuration (example 24), reduced to its name. It is not required: [Django] would generate one; we write it so that each application has its own.

docs.title: 11.8.2. models/models.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# models/models.py: the Django MODELS, one class per table of the
# dbrdvmedecins2 database (see example 28).
#
# The tables already exist: they are created by the script
# database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql, the same as that of the other versions of
# the application. Each model tells Django so with managed = False: Django never
# creates, modifies or deletes these tables (no migrations).
#
# The foreign keys (ForeignKey, OneToOneField) are declared with
# on_delete=DO_NOTHING: when a row is deleted, Django does not look itself for
# the rows that reference it. It is the business layer that deletes, in the right
# order, what must be deleted (see business/service.py); the database constraints
# would refuse an incomplete deletion anyway.
#
# All the tables have a [version] column: the optimistic lock, which the DAO
# layer uses for its UPDATEs (see dao/persons.py).
# =========================================================================

from django.db import models


# the three roles of a user (column users.role):
#   - ADMIN  : the administrator - appointments + management of doctors and clients;
#   - DOCTOR : a doctor - books and cancels appointments;
#   - USER   : a client (patient) - books for themselves, manages their account.
# TextChoices: a Django ENUMERATION, each value of which is a string (the one
# stored in the database); Role("ADMIN") goes the other way
class Role(models.TextChoices):
    ADMIN = "ADMIN"
    DOCTOR = "DOCTOR"
    USER = "USER"


# a user allowed to log in (table [users]). Each doctor and each
# client owns THEIR account (column [user] of the tables [doctors] and [clients]).
# SQL uniqueness constraint: unq_users_login (a login belongs to one account
# only), recognized by its NAME in the business layer (see business/service.py)
class User(models.Model):
    id = models.AutoField(primary_key=True)
    version = models.IntegerField(default=0)
    login = models.CharField(max_length=30)
    # the HASHED password (bcrypt), never the password itself
    password = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    # the name displayed once logged in: "Marie PELISSIER"
    name = models.CharField(max_length=40)
    # choices: the possible values of the column
    role = models.CharField(max_length=10, choices=Role.choices)

    class Meta:
        db_table = "users"
        managed = False

    def __str__(self):
        return self.login


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# what doctors (table [doctors]) and clients (table
# [clients]) have in common: a title, a last name, a first name - and the associated
# user account (column [user]).
#
# The two tables have exactly the same columns: they are described ONCE,
# in this ABSTRACT model (abstract = True: a "Person" is never created, and
# it has no table of its own), which Doctor and Client inherit; each only specifies
# the name of its table.
#
# Beware: [Client] here means a PATIENT of the medical practice, not an HTTP
# client! It is the vocabulary of the original business domain, kept as is.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
class Person(models.Model):
    id = models.AutoField(primary_key=True)
    version = models.IntegerField(default=0)
    # Mr, Mme, Melle
    title = models.CharField(max_length=5)
    last_name = models.CharField(max_length=20)
    first_name = models.CharField(max_length=20)
    # the RELATIONSHIP to the user account: a person has ONE account, designated by
    # the foreign key [user] (db_column). OneToOneField: one account per person,
    # one person per account. person.account returns a User object, read from the database on
    # first access - or by the query itself, if it asks for it (select_related, see
    # dao/persons.py). related_name: the name of the reverse relationship,
    # user.doctor or user.client (%(class)s: the name of the model, in lower case)
    account = models.OneToOneField(User, db_column="user", on_delete=models.DO_NOTHING,
                                   related_name="%(class)s")

    class Meta:
        abstract = True

    # "Mme Alice DURAND"
    def label(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.title} {self.first_name} {self.last_name}"

    def __str__(self):
        return self.label()


# a doctor (table [doctors]). SQL uniqueness constraint: unq_doctors_first_name_last_name
# (two doctors cannot have the same first and last names)
class Doctor(Person):
    class Meta:
        db_table = "doctors"
        managed = False


# a client, that is to say a PATIENT (table [clients]). SQL uniqueness constraint:
# unq_clients_first_name_last_name
class Client(Person):
    class Meta:
        db_table = "clients"
        managed = False


# a time slot of a doctor (table [slots]): 8:00 - 8:20, etc. The
# slots are created by the SQL script: the application only reads them
class Slot(models.Model):
    id = models.AutoField(primary_key=True)
    version = models.IntegerField(default=0)
    # several slots for the same doctor: a foreign key, [doctor_id]
    doctor = models.ForeignKey(Doctor, db_column="doctor_id", on_delete=models.DO_NOTHING,
                               related_name="slots")
    start_hour = models.IntegerField()
    start_minute = models.IntegerField()
    end_hour = models.IntegerField()
    end_minute = models.IntegerField()

    class Meta:
        db_table = "slots"
        managed = False

    # "8:00 - 8:20"; :02d: on two digits, "8:05" rather than "8:5"
    def time_range(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.start_hour}:{self.start_minute:02d} - {self.end_hour}:{self.end_minute:02d}"


# an appointment (table [appointments]): a client, on a slot, on a given day.
# SQL uniqueness constraint: unq1_appointments (day, slot_id) - a slot is booked
# only once per day; recognized by its name in the business layer
class Appointment(models.Model):
    id = models.AutoField(primary_key=True)
    version = models.IntegerField(default=0)
    # DateField: the [day] column (SQL type DATE) becomes a Python date object
    day = models.DateField()
    slot = models.ForeignKey(Slot, db_column="slot_id", on_delete=models.DO_NOTHING,
                             related_name="appointments")
    client = models.ForeignKey(Client, db_column="client_id", on_delete=models.DO_NOTHING,
                               related_name="appointments")

    class Meta:
        db_table = "appointments"
        managed = False
  • lines 29–32: the three roles, in the form of an enumeration of [Django] ([models.TextChoices]), itself built on the enumerations of [Python] (the [enum] module): a type whose only possible values are its members: [Role.ADMIN], [Role.DOCTOR], and [Role.USER]. Each element has a value, in this case the string in base; an element of [TextChoices] is itself a string: [Role.ADMIN == "ADMIN"] is true. [Role("ADMIN")] returns the corresponding element (and sets [ValueError] to an unknown value). [Role.choices] returns the list of (value, label) pairs, which can be passed to the [choices] parameter of a field;
  • lines 39–55: the schema for table [users]: the primary key, the version (the optimistic lock, example 28), followed by the columns. [choices] (line 48) documents the possible values for the column; [Django] uses this to validate a form based on the schema and for the administration interface; the database itself does not perform any checks. [managed = False]: the table is created by the script SQL (Example 28);
  • lines 71–95: the tables [doctors] and [clients] have the same columns. Their shared description is written once, in an abstract template ([abstract = True], line 88): a template that has no table of its own and serves only to be inherited. The templates [Doctor] and [Client] inherit from it: each has the fields of [Person] in its own table. ([Django] also supports true template hierarchies, where each child class has a table linked to that of the parent class; this is not the case here, where the two tables are independent);
  • Lines 84–85: The relationship to the account. [OneToOneField]: A person has an account, and an account belongs to at most one person. [db_column] refers to the foreign key column, [user] (without this parameter, [Django] would refer to it as [account_id], the field name followed by [_id]). [on_delete] specifies what [Django] does when the account is deleted: [DO_NOTHING], nothing (the comment on lines 10–14 explains this choice; [CASCADE] would also delete the person, while [PROTECT] would reject the deletion). The attribute [account] is a [User] object, not a number: that is the purpose of a ORM. When the ORM reads a person, it also reads their account if the request specifies it ([select_related]; see the DAO layer); otherwise, it will retrieve it via an additional request upon the first access to [person.account]. The number itself is always available, without a query, under the name [account_id]. [related_name] refers to the inverse relationship: [user.doctor] or [user.client], the person associated with an account; [%(class)s] is replaced by the template name, in lowercase, which gives a different name to each of the two templates that inherit the field;
  • lines 91–95: the name of a person, “Ms. Alice DURAND,” used by all pages;
  • lines 100–111: two templates that specify only their table; everything else is inherited. A [Client] is a patient at the practice, not a client HTTP: this is the vocabulary of the original business domain, preserved in all versions of the application;
  • lines 116–133: an appointment slot. [ForeignKey] (line 120): multiple appointment slots for the same doctor, via the foreign key [doctor_id]; the inverse relationship, [doctor.slots], returns a doctor’s time slots. The method [time_range] returns “8:00 - 8:20”: in an f-string, [{self.start_minute:02d}] writes an integer of at least two digits, padded with zeros ([8:05] rather than [8:5]);
  • lines 139–151: an appointment. The column [day] (type SQL [DATE]) becomes a [date] object of type [Python] ([DateField]); the [date] objects are immutable ([day + timedelta(days=1)] is returned the next day, [day] remains unchanged). Two relationships: one to the time slot and one to the appointment’s client.

docs.title: 11.9.1. domain/schedule.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# domain/schedule.py: the schedule of a doctor for a given day. "Business"
# objects COMPUTED by the business layer (BusinessService.get_doctor_day_schedule),
# which correspond to no table, then formatted for the template by the
# schedule view (web/views/schedule.py).
#
# frozen=True: the attributes are set once and for all by the constructor -
# exactly what is needed for a computed object, which nobody modifies afterwards.
# =========================================================================

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date

from models.models import Appointment, Doctor, Slot


# a time slot, and the appointment possibly booked on this slot on a given
# day (None if the slot is free)
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DoctorDaySlot:
    slot: Slot
    appointment: Appointment | None


# the complete schedule of a doctor for a given day: the list of their slots,
# each free or taken
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DoctorDaySchedule:
    doctor: Doctor
    day: date
    doctor_day_slots: list[DoctorDaySlot]

Two calculated objects that do not correspond to any table: a time slot and its potential appointment on a given day; a doctor’s schedule for a single day, the list of their time slots. These are immutable data classes (example 03), whose attributes are typed: [Appointment | None] (an appointment, or [None] for an available time slot), [list[DoctorDaySlot]] (a list of time slots). [Python] does not validate these types at runtime, but the editors ([Pylance]) and analysis tools ([mypy]) read them.

docs.title: 11.10. The DAO layer
docs.text: The DAO layer (Example 28) groups the queries: one module per table (doctors and clients share theirs), with no business rules. Its methods do not start a transaction: the business layer calls them within its own transactions. They are written using the [QuerySet] from the ORM (Example 28); the values there are query parameters: no SQL injection is possible. The DAO are classes, of which the business layer creates one object for each; they have no state: they are collections of functions.

docs.title: 11.10.1. dao/persons.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# dao/persons.py: the DAO layer common to doctors and clients.
#
# The DAOs of doctors and clients would be identical: the PersonDao class
# writes them only once. self.model is the model concerned (Doctor or
# Client): the queries apply to ITS table.
#
# The queries are written with the Django ORM (see example 28), which translates them
# into SQL. The values (first name, last name...) become PARAMETERS of the SQL statement:
# no string concatenation, hence no SQL injection. These methods open
# no transaction: it is the business layer that calls them, inside its own.
# =========================================================================

from django.db.models import F, QuerySet

from models.models import Client, Doctor, Person


class PersonDao:
    # model: the CLASS of the model, Doctor or Client (in Python, a class is
    # a value like any other, which can be stored in a variable)
    def __init__(self, model: type[Person]):
        self.model = model

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # a query on the table of the model, user account included.
    # select_related("account"): the SQL join with the [users] table
    #   SELECT doctors.*, users.* FROM doctors INNER JOIN users ON ...
    # the accounts are loaded BY THE SAME query. Without it, each access to
    # person.account would trigger its own query
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _query(self) -> QuerySet:
        return self.model.objects.select_related("account")

    # list sorted by last name then first name
    def list(self) -> list[Person]:
        return list(self._query().order_by("last_name", "first_name"))

    # a person and their account; None if they do not exist
    def read(self, id: int) -> Person | None:
        return self._query().filter(id=id).first()

    # the person whose user account is [user_id]; account_id: the
    # column of the foreign key itself, without a join
    def read_by_user(self, user_id: int) -> Person | None:
        return self._query().filter(account_id=user_id).first()

    # the person with these first and last names, if there is one. The comparison is
    # made by MySQL, hence with the collation of the database (utf8mb4_unicode_ci: regardless
    # of case and accents) - exactly the same rule as
    # that of the SQL uniqueness constraint
    def namesake(self, first_name: str, last_name: str) -> Person | None:
        return self._query().filter(first_name=first_name, last_name=last_name).first()

    # INSERT: the database generates the id, which Django stores in the created object
    def add(self, title: str, last_name: str, first_name: str, account) -> Person:
        return self.model.objects.create(title=title, last_name=last_name, first_name=first_name, account=account)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # UPDATE with OPTIMISTIC LOCK (see example 28):
    #   UPDATE doctors SET title = ?, last_name = ?, first_name = ?, version = version + 1
    #   WHERE id = ? AND version = ?
    # returns False if no row was modified: the record has changed (or disappeared)
    # since it was read
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def update(self, id: int, version: int, title: str, last_name: str, first_name: str) -> bool:
        return self.model.objects.filter(id=id, version=version).update(
            title=title, last_name=last_name, first_name=first_name, version=F("version") + 1) == 1

    # DELETE FROM doctors WHERE id = ?
    def delete(self, id: int) -> None:
        self.model.objects.filter(id=id).delete()


# the DAO of the doctors: everything is inherited from PersonDao
class DoctorDao(PersonDao):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(Doctor)


# the DAO of the clients: that of the persons, plus a locking method
class ClientDao(PersonDao):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(Client)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # puts a LOCK on the row of a client until the end of the current
    # transaction (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), and returns its id (None if the client does not
    # exist). A second transaction that requests the same lock WAITS until the
    # first one is finished. select_for_update: the "pessimistic" lock of
    # Django, which requires an open transaction.
    # Used for booking an appointment (see BusinessService.add_appointment): two
    # simultaneous bookings for the same patient are thus processed one
    # AFTER the other, and the second sees the appointment created by the first.
    # values_list("id", flat=True): the single id column, without a Client object
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def lock(self, id: int) -> int | None:
        return Client.objects.select_for_update().filter(id=id).values_list("id", flat=True).first()
  • Lines 19–23: The DAO objects for doctors and clients would be identical, except for the template: the [PersonDao] class creates them once and receives the template as a parameter to its constructor. [type[Person]] is the annotation of a class (not an object): [Person] or one of its child classes;
  • lines 32–33: the base query, common to all methods. [select_related("account")] instructs ORM to also retrieve each person’s account using a join ([INNER JOIN users]; see the console output above): a single query, instead of one additional query per person. Without it, displaying the list of doctors with their logins would require one query for the list, then one per doctor: this is the so-called “N + 1 queries” problem, the most common pitfall of ORM. The underscore at the beginning of the method name indicates that it is internal to the class (example 06);
  • lines 36–46: the reads. [account_id] (line 46) refers to the foreign key column itself: the condition applies to the people table, without a join;
  • lines 52–53: searching for a homonym. The comparison is performed by [MySQL], using the database’s collation: case-insensitive and ignoring accents, exactly like the uniqueness constraint (example 28);
  • lines 56–57: the insert; [account] is an instance of [User], which has already been inserted;
  • lines 66–68: the update, with its optimistic lock (Example 28): [update] returns the number of modified lines, 0 if the version has changed;
  • lines 71–72: the deletion, via a [QuerySet]: [delete()] sends a [DELETE] for all the lines it designates;
  • lines 76–78: the DAO for doctors, which inherits everything. [super().__init__(Doctor)] calls the parent class constructor with the template;
  • lines 82–98: the DAO for clients, with one additional method. [select_for_update()] adds to the [FOR UPDATE] query: [MySQL] places a lock on the read rows until the end of the current transaction. A second transaction requesting the same lock waits until the first one is complete. This is a “pessimistic” lock: it blocks the transaction, rather than detecting conflicts after the fact like an optimistic lock. It is only permitted within a transaction (otherwise, ORM throws an exception). [values_list("id", flat=True)] reads only the [id] column: a list of integers, not objects. The code comment explains the purpose of this lock; we’ll revisit this when discussing the business layer.

docs.title: 11.10.2. dao/slots.py
docs.text:
# dao/slots.py: the DAO layer of the time slots

from models.models import Slot


class SlotDao:
    # a slot and its doctor (a join)
    def read(self, id: int) -> Slot | None:
        return Slot.objects.select_related("doctor").filter(id=id).first()

    # the slots of a doctor, in chronological order. doctor_id: the column
    # of the foreign key, compared to an id
    def list_by_doctor(self, doctor_id: int) -> list[Slot]:
        return list(Slot.objects.filter(doctor_id=doctor_id).order_by("start_hour", "start_minute"))

    # deletes all the slots of a doctor (deletion of a doctor):
    #   DELETE FROM slots WHERE doctor_id = ?
    def delete_by_doctor(self, doctor_id: int) -> None:
        Slot.objects.filter(doctor_id=doctor_id).delete()

A doctor’s appointment slots, in chronological order; an appointment slot and its doctor (a join); the deletion of a doctor’s appointment slots (which precedes the deletion of the doctor, due to the foreign key constraint).

docs.title: 11.10.3. dao/appointments.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# dao/appointments.py: the DAO layer of the appointments.
#
# The [appointments] table does not reference the doctor directly: it goes through the slot.
# The Django ORM writes the join itself when a filter follows a relationship:
# slot__doctor_id (two underscores: "the doctor of the slot").
# =========================================================================

from datetime import date

from models.models import Appointment, Client, Slot


class AppointmentDao:
    # an appointment, its client and its slot
    def read(self, id: int) -> Appointment | None:
        return Appointment.objects.select_related("client", "slot").filter(id=id).first()

    # the appointments of a doctor on a given day, with their client
    def doctor_day_appointments(self, doctor_id: int, day: date) -> list[Appointment]:
        return list(Appointment.objects.select_related("client")
                    .filter(day=day, slot__doctor_id=doctor_id))

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # the appointments of a client from the day [since] (included), in chronological
    # order, with the slot AND the doctor of that slot (two joins:
    # select_related("slot__doctor")). day__gte: day >= since (gte:
    # "greater than or equal")
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def client_upcoming_appointments(self, client_id: int, since: date) -> list[Appointment]:
        return list(Appointment.objects.select_related("slot__doctor")
                    .filter(client_id=client_id, day__gte=since)
                    .order_by("day", "slot__start_hour", "slot__start_minute"))

    # number of appointments of a client from the day [since] (included):
    # count() makes the database count (SELECT COUNT(*) ...)
    def count_client_upcoming(self, client_id: int, since: date) -> int:
        return Appointment.objects.filter(client_id=client_id, day__gte=since).count()

    # number of appointments (past or future) of a doctor
    def count_by_doctor(self, doctor_id: int) -> int:
        return Appointment.objects.filter(slot__doctor_id=doctor_id).count()

    # INSERT INTO appointments ...
    def add(self, day: date, slot: Slot, client: Client) -> Appointment:
        return Appointment.objects.create(day=day, slot=slot, client=client)

    def delete(self, id: int) -> None:
        Appointment.objects.filter(id=id).delete()

    # deletes ALL the appointments (past and future) of a client
    def delete_by_client(self, client_id: int) -> None:
        Appointment.objects.filter(client_id=client_id).delete()
  • Lines 20–22: a doctor’s appointments on a given day. The [appointments] table does not directly reference the doctor: [slot__doctor_id] (two underscores) follows the relationship to the time slot, then compares the [doctor_id] column of the time slot. ORM writes the join itself ([INNER JOIN slots]; see the console output above). The client for each appointment is retrieved by the same query;
  • lines 30–33: a client’s upcoming appointments. [select_related("slot__doctor")] joins two tables: the time slot, then the client’s doctor (two joins). [day__gte]: The suffix [gte] (“greater than or equal,” example 28) performs a comparison using [>=]. The sort also follows the relationships;
  • lines 37–42: [count()] counts the base ([SELECT COUNT(*)]) without reading the lines;
  • lines 45–53: insertions and deletions.

docs.title: 11.10.4. dao/users.py
docs.text:
# dao/users.py: the DAO layer of the user accounts. Creating (or deleting) a
# doctor or a client also creates (or deletes) their account - see business/service.py

from django.db.models import F

from models.models import User


class UserDao:
    # None if no user has this login
    def read_by_login(self, login: str) -> User | None:
        return User.objects.filter(login=login).first()

    def add(self, login: str, hash: str, name: str, role: str) -> User:
        return User.objects.create(login=login, password=hash, name=name, role=role)

    # UPDATE with optimistic lock (see dao/persons.py); hash None: the
    # password is unchanged. **fields: the dictionary, "unpacked" into named parameters
    def update(self, id: int, version: int, login: str, name: str, hash: str | None) -> bool:
        fields = {"login": login, "name": name, "version": F("version") + 1}
        if hash is not None:
            fields["password"] = hash
        return User.objects.filter(id=id, version=version).update(**fields) == 1

    def delete(self, id: int) -> None:
        User.objects.filter(id=id).delete()

User accounts. The modification (lines 19–23) has an optional parameter: the hash of the new password, or [None] to keep the existing one. The columns to be modified are grouped into a dictionary, which [**fields] passes to [update] as named parameters (the “unpacking” of a dictionary, example 08).

docs.title: 11.11. The business layer
docs.text: The business layer (example 28): business rules and transactions. It knows nothing about the web: no requests, no responses, no templates.

docs.title: 11.11.1. business/dates.py
docs.text:
# business/dates.py: today's date. It is used by BUSINESS RULES (no
# booking in the past, a single UPCOMING appointment per patient): it therefore lives
# in the business layer. The web layer reuses it.

from datetime import date

from django.utils import timezone


# today, in the time zone of the application (TIME_ZONE setting)
def today() -> date:
    return timezone.localdate()

Today's date, in the application's time zone ([TIME_ZONE], see [config/settings.py]): [timezone.localdate()] converts Coordinated Universal Time to this time zone and then returns the date. The current date is used for two business rules (no appointments in the past, only one upcoming appointment): it is therefore calculated here, in a single location.

docs.title: 11.11.2. business/errors.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# business/errors.py: the exception raised by the business layer when a BUSINESS
# RULE is violated (login already taken, doctor who still has appointments,
# slot already booked...).
#
# It carries a CODE (LOGIN_TAKEN...), which the web layer can test, and the message
# intended for the user. This message is translated into French or English at the
# time it is displayed, in the language of the page: gettext_lazy returns a
# "lazy" translation, which is only computed when its text is requested
# (str), and not when the module is loaded (see example 22 and the locale folder).
#
# A BusinessError is not an anomaly: it is a normal answer ("this login
# is already used"), displayed to the user. Any other exception is a real
# anomaly, which ends in the 500 error page.
# =========================================================================

from django.utils.translation import gettext_lazy as _

# the codes of the business errors
LOGIN_TAKEN = "LOGIN_TAKEN"
DOCTOR_ALREADY_EXISTS = "DOCTOR_ALREADY_EXISTS"
CLIENT_ALREADY_EXISTS = "CLIENT_ALREADY_EXISTS"
DOCTOR_HAS_APPOINTMENTS = "DOCTOR_HAS_APPOINTMENTS"
SLOT_ALREADY_BOOKED = "SLOT_ALREADY_BOOKED"
CONCURRENT_UPDATE = "CONCURRENT_UPDATE"
DOCTOR_NOT_FOUND = "DOCTOR_NOT_FOUND"
CLIENT_NOT_FOUND = "CLIENT_NOT_FOUND"
PAST_DATE = "PAST_DATE"
PATIENT_HAS_APPOINTMENT = "PATIENT_HAS_APPOINTMENT"

# the message of each code
MESSAGES = {
    LOGIN_TAKEN: _("This login is already used by another account."),
    DOCTOR_ALREADY_EXISTS: _("A doctor with this first and last name already exists."),
    CLIENT_ALREADY_EXISTS: _("A patient with this first and last name already exists."),
    DOCTOR_HAS_APPOINTMENTS: _("This doctor has appointments: cancel them before deleting the doctor."),
    SLOT_ALREADY_BOOKED: _("This slot has just been booked by someone else."),
    CONCURRENT_UPDATE: _("This record was changed by another user in the meantime. "
                         "Go back to the list and reopen it before trying again."),
    DOCTOR_NOT_FOUND: _("This doctor does not exist (any more)."),
    CLIENT_NOT_FOUND: _("This patient does not exist (any more)."),
    PAST_DATE: _("Appointments cannot be booked for a past date."),
    PATIENT_HAS_APPOINTMENT: _("This patient already has an upcoming appointment: it must be cancelled "
                               "before booking another one."),
}


class BusinessError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, code: str):
        super().__init__(code)
        self.code = code

    # the message, in the language of the current request; @property: it is written
    # error.message, without parentheses
    @property
    def message(self) -> str:
        return str(MESSAGES[self.code])
  • lines 20–29: business error codes and constants (example 09). The web layer can check an error code to associate it with the correct field in a form (see below);
  • Lines 32–45: The message for each code, marked “to be translated.” [gettext_lazy], imported under the short name [_] (as used in Example 22), provides a lazy translation: an object that retrieves its translation only when the text is requested. A standard translation ([gettext]) would be performed when the module loads, at startup, once and for all, in the default language; the lazy translation is performed each time the content is displayed, in the language of the current request. Two strings written side by side are concatenated by [Python] (line 38);
  • lines 48–57: the business-layer exception (example 28), which carries its own code. The [message] property (example 14) renders the message in the language of the request; [str] forces lazy translation.

A [BusinessError] is not an error: it is a normal response (“this login is already in use”), displayed to the user. Any other exception is a true error, which results in a 500 error page.

# business/person_data.py: the data entered in a "doctor" or "client" form,
# as the web layer passes them to the business layer

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PersonData:
    title: str          # Mr, Mme, Melle
    last_name: str
    first_name: str
    # creation: optional (None), defaults to the last name in lower case
    # update: optional, the login is unchanged if it is missing
    login: str | None = None
    # creation: optional, defaults to the login
    # update: optional, the password is unchanged if it is missing
    password: str | None = None
    # update: the version of the record at the time the form was
    # displayed (optimistic lock)
    version: int | None = None

A person’s data, as transmitted by the web layer to the business layer (example 28). The last three attributes have a default value, [None]: they are optional. A comment following an attribute (line 9) is allowed: the comment extends from [#] to the end of the line.

docs.title: 11.11.4. business/business.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# business/business.py: the CONTRACT of the business layer: reads, schedule,
# appointments, management of doctors and clients.
#
# An abstract class (ABC, see example 06) describes the methods a class must
# have, without saying how they are written. BusinessService (the business layer) and
# ApplicationModel (the cache of the web layer) both inherit from it; Python
# refuses to create an object of a class that lacks an abstract method.
#
# X | None: a result that may be missing (a doctor who does not exist...).
# =========================================================================

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from datetime import date

from domain.schedule import DoctorDaySchedule
from models.models import Appointment, Client, Doctor, Slot

from .person_data import PersonData


class Business(ABC):
    # ------------------------------------------------ reads
    @abstractmethod
    def get_all_clients(self) -> list[Client]: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def get_all_doctors(self) -> list[Doctor]: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def get_all_slots(self, doctor_id: int) -> list[Slot]: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def get_doctor_day_appointments(self, doctor_id: int, day: date) -> list[Appointment]: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def get_client_by_id(self, id: int) -> Client | None: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def get_doctor_by_id(self, id: int) -> Doctor | None: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def get_appointment_by_id(self, id: int) -> Appointment | None: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def get_slot_by_id(self, id: int) -> Slot | None: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def get_doctor_day_schedule(self, doctor_id: int, day: date) -> DoctorDaySchedule | None: ...

    # the client (patient) whose user account is [user_id]
    @abstractmethod
    def get_client_by_user_id(self, user_id: int) -> Client | None: ...

    # the appointments of a client, today or in the future, with slot and doctor
    @abstractmethod
    def get_client_upcoming_appointments(self, client_id: int) -> list[Appointment]: ...

    # ------------------------------------------------ appointments (ADMIN, DOCTOR, USER)
    # raises a BusinessError if:
    #  - the day is past (PAST_DATE);
    #  - the patient already has an upcoming appointment (PATIENT_HAS_APPOINTMENT);
    #  - the slot is already taken that day (SLOT_ALREADY_BOOKED).
    @abstractmethod
    def add_appointment(self, day: date, slot: Slot, client: Client) -> Appointment: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def delete_appointment(self, appointment: Appointment) -> None: ...

    # ------------------------------------------------ doctors (ADMIN)
    # creates the doctor AND their user account (role DOCTOR)
    @abstractmethod
    def add_doctor(self, data: PersonData) -> Doctor: ...

    # updates the doctor AND their user account
    @abstractmethod
    def edit_doctor(self, id: int, data: PersonData) -> Doctor: ...

    # deletes the doctor, their slots AND their account - refused if they have appointments
    @abstractmethod
    def delete_doctor(self, id: int) -> None: ...

    # ------------------------------------------------ clients
    # (the ADMIN; add_client is also used for the registration of a patient,
    # edit_client and delete_client by the patient for their own account)
    # creates the client AND their user account (role USER)
    @abstractmethod
    def add_client(self, data: PersonData) -> Client: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def edit_client(self, id: int, data: PersonData) -> Client: ...

    # deletes the client, their account AND all their appointments (past and future)
    @abstractmethod
    def delete_client(self, id: int) -> None: ...

The business layer contract, an abstract class (example 06): all methods, along with their parameters and types, and, in comments, the rules they enforce. The body of an abstract method can be written on the same line as its signature ([: ...]). Two classes inherit from this contract: [BusinessService], the business layer itself, and [ApplicationModel], the web layer facade (discussed later), which can thus replace the business layer wherever a [Business] object is expected.

docs.title: 11.11.5. business/descriptor.py
docs.text:
# business/descriptor.py: everything that distinguishes a doctor from a client for the
# business rules (see business/service.py). Doctors and clients follow the
# same rules: the common code is written ONCE, and parameterized by a descriptor.

from collections.abc import Callable
from dataclasses import dataclass

from dao.persons import PersonDao


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Descriptor:
    dao: PersonDao
    role: str                   # DOCTOR or USER
    not_found_code: str         # error if the person does not exist
    already_exists_code: str    # error if the same first and last names already exist
    # optional (None): if present, the deletion is REFUSED as long as the
    # person has appointments (count_appointments(id) > 0), with the error has_appointments_code.
    # Callable[[int], int]: a function that receives an integer and returns an integer
    count_appointments: Callable[[int], int] | None
    has_appointments_code: str | None
    # optional: what must be deleted BEFORE the person (the rows that
    # reference them through a foreign key); receives their id
    before_delete: Callable[[int], None] | None

Doctors and clients follow the same management rules, with a few minor differences: their account roles, their error codes, and what prevents or facilitates their deletion. A descriptor consolidates these details; the common code, in [BusinessService], is defined once and receives the descriptor. The last three attributes are functions: [Callable[[int], int]] declares a function that takes an integer and returns an integer (the module [collections.abc] provides these abstract types); [| None]: or nothing.

docs.title: 11.11.6. business/provider.py
docs.text:
# business/provider.py: the provider of the business layer (see example 06):
# ONE BusinessService object, created on the first request, then shared by all the
# requests as long as the server runs. It has no state specific to a request:
# sharing it is safe, even between several threads

from functools import cache

from .service import BusinessService


@cache
def business() -> BusinessService:
    return BusinessService()

The business layer provider (example 06): a single [BusinessService] object, created on the first request, then shared by all requests. This is safe, even with multiple execution threads (example 20): the object has no request-specific state (its DAO objects do not have any either), and each thread has its own connection to the database (the ORM of [Django] opens one connection per execution thread).

docs.title: 11.11.7. business/service.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# business/service.py: the implementation of the business layer.
#
# The management of doctors and clients obeys three business rules:
#
#   1. a person (doctor or client) and their user account ALWAYS go
#      together: they are created, updated and deleted together, in the same
#      TRANSACTION - either everything succeeds, or nothing is written;
#   2. the login is unique in the whole application, and two doctors (or two
#      clients) cannot have the same first and last names;
#   3. deletion:
#      - a DOCTOR who has appointments cannot be deleted (their patients
#        would lose their appointment without being warned): they must first be
#        cancelled. Their time slots disappear with them;
#      - a CLIENT, on the other hand, disappears with ALL their appointments (past and future) -
#        whether the deletion comes from the ADMIN or from the patient themselves.
#
# And two rules for booking appointments, whatever the role of the one who
# books (ADMIN, DOCTOR or the patient themselves):
#   4. no appointment in the past;
#   5. a patient has only ONE upcoming appointment at a time.
#
# Doctors and clients follow exactly the same rules: the common code is
# written ONCE (methods _xxx_person), and parameterized by a descriptor that says
# which type of person we are dealing with.
#
# The TRANSACTIONS are opened by the _transaction method (at the end of the file),
# which also translates into BusinessError the errors reported by the database.
# =========================================================================

import re
from collections.abc import Callable
from datetime import date

from django.db import IntegrityError, transaction

from dao.slots import SlotDao
from dao.persons import ClientDao, DoctorDao
from dao.appointments import AppointmentDao
from dao.users import UserDao
from domain.schedule import DoctorDaySchedule, DoctorDaySlot
from models.models import Appointment, Client, Doctor, Person, Role, Slot
from security import passwords

from . import errors
from .dates import today
from .descriptor import Descriptor
from .person_data import PersonData
from .errors import BusinessError
from .business import Business

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Database errors -> BusinessError
#
# When a UNIQUE constraint refuses a write, Django raises an IntegrityError,
# whose message is that of MySQL. It quotes the NAME of the constraint:
#   (1062, "Duplicate entry 'Marie-PELISSIER' for key 'doctors.unq_doctors_first_name_last_name'")
# (MySQL 8 prefixes the name with that of the table, MariaDB does not). That is why
# the SQL script NAMES all its constraints. The regular expression CONSTRAINT
# extracts this name: (?:[^'.]*\.)? skips the optional prefix, ([^']+) captures the name
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CONSTRAINT_ERRORS = {
    "unq_users_login": errors.LOGIN_TAKEN,
    "unq_doctors_first_name_last_name": errors.DOCTOR_ALREADY_EXISTS,
    "unq_clients_first_name_last_name": errors.CLIENT_ALREADY_EXISTS,
    "unq1_appointments": errors.SLOT_ALREADY_BOOKED,
}

CONSTRAINT = re.compile(r"for key '(?:[^'.]*\.)?([^']+)'")


# a BusinessError CONCURRENT_UPDATE, raised INSIDE a transaction so that it
# is rolled back: an UPDATE modified no row (optimistic lock)
class _StaleVersion(Exception):
    pass


class BusinessService(Business):
    # the DAOs, created once and for all; they have no state: a single object of
    # each serves all the requests
    def __init__(self):
        self.doctors = DoctorDao()
        self.clients = ClientDao()
        self.slots = SlotDao()
        self.appointments = AppointmentDao()
        self.users = UserDao()

        self.doctor = Descriptor(
            dao=self.doctors,
            role=Role.DOCTOR,
            not_found_code=errors.DOCTOR_NOT_FOUND,
            already_exists_code=errors.DOCTOR_ALREADY_EXISTS,
            # self.appointments.count_by_doctor: the method itself, without calling it (a
            # "bound method" of the object self.appointments, which will be called later)
            count_appointments=self.appointments.count_by_doctor,
            has_appointments_code=errors.DOCTOR_HAS_APPOINTMENTS,
            # a doctor without appointments may still have time slots:
            # they make no sense without them, they are deleted with them (otherwise the
            # foreign key slots.doctor_id would forbid the deletion)
            before_delete=self.slots.delete_by_doctor)

        self.client = Descriptor(
            dao=self.clients,
            role=Role.USER,
            not_found_code=errors.CLIENT_NOT_FOUND,
            already_exists_code=errors.CLIENT_ALREADY_EXISTS,
            # no count_appointments: the deletion of a client is never refused;
            # their appointments (past and future) are deleted with them (otherwise
            # the foreign key appointments.client_id would forbid the deletion)
            count_appointments=None,
            has_appointments_code=None,
            before_delete=self.appointments.delete_by_client)

    # =======================================================================
    # reads
    # =======================================================================

    def get_all_clients(self) -> list[Client]:
        return self.clients.list()

    def get_all_doctors(self) -> list[Doctor]:
        return self.doctors.list()

    def get_all_slots(self, doctor_id: int) -> list[Slot]:
        return self.slots.list_by_doctor(doctor_id)

    def get_doctor_day_appointments(self, doctor_id: int, day: date) -> list[Appointment]:
        return self.appointments.doctor_day_appointments(doctor_id, day)

    def get_client_by_id(self, id: int) -> Client | None:
        return self.clients.read(id)

    def get_doctor_by_id(self, id: int) -> Doctor | None:
        return self.doctors.read(id)

    def get_appointment_by_id(self, id: int) -> Appointment | None:
        return self.appointments.read(id)

    def get_slot_by_id(self, id: int) -> Slot | None:
        return self.slots.read(id)

    def get_client_by_user_id(self, user_id: int) -> Client | None:
        return self.clients.read_by_user(user_id)

    def get_client_upcoming_appointments(self, client_id: int) -> list[Appointment]:
        return self.appointments.client_upcoming_appointments(client_id, today())

    # the schedule of a doctor on a given day: their slots, and for each one the
    # appointment booked that day (None if it is free)
    def get_doctor_day_schedule(self, doctor_id: int, day: date) -> DoctorDaySchedule | None:
        doctor = self.get_doctor_by_id(doctor_id)
        if doctor is None:
            return None
        # a dictionary COMPREHENSION: slot no. -> appointment booked on this slot
        bookings = {a.slot_id: a for a in self.get_doctor_day_appointments(doctor_id, day)}
        # get(key): the value, or None if the key is missing
        doctor_day_slots = [DoctorDaySlot(slot, bookings.get(slot.id))
                            for slot in self.get_all_slots(doctor_id)]
        return DoctorDaySchedule(doctor, day, doctor_day_slots)

    # =======================================================================
    # appointments
    # =======================================================================

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # booking an appointment, in a transaction:
    #   1. no appointment in the past;
    #   2. the patient's row is LOCKED (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE): if the same
    #      patient books two slots at the same moment (two tabs, double
    #      click...), the second transaction waits for the end of the first - and then sees
    #      the appointment it has just created;
    #   3. a single upcoming appointment per patient;
    #   4. finally the insertion. If the slot has just been taken by ANOTHER patient,
    #      it is the SQL constraint unq1_appointments (day, slot_id) that refuses
    #      the insertion - translated into BusinessError by _transaction.
    # A function defined INSIDE a method (work) sees the variables of
    # that method (day, slot, client): it is a "closure"
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def add_appointment(self, day: date, slot: Slot, client: Client) -> Appointment:
        def work():
            if day < today():
                raise BusinessError(errors.PAST_DATE)
            patient_id = self.clients.lock(client.id)
            if patient_id is None:
                raise BusinessError(errors.CLIENT_NOT_FOUND)
            if self.appointments.count_client_upcoming(patient_id, today()) > 0:
                raise BusinessError(errors.PATIENT_HAS_APPOINTMENT)
            return self.appointments.add(day, slot, client)
        return self._transaction(work)

    def delete_appointment(self, appointment: Appointment) -> None:
        # lambda: an anonymous function reduced to an expression
        self._transaction(lambda: self.appointments.delete(appointment.id))

    # =======================================================================
    # doctors and clients - the public methods delegate to the common
    # methods, with the right descriptor
    # =======================================================================

    def add_doctor(self, data: PersonData) -> Doctor:
        return self._add_person(self.doctor, data)

    def edit_doctor(self, id: int, data: PersonData) -> Doctor:
        return self._edit_person(self.doctor, id, data)

    def delete_doctor(self, id: int) -> None:
        self._delete_person(self.doctor, id)

    def add_client(self, data: PersonData) -> Client:
        return self._add_person(self.client, data)

    def edit_client(self, id: int, data: PersonData) -> Client:
        return self._edit_person(self.client, id, data)

    # the client, their account AND all their appointments (ADMIN, or the patient themselves
    # from "Manage my account": same method, same rule)
    def delete_client(self, id: int) -> None:
        self._delete_person(self.client, id)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # creation: the user account, THEN the person (who references it through their
    # foreign key [user]), in ONE transaction
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _add_person(self, d: Descriptor, data: PersonData) -> Person:
        last_name = data.last_name.strip().upper()
        first_name = data.first_name.strip()
        # the rules of the dbrdvmedecins2 database: login = last name in lower case,
        # password = login - unless the ADMIN (or the patient) entered other ones
        login = (data.login or last_name).lower()
        password = data.password or login

        def work():
            self._check_person_unique(d, first_name, last_name, None)
            self._check_login_free(login)
            account = self.users.add(login, passwords.hash_password(password), f"{first_name} {last_name}", d.role)
            return d.dao.add(data.title, last_name, first_name, account)
        return self._transaction(work)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # update: the person AND their account (the displayed name "first name LAST NAME" must
    # follow; the login and the password only change if they were entered).
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _edit_person(self, d: Descriptor, id: int, data: PersonData) -> Person:
        def work():
            person = d.dao.read(id)
