            if person is None:
                raise BusinessError(d.not_found_code)
            # optimistic lock: if the version in the database is no longer that of the
            # form, someone has modified this record in the meantime - we refuse
            # rather than silently overwrite their changes
            if data.version is not None and data.version != person.version:
                raise BusinessError(errors.CONCURRENT_UPDATE)
            last_name = data.last_name.strip().upper()
            first_name = data.first_name.strip()
            self._check_person_unique(d, first_name, last_name, id)
            # their account: the displayed name, and, if they were entered, the login and the
            # password
            account = person.account
            login = data.login.lower() if data.login else account.login
            if login != account.login:
                self._check_login_free(login)
            hash = passwords.hash_password(data.password) if data.password else None
            # the UPDATEs, with their optimistic lock: if the record (or the account) has
            # been modified AFTER the read above, no row is modified
            if not d.dao.update(id, person.version, data.title, last_name, first_name):
                raise _StaleVersion()
            if not self.users.update(account.id, account.version, login, f"{first_name} {last_name}", hash):
                raise _StaleVersion()
            # the person read again, with their account: the saved values
            return d.dao.read(id)
        return self._transaction(work)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # deletion, in ONE transaction, in the order imposed by the foreign
    # keys:
    #   1. possible refusal if appointments remain (doctor);
    #   2. what references the person (slots of a doctor, appointments of a
    #      client);
    #   3. the person (who references their account), then their account.
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _delete_person(self, d: Descriptor, id: int) -> None:
        def work():
            person = d.dao.read(id)
            if person is None:
                raise BusinessError(d.not_found_code)
            if d.count_appointments is not None and d.count_appointments(id) > 0:
                raise BusinessError(d.has_appointments_code)
            if d.before_delete is not None:
                d.before_delete(id)
            d.dao.delete(id)
            self.users.delete(person.account_id)
        self._transaction(work)

    # refuses first and last names already used by ANOTHER person of the same type
    # (current_id: the person being updated, who obviously has the right
    # to keep their own first and last names; None for a creation)
    def _check_person_unique(self, d: Descriptor, first_name: str, last_name: str,
                             current_id: int | None) -> None:
        namesake = d.dao.namesake(first_name, last_name)
        if namesake is not None and namesake.id != current_id:
            raise BusinessError(d.already_exists_code)

    def _check_login_free(self, login: str) -> None:
        if self.users.read_by_login(login) is not None:
            raise BusinessError(errors.LOGIN_TAKEN)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # runs [work] in a transaction (transaction.atomic, see example 28):
    # if the function ends normally, the transaction is committed (COMMIT);
    # if an exception comes out of it (BusinessError included), it is rolled back
    # (ROLLBACK): nothing is written.
    #
    # The "free login" and "unique first + last name" checks are made BEFORE
    # the write, to give a clear message. But two ADMINs could
    # save the same login (or the same doctor) at the same moment: in this
    # rare case, it is an SQL uniqueness constraint that refuses the second write.
    # Likewise, two simultaneous updates of the same record are settled by the
    # optimistic lock. These errors are therefore intercepted AROUND the transaction,
    # to translate them into BusinessError. Any other error is a real anomaly:
    # it is left to propagate.
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _transaction(self, work: Callable):
        try:
            with transaction.atomic():
                return work()
        except IntegrityError as e:
            # str(e): the MySQL message
            found = CONSTRAINT.search(str(e))
            if found and found.group(1) in CONSTRAINT_ERRORS:
                # from e: the new exception keeps track of the one that caused it
                raise BusinessError(CONSTRAINT_ERRORS[found.group(1)]) from e
            raise
        except _StaleVersion as e:
            raise BusinessError(errors.CONCURRENT_UPDATE) from e

docs.title: 11.11.7.1. Dependencies and Descriptors
docs.text:
• lines 62–69: translation of database errors into business errors (see “Transactions,” below);
  • lines 74–75: an internal exception, which signals a [UPDATE] with no effect (the optimistic lock);
  • lines 81–86: the DAO objects, created once and for all by the constructor;
  • lines 88–112: the two descriptors. The functions are methods of the DAO, passed without parentheses (line 95): these are bound methods—functions that retain a reference to their object—and will be called later ([d.count_appointments(id)], line 286). A doctor who has appointments cannot be deleted; their time slots are deleted along with them. A client is deleted along with their appointments. The parameters are named: you can immediately see what each value is for.

docs.title: 11.11.7.2. Read operations and the calendar
docs.text:
• lines 118–146: the readings, delegated to the DAO layer. The current date is calculated here (line 146), not by DAO: this is a business rule (“upcoming”);
  • lines 150–159: a doctor’s schedule for a given day. A read-only dictionary (example 18) associates each time slot number with the appointment booked for that slot on that day ([a.slot_id]: the foreign key, without a query; see the templates); then, for each of the doctor’s time slots, the corresponding appointment, or [None]. Only two queries, regardless of the number of time slots: the day’s appointments and the time slots (plus the doctor’s notes), as shown in the console (“Development Mode”).

docs.title: 11.11.7.3. Appointment Scheduling
docs.text:
• Lines 179–189: Scheduling an appointment in a transaction. The function [work], defined in the method, receives its parameters ([day], [slot], [client]): this is a closure (example 08). It is passed to [_transaction], which executes it within a transaction;
  • lines 181–182: no appointments in the past;
  • lines 183–185: the “pessimistic” lock on the patient’s record ([SELECT ... FOR UPDATE]; see layer DAO). Here’s why. The “only one upcoming appointment” rule is verified by a count (line 186), then the appointment is inserted (line 188). If the same patient books two time slots at the same time (two tabs, a double-click), two transactions could both count zero appointments and then both insert the appointment: no database constraint would prevent this, since the two time slots are different. The lock on the patient’s row causes the second transaction to wait until the first one is complete: it then counts one appointment and fails. The database cannot enforce this rule on its own: it is the business layer that enforces it, with the database’s assistance;
  • lines 186–187: only one upcoming appointment per patient;
  • line 188: the insertion. If the time slot has just been taken by another patient, it is the database constraint [unq1_appointments] that rejects the insertion, and [_transaction] translates the error (further on);
  • lines 191–193: canceling an appointment. [lambda: ...] is an anonymous function, reduced to a single expression (in this case, a call): the equivalent of a three-line function [def].

docs.title: 11.11.7.4. Managing Doctors and Patients
docs.text:
• lines 200–218: public methods delegate to common methods, using the correct descriptor;
  • lines 224–237: creating a person. The name is capitalized ([PELISSIER], the database convention), and spaces surrounding the input are removed. The rules of the [dbrdvmedecins2] database: By default, the login is the name in lowercase, and the password is, by default, the login ([a or b]: [a] if it is “true” (a non-empty string), [b] otherwise). In the transaction: the validations (homonym check, free username), then the account (with the password hash; see [security/passwords.py]), then the person, who references the account by its foreign key: the order is fixed;
  • lines 243–271: modifying a person and their account. The form version is compared to the version read (line 251): this is the first level of the optimistic lock, which returns a clear message. The second level is that of the [UPDATE] (lines 265–268): if the record has been modified between the read operation (line 245) and the write operation, [UPDATE] does not modify anything, and the exception [_StaleVersion] rolls back the entire transaction (so the account is not modified either). The login and password change only if they have been entered; the displayed account name follows the person;
  • lines 281–292: deletion, in the order dictated by the foreign keys: the reference to the person (their time slots or appointments), the person, then their account. [person.account_id] is the foreign key, read without a query;
  • lines 297–305: the two uniqueness checks, performed before the write operation, to ensure a clear message. A person being edited has the right to retain their own first and last names: [current_id] excludes this.

docs.title: 11.11.7.5. Database Transactions and Errors
docs.text:
• lines 322–334: every write operation is executed within a transaction ([transaction.atomic], example 28): if [work] completes normally, the transaction is committed ([COMMIT]); if an exception occurs (including a [BusinessError]), it is rolled back ([ROLLBACK]): nothing is written. The business layer thus determines the scope of transactions: one business operation, one transaction;
  • Lines 326–332: The checks performed before writing are not always sufficient: two administrators could save the same login at the same time. In this case, a database uniqueness constraint rejects the second write, and ORM triggers a [IntegrityError], whose message is that of [MySQL]: [(1062, "Duplicate entry 'Marie-PELISSIER' for key 'doctors.unq_doctors_first_name_last_name'")]. The regular expression [CONSTRAINT] (line 69) extracts the name of the constraint ([search] searches for the expression in the string; [group(1)] returns what the first group captured in parentheses; [(?:...)] is a non-capturing group, and [?] makes it optional: [MySQL] 8 prefixes the name with the table name, [MariaDB] does not). This is why the script SQL names all its constraints. A known constraint becomes the corresponding [BusinessError]; another, [IntegrityError], is re-raised as-is ([raise] with no parameters): this is a genuine anomaly. [raise ... from e] attaches the original exception to the new one (example 28);
  • Lines 333–334: A failed optimistic lock results in the error [CONCURRENT_UPDATE]. The exception [_StaleVersion] is thrown within the block [atomic] to roll back the transaction, then propagated outside the block.

Exceptions are caught outside the [with transaction.atomic()] block, not inside it: after a database error, the transaction is no longer valid and must first be rolled back, which is what exiting the block does (Example 28).

docs.title: 11.12. Authentication and Security
docs.text: The [security] file covers everything related to authentication (who is the user?), permissions (does the user have access to this page?), and protection against bots. This is the complete version of Examples 25 through 27.

docs.title: 11.12.1. security/passwords.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# security/passwords.py: the hashing of the passwords, with the bcrypt algorithm
# (bcrypt library), 10 rounds, like the hashes of the SQL script.
#
# A HASH is one-way: the password cannot be recovered from
# it. To check an entered password, it is hashed with the "salt" (a
# random value) contained in the stored hash, and the two
# results are compared: that is what bcrypt.checkpw does.
#
# The hashes of the SQL script start with $2b$; those of the other versions of
# the application, which share the same database, with $2y$ (PHP) or $2a$ (Java):
# bcrypt checks the three forms.
#
# bcrypt only takes into account the first 72 BYTES of the password (and the
# library refuses to hash more): the forms therefore limit the
# length of the passwords (see web/forms.py).
# =========================================================================

import bcrypt

# the number of rounds: the hash costs 2^10 elementary computations
ROUNDS = 10
MAX_BYTES = 72


def hash_password(password: str) -> str:
    # encode: the string into bytes (UTF-8); decode: the bytes into a string
    return bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt(ROUNDS)).decode()


def check_password(password: str, hash: str) -> bool:
    data = password.encode()
    if len(data) > MAX_BYTES:
        return False
    return bcrypt.checkpw(data, hash.encode())

Passwords in the database are hashed by [bcrypt] (the SQL script mentioned above), not by PBKDF2, the default algorithm of [Django] (Example 25). The [bcrypt] library verifies them directly:

  • lines 26–28: the hash of a password. [gensalt(10)] generates a random salt with a cost of 10; [hashpw] calculates the hash, which contains the algorithm, the cost, and the salt (Example 25). The library operates on bytes: [encode()] converts the string to bytes ([UTF-8]), and [decode()] performs the reverse operation;
  • lines 31–35: verification. [checkpw] retrieves the cost and salt from the stored hash, hashes the entered password using them, and compares the results (in constant time, Example 23). [bcrypt] considers only the first 72 bytes of a password, and the library, since version 5, refuses to hash any more than that (it throws an exception): a longer password is therefore rejected outright. Forms also limit password length (web layer, discussed later).

[Django] could have verified these hashes itself, using its [BCryptPasswordHasher] algorithm (setting [PASSWORD_HASHERS]): but it expects hashes prefixed with [bcrypt$], and the database is shared with other versions of the application, which do not recognize this prefix.

docs.title: 11.12.2. security/connected_user.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# security/connected_user.py: the logged-in user, as described by their JWT token
# (see example 25).
#
# The claims of our tokens (see security/auth.py):
#   sub   : the id of the user account (JWT convention: "subject"), as text
#   login : the login
#   name  : the displayed name ("Marie PELISSIER"), for the navigation bar
#   role  : ADMIN, DOCTOR or USER
#   iat, exp : creation and expiration dates of the token
#
# This object does NOT come from the database: it is rebuilt, on each request, from
# the token, whose signature guarantees the content.
# =========================================================================

from dataclasses import dataclass

from models.models import Role


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ConnectedUser:
    user_id: int
    login: str
    name: str
    role: str

    # the user described by the claims of an already checked token; None if a claim
    # is missing or does not have the expected form. @staticmethod: a function stored in
    # the class, which receives neither object nor class
    @staticmethod
    def from_claims(claims: dict) -> "ConnectedUser | None":
        role = claims.get("role")
        sub = str(claims.get("sub", ""))
        # Role.values: the values of the enumeration; isdigit: only digits
        if role not in Role.values or not sub.isdigit() or "login" not in claims or "name" not in claims:
            return None
        return ConnectedUser(int(sub), str(claims["login"]), str(claims["name"]), role)

    @property
    def is_admin(self) -> bool:
        return self.role == Role.ADMIN

    @property
    def is_doctor(self) -> bool:
        return self.role == Role.DOCTOR

    @property
    def is_patient(self) -> bool:
        return self.role == Role.USER

The logged-in user, as described by their token (example 25). This object does not come from the database: it is reconstructed with each request from the token, whose signature guarantees its content.

  • Lines 31–38: a static method ([@staticmethod]): a method defined within the class that takes neither an object nor a class as an argument, and is called [ConnectedUser.from_claims(claims)]. It constructs the user object based on the claims in a token that has already been verified. Even if signed by us, a token is carefully verified: an unknown role, an identifier that is not a number, or a missing claim will result in the user being denied access ([None]). [Role.values] is the list of enumeration values; [isdigit] verifies that a string consists only of digits. The annotation for the returned type is enclosed in quotation marks: the class is not yet fully defined at this point;
  • lines 40–50: three properties for templates (example 26).

docs.title: 11.12.3. security/auth.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# security/auth.py: the authentication logic:
#   - validate()         : checks a login / password pair;
#   - set_token()        : builds the JWT token of a validated user, and
#                          puts it in a cookie of the response;
#   - user()             : the user described by a token.
#
# Where does the JWT token travel? In a COOKIE (see example 25): a browser that
# displays ordinary HTML pages thus presents it by itself, on each request.
# The options of this cookie matter for security:
#   - HttpOnly: the JavaScript of the page cannot read the cookie (an injected
#     script could therefore not steal the token);
#   - SameSite=Lax: the browser does NOT send the cookie with a POST coming from another
#     site (first protection against the so-called CSRF attack; the second is
#     the anti-CSRF token of the forms);
#   - Secure: in production (HTTPS), the cookie never travels unencrypted;
#   - lifetime: the cookie disappears at the same time as the token expires.
# =========================================================================

import time

import jwt
from django.conf import settings
from django.core.exceptions import ImproperlyConfigured

from dao.users import UserDao
from models.models import User

from . import passwords
from .connected_user import ConnectedUser

# the name of the cookie that carries the token
COOKIE = "rdvmedecins_jwt"

# HMAC-SHA256 requires a key of at least 256 bits: we say it clearly, as soon as the
# module is loaded, rather than letting the library fail further on
if len(settings.JWT_SECRET) < 32:
    raise ImproperlyConfigured("JWT_SECRET must be at least 32 characters long (see .env).")

_users = UserDao()


# None if the login does not exist or if the password is wrong
def validate(login: str, password: str) -> User | None:
    user = _users.read_by_login(login)
    if user is None or not passwords.check_password(password, user.password):
        return None
    return user


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# the JWT token of [user], put in the cookie that carries it. The token is
# SIGNED (HMAC-SHA256) with the secret key: the browser can read it (it is not
# encrypted), but not modify it - any modification would make the signature
# invalid.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
def set_token(response, user: User):
    now = int(time.time())
    duration = settings.JWT_DURATION_MINUTES * 60
    claims = {
        "sub": str(user.id),
        "login": user.login,
        "name": user.name,
        "role": user.role,
        "iat": now,
        "exp": now + duration,
    }
    token = jwt.encode(claims, settings.JWT_SECRET, algorithm="HS256")
    response.set_cookie(COOKIE, token, max_age=duration, secure=settings.COOKIE_SECURE,
                        httponly=True, samesite="Lax")
    return response


# clears the token cookie: the response carries a cookie of the same name, empty, already expired
def clear_token(response):
    response.delete_cookie(COOKIE, samesite="Lax")
    return response


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# the user described by a token; None if the token is expired, forged or
# malformed. jwt.decode checks the signature AND the expiration date (claim exp).
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
def user(token: str) -> ConnectedUser | None:
    try:
        claims = jwt.decode(token, settings.JWT_SECRET, algorithms=["HS256"])
    except jwt.InvalidTokenError:
        return None
    return ConnectedUser.from_claims(claims)

The authentication service from Example 25, with a few differences:

  • Lines 37–38: The token key is verified when the module loads, that is, when the application starts: If the key is too short, the process stops entirely, with a clear error message ([ImproperlyConfigured] is the exception to [Django] for an incorrect configuration), rather than a simple warning like [PyJWT] (Example 25);
  • lines 44–48: verification of a username and password by the DAO layer (the account, retrieved from the database) and by the password module. The web layer calls this module directly: authentication is a security matter, not a business rule;
  • lines 57–71: generating the token and storing it in a cookie in the response (Example 25). The account ID ([sub]) is written in plain text: the JWT standard requires this. The cookie is [Secure] in production ([COOKIE_SECURE], see [config/settings.py]);
  • lines 75–77: Deletion of the cookie: a cookie with the same name, empty, and already expired (Example 25);
  • lines 84–89: the user is identified by a token, or [None] (example 25).

docs.title: 11.12.4. security/access.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# security/access.py: THE ACCESS RULE of each URL.
#
# The rules are examined in order; the first one whose pattern (a
# regular expression) matches the path of the URL applies:
#   - a few PUBLIC URLs: the home page, login, the choice of language, the
#     creation of an account;
#   - URLs reserved to certain roles (a set of roles: ONE of them is enough);
#   - all the OTHERS require an authenticated user (last rule).
# It is the rule "everything is forbidden except what is allowed": a URL added
# later, which we forgot to protect, is protected automatically.
#
# The AccessControl middleware (see security/middleware.py) applies these rules: a
# refused anonymous visitor is sent to the login page; an
# authenticated user without the required role gets a 403 error page.
# =========================================================================

import re

from models.models import Role

# two special values instead of a set of roles
PUBLIC = "PUBLIC"
AUTHENTICATED = "AUTHENTICATED"

# re.compile: the regular expression, parsed once and for all
RULES = [
    (re.compile(r"^/$"), PUBLIC),
    (re.compile(r"^/(login|logout)$"), PUBLIC),
    (re.compile(r"^/language/"), PUBLIC),
    (re.compile(r"^/register"), PUBLIC),
    # a patient cancels THEIR appointment from "My area", not from the schedule
    (re.compile(r"^/schedule/cancel$"), {Role.ADMIN, Role.DOCTOR}),
    (re.compile(r"^/(doctors|clients)"), {Role.ADMIN}),
    (re.compile(r"^/my-"), {Role.USER}),
    (re.compile(r"^/"), AUTHENTICATED),
]


# the rule of the path [path]: PUBLIC, AUTHENTICATED, or a set of roles
def rule(path: str):
    for pattern, requirement in RULES:
        if pattern.match(path):
            return requirement
    return AUTHENTICATED

The application’s access rules, grouped into a single list. Example 26 protected each view with a decorator; here, protection is centralized, as was done by the [access_control] rules of [Symfony]:

  • lines 27–37: Each rule associates a pattern (a regular expression, compiled once and for all by [re.compile]) with a requirement: [PUBLIC], [AUTHENTICATED], or a set of roles, any one of which is sufficient. [^] marks the start of the path, [$] marks its end; [(login|logout)]: either one. The public URL pages are the home page, login, language selection, and account creation. Next are the URL pages reserved for certain roles: cancellation from the calendar (a patient cancels from “My area”), management of doctors and clients, and the patient’s account. The last rule, [^/], applies to all remaining URL rules and requires an authenticated user;
  • lines 41–45: the path rule: the first one that matches ([match]: the recognized expression at the beginning of the string).

This is the “everything is prohibited except what is permitted” rule: a URL added later—which might have been forgotten to be protected—is automatically protected. The opposite error (a public URL that was forgotten to be made public) is immediately obvious; the error of a forgotten protected page is much less so.

docs.title: 11.12.5. security/middleware.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# security/middleware.py: the two security middlewares (see examples 24 to 26).
#
#   1. Authentication, BEFORE routing: who is the user? From the
#      JWT token of their cookie. It refuses nothing itself: a missing or
#      invalid token leaves the visitor ANONYMOUS (request.user is None); the
#      cookie of an invalid token is cleared from the response;
#   2. AccessControl, AFTER routing (process_view): is the user allowed
#      to access this URL? The rules are in security/access.py. A URL
#      that has no route does not get this far: it gets a 404 page.
# =========================================================================

from django.contrib import messages
from django.core.exceptions import PermissionDenied
from django.shortcuts import redirect
from django.utils.translation import gettext as _

from . import access, auth


class Authentication:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        token = request.COOKIES.get(auth.COOKIE, "")
        request.user = auth.user(token) if token else None
        response = self.get_response(request)
        # an invalid token (expired, forged): the cookie is cleared, on the response
        # whatever it is - unless the request has just set a new one (a
        # successful login)
        if token and request.user is None and auth.COOKIE not in response.cookies:
            auth.clear_token(response)
        return response


class AccessControl:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        return self.get_response(request)

    def process_view(self, request, view_func, view_args, view_kwargs):
        # path_info: the path of the URL, without its parameters
        requirement = access.rule(request.path_info)
        if requirement == access.PUBLIC:
            return None
        user = request.user
        if user is None:
            # an anonymous visitor: off to the login page. If they had a
            # token cookie, it means their token is no longer valid (expired,
            # forged): their session has expired, we tell them so
            if auth.COOKIE in request.COOKIES:
                messages.error(request, _("Your session has expired: please log in again."))
            return redirect("login")
        if requirement != access.AUTHENTICATED and user.role not in requirement:
            # authenticated, but without the required role: 403 error (handler403 view, see config/urls.py)
            raise PermissionDenied("insufficient role")
        return None

The two security middleware components:

  • lines 21–34: authentication (example 25), before routing. It does not reject anything: a missing or invalid token leaves the visitor anonymous. It deletes the cookie associated with an invalid token in the response, regardless of what that response is, unless the response sets a new one (a successful login): [response.cookies] is the dictionary of cookies that the response sets;
  • Lines 37–60: access control, after routing (its method [process_view], Example 24). A URL that has no route therefore does not reach this point: it receives a 404 page directly, without the visitor being asked to log in. [request.path_info] is the path of URL, without its parameters. An anonymous visitor who is denied access is sent to the login page; if they had a token cookie, it means their token is no longer valid: a pop-up message informs them that their session has expired (see the screenshot titled “End of Session”). An authenticated user who does not have the required role triggers [PermissionDenied]: since the exception is thrown in [process_view]—not in the view—[Django] itself transforms it into a response via the application’s [handler403] view (Example 24), in both debug and production modes.

The message is translated by [gettext] (line 16), not by [gettext_lazy]: it is translated during the request, in its language; lazy translation is only useful for text defined when a module is loaded.

docs.title: 11.12.6. security/errors.py
docs.text:
# security/errors.py: the token is valid, but the account it designates no longer
# exists: it has been deleted since login (by the patient themselves in another
# tab, or by the ADMIN). This case is treated as an expired session: the
# ErrorPage middleware clears the cookie and redirects to the login page.


class InvalidSession(Exception):
    pass

A special case: the token is valid, but the account it refers to no longer exists (the patient deleted it in another tab, or the administrator deleted it). Views that require the account then throw this exception, which the [ErrorPage] middleware treats as an expired session (see below).

docs.title: 11.12.7. security/captchas.py and captcha_drawing.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# security/captchas.py: a CAPTCHA ("test to tell a human from a robot")
# made by the server itself, without any external service (see example 27).
#
# How it works:
#   1. generate() draws a random text, makes an image of it, and stores the right
#      answer IN THE CACHE of the server, under a random identifier;
#   2. the page displays the image and puts the identifier in a hidden field of the
#      form (the answer itself never leaves the server);
#   3. verify(id, input) compares the input with the expected answer, then FORGETS
#      this captcha: each image is used only once, a robot cannot replay
#      an answer already found.
#
# Why the cache, and not a simple variable of the module? Because a production
# server starts SEVERAL processes (see README.md), which do not share their
# memory: the request that checks the captcha is not necessarily processed by the
# process that made it. The cache of the application (files, see
# config/settings.py) is, for its part, shared by all.
# =========================================================================

import secrets
from dataclasses import dataclass

from django.core.cache import cache

from . import captcha_drawing

# validity duration of an image, in seconds: 10 minutes to fill in the form
LIFETIME = 600


# a captcha: its identifier, to put in the hidden field [captcha_id] of the
# form, and its image (SVG), to insert as is in the page
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Captcha:
    id: str
    svg: str


def generate() -> Captcha:
    text = captcha_drawing.random_text(5)        # 5 characters
    id = secrets.token_hex(12)                     # an identifier impossible to guess
    # the cache will forget the answer by itself after 10 minutes
    cache.set(f"captcha.{id}", text, LIFETIME)
    return Captcha(id, captcha_drawing.svg(text))


# true if [answer] is the right answer to the captcha [id] (regardless of
# case). The captcha is consumed in all cases.
def verify(id: str, answer: str) -> bool:
    # the identifier comes from the browser: 24 hexadecimal digits, or nothing
    if len(id) != 24 or any(c not in "0123456789abcdef" for c in id) or not answer:
        return False
    expected = cache.get(f"captcha.{id}")
    # delete returns True if the item existed: if two requests present the same
    # captcha at the same moment, only one really deletes it - the other fails
    if expected is None or not cache.delete(f"captcha.{id}"):
        return False
    return expected.casefold() == answer.strip().casefold()

The CAPTCHA service from Example 27, with two additional precautions:

  • lines 51–52: The identifier comes from the browser; we verify that it consists of 24 hexadecimal digits (those of [token_hex(12)]) before using it as the cache key. [any] returns [True] if any of the elements produced by the generating expression is true;
  • lines 53–56: [cache.delete] returns [True] if the element existed. If two requests present the same CAPTCHA at the same time, only one actually removes it; the other fails. An image is used only once.

The file's comment (lines 17–22) explains why the CAPTCHAs are stored in the cache (a set of files shared by all server processes) rather than in a module variable. The file [security/captcha_drawing.py] is the one from Example 27, with a longer header comment: each character is drawn with lines, never written as text, otherwise a bot would simply have to read the image’s source code.

docs.title: 11.12.8. security/limiter.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# security/limiter.py: second barrier against robots (the first is the
# captcha): attempts are COUNTED, and beyond a threshold they are BLOCKED for a
# while (see example 27).
#
#   - login: after LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES failures (wrong captcha or wrong
#     password) for the same login from the same IP address, this pair is blocked
#     until the end of a window of LOGIN_BLOCK_MINUTES minutes, counted from
#     the first failure. The same IP address is also blocked if it accumulates
#     LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES_IP failures, all logins together (a robot trying
#     thousands of different logins);
#   - account creation: at most REGISTRATION_MAX_PER_HOUR accounts created per hour
#     from the same IP address.
#
# Beware in a classroom: all the computers often go out to the Internet through the
# SAME IP address. That is why the login block applies first to the
# (IP, login) pair - a student who mistypes their password does not block their
# neighbours - and why the thresholds are configurable (.env file).
#
# Each counter is stored in the cache (see security/captchas.py), with the end
# of its window: {"count": 3, "end": 1790531419.2}.
# =========================================================================

import hashlib
import math
import time

from django.conf import settings
from django.core.cache import cache


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- login
# number of remaining minutes of block (0 = the attempt is allowed)
def login_block_minutes(ip: str, login: str) -> int:
    return max(_remaining_minutes(_login_key(ip, login), settings.LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES),
               _remaining_minutes(f"login_ip.{ip}", settings.LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES_IP))


# one more failure; the first one opens a window of LOGIN_BLOCK_MINUTES minutes,
# at the end of which the counter starts again from zero
def login_failure(ip: str, login: str) -> None:
    duration = settings.LOGIN_BLOCK_MINUTES * 60
    _count(_login_key(ip, login), duration)
    _count(f"login_ip.{ip}", duration)


# a successful login resets the counter of THIS login
def login_success(ip: str, login: str) -> None:
    cache.delete(_login_key(ip, login))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- registration
def registration_block_minutes(ip: str) -> int:
    return _remaining_minutes(f"registration.{ip}", settings.REGISTRATION_MAX_PER_HOUR)


def registration_success(ip: str) -> None:
    _count(f"registration.{ip}", 3600)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- common mechanics
# the key of the (IP, login) pair. The login comes from the browser: it may contain
# anything (spaces...). Its SHA-256 fingerprint, made of 64 hexadecimal
# digits, gives a cache key that is always valid
def _login_key(ip: str, login: str) -> str:
    fingerprint = hashlib.sha256(f"{ip}|{login.strip().lower()}".encode()).hexdigest()
    return f"login.{fingerprint}"


# the minutes left until the end of the window if the counter has reached the
# limit, 0 otherwise; the seconds are rounded UP to the minute (ceil):
# 30 s -> "1 minute"
def _remaining_minutes(key: str, limit: int) -> int:
    state = cache.get(key)
    if state is None or state["count"] < limit:
        return 0
    return max(1, math.ceil((state["end"] - time.time()) / 60))


# one more attempt in the current window (or in a new window of
# [duration] seconds). The cache forgets the counter at the end of the window (timeout).
# The read then the write are not ATOMIC: two simultaneous attempts
# could count as only one. For a failure counter, it does not matter
def _count(key: str, duration: int) -> None:
    state = cache.get(key) or {"count": 0, "end": time.time() + duration}
    state["count"] += 1
    cache.set(key, state, timeout=max(1, math.ceil(state["end"] - time.time())))

The attempt limit in Example 27, more refined:

  • lines 34–49: the login. Failed attempts are counted for each pair (address IP, username): five failed attempts (setting [LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES]) block that username from that address for fifteen minutes, starting from the first failed attempt. In a classroom, where all computers often access the Internet via the same address IP, a student who enters the wrong password does not block their neighbors. However, the same address is also blocked if it accumulates 25 failed attempts across all logins: this is the case for a bot that tries thousands of different logins. A successful login clears the failed attempts for that login;
  • lines 53–58: account creation: a maximum of ten accounts per hour per IP address;
  • lines 65–67: the pair’s key (IP, login). The login comes from the browser: it can contain anything. Its fingerprint SHA-256 ([hashlib.sha256], from the standard library), consisting of 64 hexadecimal digits, yields a cache key that is always valid and of fixed length;
  • lines 73–77: the remaining lockout minutes, rounded up to the next minute ([math.ceil]: 30 seconds equal “1 minute”);
  • lines 84–87: the counter, within a fixed window (Example 27). [cache.get(key) or {...}]: the current state, or a new state. The code comment acknowledges the weakness of Example 27 (two simultaneous failures may count as only one); for a failure counter, this is not a serious issue.

docs.title: 11.12.9. security/registration_pass.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# security/registration_pass.py: the "pass" of account creation.
#
# To open the "Create a patient account" page, the captcha of the authentication page
# must first have been typed (see web/views/registration.py, POST
# /register/access). The server then issues a pass:
#   - a random identifier, stored in an HttpOnly cookie;
#   - valid for 15 minutes (the time to fill in the form, even after several
#     attempts following input errors);
#   - consumed as soon as an account is created: ONE solved captcha = ONE account at most.
#     A robot cannot create accounts in series.
#
# Without a valid pass, GET and POST /register redirect to the
# authentication page (see the @registration_pass_required decorator): typing
# the URL /register directly does not bypass the captcha.
#
# Like the captchas, the passes live in the cache.
# =========================================================================

import secrets
from functools import wraps

from django.conf import settings
from django.contrib import messages
from django.core.cache import cache
from django.shortcuts import redirect
from django.utils.translation import gettext as _

COOKIE = "rdvmedecins_registration"
# the cookie is sent by the browser only to the /register... addresses
PATH = "/register"
# lifetime of a pass, in minutes
LIFETIME = 15


# issues a new pass, in a cookie of the response
def issue(response):
    id = secrets.token_hex(12)
    cache.set(f"pass.{id}", True, LIFETIME * 60)
    response.set_cookie(COOKIE, id, max_age=LIFETIME * 60, path=PATH,
                        secure=settings.COOKIE_SECURE, httponly=True, samesite="Lax")
    return response


# true if [id] is an existing, unexpired pass
def is_valid(id: str | None) -> bool:
    return bool(id) and id.isalnum() and cache.get(f"pass.{id}") is not None


# the pass has been used: it is forgotten...
def consume(id: str | None) -> None:
    if id and id.isalnum():
        cache.delete(f"pass.{id}")


# ... and its cookie is cleared by a cookie of the same name and the same path, already expired
def clear_cookie(response):
    response.delete_cookie(COOKIE, path=PATH, samesite="Lax")
    return response


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# @registration_pass_required: a decorator (see example 26), put on the views that
# require a pass (GET and POST /register). Without a valid pass,
# the view is not called: back to the authentication page, with a message
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
def registration_pass_required(view):
    @wraps(view)
    def wrapper(request, *args, **kwargs):
        if not is_valid(request.COOKIES.get(COOKIE)):
            messages.error(request, _("To create an account, first type the characters shown in the image "
                                      "correctly, then click \"Create a patient account\"."))
            return redirect("login")
        return view(request, *args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper

The account creation token. To create an account, you must first enter the CAPTCHA from the login page (the “Create a patient account” button): the server then issues a token, a random identifier stored in the cache and in a cookie. Without a passcode, the account creation page redirects to the login page: typing URL or [/register] directly does not bypass the CAPTCHA; and a passcode is only used to create an account: a bot cannot create accounts in bulk.

  • lines 29–33: the cookie is sent by the browser only to addresses beginning with [/register] (cookie parameter [path]): it does not travel with other requests;
  • lines 37–42: the cookie is issued for fifteen minutes—enough time to fill out the form, even if you have to try several times after making input errors;
  • lines 46–59: verification, usage, and deletion of the cookie (which must have the same path as the cookie to be deleted). [isalnum] verifies that the identifier consists only of letters and numbers;
  • lines 67–75: the decorator [@registration_pass_required] (example 26), applied to the account creation view.

docs.title: 11.13. The Web Layer: Shared Services
docs.text: The [web] folder contains the [Django] application for the web layer (declared in [INSTALLED_APPS]; see [config/settings.py]; its file [web/apps.py] contains only its name). It brings together the routes, views, forms, and what all views have in common: that is the focus of this section.

docs.title: 11.13.1. web/application.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# web/application.py: the cache / facade of the business layer (the equivalent of the
# [ApplicationModel] class of the other versions of the application): the lists of
# doctors and clients are read from the database once, then served from the cache.
#
# Why the Django CACHE, and not simply an attribute of this object? A
# Python process does keep its objects from one request to the next (see example 20);
# but a production server starts SEVERAL processes, each of which would have ITS
# copy of the lists: the ADMIN who adds a doctor would only update that of the
# process that handled their request. The cache of the application (files, see
# config/settings.py) is, for its part, shared by all the processes.
#
# These lists can CHANGE (the ADMIN adds, updates, deletes doctors and
# clients): each write therefore goes through this facade, which FORGETS the list
# concerned right after; the next request that needs it reads it again from the database. That is
# the whole point of a SINGLE entry point to the business layer: the rule
# "write => cache update" is written only here.
# =========================================================================

from datetime import date
from functools import cache as once

from django.core.cache import cache

from domain.schedule import DoctorDaySchedule
from business.person_data import PersonData
from business.provider import business
from business.business import Business
from models.models import Appointment, Client, Doctor, Slot

DOCTORS = "rdvmedecins.doctors"
CLIENTS = "rdvmedecins.clients"


# same contract as the business layer
class ApplicationModel(Business):
    def __init__(self):
        self.business = business()

    # ------------------------------------------------ reads from the cache
    # get_or_set(key, function, timeout): the value of the cache if it exists; otherwise,
    # the function is called, and its result stored in the cache (timeout=None:
    # without time limit) before being returned. The objects are stored there serialized
    # (pickle module): each request that reads them gets copies of them
    def get_all_doctors(self) -> list[Doctor]:
        return cache.get_or_set(DOCTORS, self.business.get_all_doctors, timeout=None)

    def get_all_clients(self) -> list[Client]:
        return cache.get_or_set(CLIENTS, self.business.get_all_clients, timeout=None)

    # the doctor whose user account is [user_id] - used to preselect,
    # for a logged-in doctor, their own schedule
    def get_doctor_by_user_id(self, user_id: int) -> Doctor | None:
        return next((d for d in self.get_all_doctors() if d.account_id == user_id), None)

    # ------------------------------------------------ simple delegations
    def get_all_slots(self, doctor_id: int) -> list[Slot]:
        return self.business.get_all_slots(doctor_id)

    def get_doctor_day_appointments(self, doctor_id: int, day: date) -> list[Appointment]:
        return self.business.get_doctor_day_appointments(doctor_id, day)

    def get_client_by_id(self, id: int) -> Client | None:
        return self.business.get_client_by_id(id)

    def get_doctor_by_id(self, id: int) -> Doctor | None:
        return self.business.get_doctor_by_id(id)

    def get_appointment_by_id(self, id: int) -> Appointment | None:
        return self.business.get_appointment_by_id(id)

    def get_slot_by_id(self, id: int) -> Slot | None:
        return self.business.get_slot_by_id(id)

    def get_doctor_day_schedule(self, doctor_id: int, day: date) -> DoctorDaySchedule | None:
        return self.business.get_doctor_day_schedule(doctor_id, day)

    # no cache here: it is the most recent data that counts (a patient who
    # has just updated or deleted their account)
    def get_client_by_user_id(self, user_id: int) -> Client | None:
        return self.business.get_client_by_user_id(user_id)

    def get_client_upcoming_appointments(self, client_id: int) -> list[Appointment]:
        return self.business.get_client_upcoming_appointments(client_id)

    def add_appointment(self, day: date, slot: Slot, client: Client) -> Appointment:
        return self.business.add_appointment(day, slot, client)

    def delete_appointment(self, appointment: Appointment) -> None:
        self.business.delete_appointment(appointment)

    # ------------------------------------------------ writes => cache forgotten
    # (delete: the item is removed from the cache)
    def add_doctor(self, data: PersonData) -> Doctor:
        doctor = self.business.add_doctor(data)
        cache.delete(DOCTORS)
        return doctor

    def edit_doctor(self, id: int, data: PersonData) -> Doctor:
        doctor = self.business.edit_doctor(id, data)
        cache.delete(DOCTORS)
        return doctor

    def delete_doctor(self, id: int) -> None:
        self.business.delete_doctor(id)
        cache.delete(DOCTORS)

    def add_client(self, data: PersonData) -> Client:
        client = self.business.add_client(data)
        cache.delete(CLIENTS)
        return client

    def edit_client(self, id: int, data: PersonData) -> Client:
        client = self.business.edit_client(id, data)
        cache.delete(CLIENTS)
        return client

    def delete_client(self, id: int) -> None:
        self.business.delete_client(id)
        cache.delete(CLIENTS)


# the provider of the facade: a single, shared object (see business/provider.py)
@once
def application() -> ApplicationModel:
    return ApplicationModel()

All versions of the application have a [ApplicationModel] class: a single entry point from the web layer to the business layer, which keeps the lists of doctors and clients in memory. These lists are requested by almost all pages (the drop-down list of doctors in the calendar, the list of patients in the booking window, the administration pages), and rarely change.

A [Python] process retains its objects from one request to the next (Example 20): the [Flask] version therefore simply stored these lists in the attributes of a single object. The header comment explains why this version instead stores them in the cache of [Django] (Example 20): a production server runs multiple processes, and each would have its own copy of the lists.

  • line 36: the class inherits the contract [Business], just like [BusinessService]: the views call the same methods, regardless of which class serves them;
  • Lines 45–49: [get_or_set(key, function, timeout)] returns the value stored under this key; if it does not exist, it calls the function (here, a bound method from the business layer, passed without parentheses, which reads the list from the database), stores its result in the cache indefinitely ([timeout=None]), and returns it. The first request that needs the list reads it from the database; subsequent requests find it in the cache. The cache stores the list serialized by module [pickle] (Example 20), and reconstructs it upon retrieval, along with the already-loaded relationships: each person’s account, retrieved via the join [select_related("account")] from layer DAO. The reconstructed objects are copies: they are used for display, never for writing (the business layer always re-reads from the database what it modifies);
  • lines 53–54: the physician associated with an account, retrieved from the cache list. [next(generator, None)] returns the first element produced by the generating expression, or [None] if there is none (example 06);
  • Lines 57–90: The other methods in the contract simply delegate to the business layer. An account’s client ([get_client_by_user_id]) is always retrieved from the database, not from the cache: the most recent data is what matters (a patient who has just modified or deleted their account);
  • Lines 94–120: the updates. Each write operation for a doctor or client clears the relevant list ([delete]): the next query that needs it will read it from the database again. This is the whole point of a single entry point: the rule “a write operation updates the cache” is implemented only here. If the write operation fails (a [BusinessError]), the exception exits the method before the [delete]: the list is not overwritten; it has not changed. An application that writes to the database via a different path (another program, another version of the application using the same database) would leave the cache out of date: in that case, it would suffice to clear the [var/cache] folder;
  • Lines 124–126: The facade provider, modeled after the business layer provider: a single object, created on the first request. [functools.cache], imported under the name [once], stores the result of a function (example 06): the function [application()] executes only once, then always returns the same object.

docs.title: 11.13.2. web/utils.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# web/utils.py: small utility functions of the web layer:
#   - dates: "yyyy-mm-dd", days "Wednesday 23 September 2026";
#   - input: reading a positive integer, a date, sent by the browser;
#   - user: the logged-in user, and their patient (Client model).
# =========================================================================

import re
from datetime import date, datetime

from django.utils import dateformat

from models.models import Client
from security.errors import InvalidSession
from security.connected_user import ConnectedUser

from .application import application


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- dates
# the date, if [text] is a date that exists in the yyyy-mm-dd format; None otherwise.
# strptime refuses dates that do not exist ("2026-02-30")
def valid_date(text: str | None) -> date | None:
    if text is None or not re.fullmatch(r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}", text):
        return None
    try:
        return datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d").date()
    except ValueError:
        return None


# "2026-09-23"
def iso(day: date) -> str:
    return day.isoformat()


# "Wednesday 23 September 2026" / "mercredi 23 septembre 2026", in the active
# language (see web/middleware.py). dateformat.format formats a date like the
# date filter of the templates: l the day of the week in full, j the day,
# F the month in full, Y the year; the names are translated by Django
def format_day(day: date) -> str:
    return dateformat.format(day, "l j F Y")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- input
# "3" -> 3; "", "abc", "-2", "+2", None -> None
def positive_integer(value: str | None) -> int | None:
    if value is None or not re.fullmatch(r"\d{1,9}", value):
        return None
    n = int(value)
    return n if n > 0 else None


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- user
# the logged-in user. The protected views are only called if they exist (see
# security/middleware.py); as a precaution, their absence is treated as an
# expired session
def user(request) -> ConnectedUser:
    if request.user is None:
        raise InvalidSession()
    return request.user


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The patient (Client model) that corresponds to the logged-in user.
#
# The JWT token only contains the id of the ACCOUNT (users.id). For a USER role, the
# corresponding client is found thanks to the clients.user column.
#
# If there is none, the account has been deleted since login while
# its token is still valid: it is treated as an expired session.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
def connected_patient(request) -> Client:
    client = application().get_client_by_user_id(user(request).user_id)
    if client is None:
        raise InvalidSession()
    return client


# the IP address of the client
def ip(request) -> str:
    return request.META.get("REMOTE_ADDR", "")

Some utility functions that all views require:

  • Lines 23–29: the date of a parameter [yyyy-mm-dd] or [None]. Two checks: the format (a regular expression; [fullmatch] requires that the entire string match), then the existence of the date: [strptime] raises a [ValueError] for February 30;
  • lines 41–42: “Wednesday 23 September 2026” or “mercredi 23 septembre 2026,” depending on the language of the query. [dateformat.format] formats a date like the [date] filter in the templates (example 16), using the same codes; the names of the days and months are translated by [Django] itself, in the active language;
  • lines 47–51: a query parameter is a string, or [None]. Only digits are accepted (up to nine: a reasonable number that the database accepts), and the number must be strictly positive;
  • lines 58–61: the logged-in user, determined by the middleware [Authentication]. Protected views are called only for an authenticated user (access control), but the absence of a user is still handled as an expired session;
  • lines 73–77: the patient ([Client]) associated with the logged-in user. The token contains only the account ID; the client is identified by the [clients.user] column. If it does not exist, the account has been deleted since the user logged in: [InvalidSession] (the [ErrorPage] middleware, discussed later);
  • lines 81–82: the client’s address (IP) for the attempt limiter. [REMOTE_ADDR] is the address of the machine that established the connection. Behind a reverse proxy (see “A production server”), this would always be the proxy’s address: you would then need to read the header it adds ([X-Forwarded-For]), and only the one it adds, since the browser can send any header.

docs.title: 11.13.3. web/contexts.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# web/contexts.py: a context processor (see example 15): the variables that
# ALL the pages need:
#   - user: the logged-in user (or None), for the navigation bar;
#   - menu: the entries of the menu of the navigation bar, which depend on the role.
#
# The menu is computed HERE, in Python, and not in the template: "Doctors" and
# "Patients" only appear for the ADMIN. It is only a display convenience: the
# real protection is the access rules (a USER who types /doctors by
# hand gets a 403 page).
# =========================================================================

from dataclasses import dataclass

from django.urls import reverse
from django.utils.translation import gettext_lazy as _

from security import auth


# a menu entry: its URL, its label, and whether it is the one of the current page
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class MenuEntry:
    url: str
    label: str
    active: bool


def user(request):
    # the user established by the Authentication middleware. As a precaution, if it
    # is missing (an error page due to an error that occurred before this middleware), it is
    # read directly from the token, so that the navigation bar is complete
    connected = getattr(request, "user", None)
    if connected is None and request.COOKIES.get(auth.COOKIE):
        connected = auth.user(request.COOKIES[auth.COOKIE])
    return {"user": connected, "menu": menu(request, connected)}


# the menu entries: (name of the route, label, prefixes of the paths for
# which the entry is active)
def menu(request, connected):
    if connected is None:
        return []
    entries = []
    if connected.is_patient:
        # active for /my-area AND /my-account
        entries.append(("area", _("My area"), ["/my-"]))
    entries.append(("schedule", _("Schedule"), ["/schedule"]))
    if connected.is_admin:
        entries.append(("doctors_list", _("Doctors"), ["/doctors"]))
        entries.append(("clients_list", _("Patients"), ["/clients"]))
    # any: true if one of the prefixes matches
    return [MenuEntry(reverse(route), label, any(request.path.startswith(p) for p in prefixes))
            for route, label, prefixes in entries]

A context processor (Example 15), declared in [config/settings.py]: the variables required by all pages, within the context of all templates:

  • [user]: the logged-in user, or [None], for the navigation bar. Usually, this is the one from the [Authentication] middleware; [getattr(object, name, default)] reads an attribute or returns the default value if it does not exist. As a precaution, if it is missing, the user is read directly from the token (lines 34–35);
  • [menu]: the navigation bar menu entries, which depend on the role (lines 41–54). Each entry is a [MenuEntry] object (a data class, lines 22–26): the URL (generated by [reverse], example 04), the translated label, and the indicator for the active entry—the one on the currently displayed page—which the template highlights. The [My area] entry is active for all URL entries that begin with [/my-]: [/my-area] and [/my-account].

The menu is calculated in [Python], not in the template (there is no logic in the templates; more on this later). Hiding the “Doctors” and “Patients” entries is merely a display convenience: the real protection comes from the access rules.

docs.title: 11.13.4. web/templatetags/rdv.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# web/templatetags/rdv.py: the tags of our templates (see example 16), loaded
# by {% load rdv %}.
#
#   {% success_zone %}: the SUCCESS flash messages, at the top of the page;
#   {% error_zone %}: the error zone, at the BOTTOM of each page, on a light pink
#   background. It gathers the three possible sources of error:
#     - [error]: the error of the displayed page (invalid date, mistyped captcha,
#       login already taken...), passed on by the view;
#     - the error flash messages, left by the previous view before a
#       redirection (slot already booked, deletion refused...);
#     - the input errors of an invalid form (see example 19): their
#       messages are displayed UNDER the fields; here, if there is no other
#       message, a simple sentence "The form contains errors.".
# =========================================================================

from django import template
from django.contrib import messages as flash
from django.utils.translation import gettext as _

register = template.Library()


# takes_context: the function receives the context of the template that calls it; messages:
# the variable of the context processor of the flash messages; level: the level of a message
@register.inclusion_tag("fragments/success.html", takes_context=True)
def success_zone(context):
    return {"texts": [m.message for m in context.get("messages", []) if m.level == flash.SUCCESS]}


@register.inclusion_tag("fragments/errors.html", takes_context=True)
def error_zone(context):
    texts = [m.message for m in context.get("messages", []) if m.level == flash.ERROR]
    if context.get("error"):
        texts.insert(0, context["error"])
    form = context.get("form")
    # a BOUND (sent) and invalid form, without any other message
    if not texts and form is not None and form.is_bound and form.errors:
        texts.append(_("The form contains errors."))
    return {"texts": texts}

Two inclusion tags (example 16), loaded into the templates by [{% load rdv %}]. Each returns a small template (a fragment, discussed later), containing the variables returned by the function:

  • Lines 26–28: [{% success_zone %}]: success flash messages (example 20), displayed at the top of the page. [takes_context=True]: The function receives the context of the template that calls it, where the message context processor has stored the variable [messages]. [level] is the level of a message ([flash.SUCCESS], [flash.ERROR]...);
  • lines 31–40: [{% error_zone %}]: the error area, at the bottom of each page. It groups the three possible sources of errors: the page error (the variable [error], passed by the view and placed at the top of the list by [insert(0, ...)]), flash error messages (set by the previous view before a redirect), and input errors from an invalid form, whose messages are displayed below the fields: the error area then simply displays the phrase, “The form contains errors.” [is_bound]: the form has received an entry (example 19).

Both tags read the same list, with each retaining only one level. A list of messages that has been read is cleared at the end of the request (example 20): each message is displayed only once.

docs.title: 11.13.5. web/middleware.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# web/middleware.py: two middlewares of the web layer (see example 24).
# =========================================================================

from django.conf import settings
from django.contrib import messages
from django.core.exceptions import BadRequest, PermissionDenied
from django.http import Http404
from django.shortcuts import redirect
from django.utils import translation
from django.utils.translation import gettext as _

from security import auth
from security.errors import InvalidSession

from .views.errors import error_page


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# the language of the request (see example 22): that of the cookie [rdvmedecins_language]
# if it is a supported language, English otherwise. Placed at the top of the list of
# middlewares, it acts for ALL the requests, even those that end in
# no route (404 page): their error page is in the right language
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
class SetLanguage:
    # the supported languages; the default language is LANGUAGE_CODE
    LANGUAGES = [code for code, name in settings.LANGUAGES]

    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        language = request.COOKIES.get(settings.LANGUAGE_COOKIE_NAME)
        if language not in self.LANGUAGES:
            language = settings.LANGUAGE_CODE
        translation.activate(language)
        # the language of the request, stored as LocaleMiddleware does (see example 22)
        request.LANGUAGE_CODE = language
        return self.get_response(request)


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# how errors become HTML pages. Three cases:
#   1. an InvalidSession (account deleted since login) -> back to the
#      login page, as for an expired session;
#   2. an HTTP error raised by a view: invalid request (BadRequest, 400),
#      insufficient role (PermissionDenied, 403), unknown object (Http404) -> the error
#      page, with the original code;
#   3. any other exception (a real anomaly): Django writes it to the
#      log, with its stack trace; in production (DEBUG false), the user
#      sees the 500 error page (handler500, see config/urls.py) - never the stack
#      trace; in development, the Django debug page.
# A refused HTTP method (405) is not an exception: the decorators
# require_GET... return an empty 405 response, which __call__ replaces with our page.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
class ErrorPage:
    CODES = {BadRequest: 400, PermissionDenied: 403, Http404: 404}

    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        response = self.get_response(request)
        if response.status_code == 405 and not response.content:
            page = error_page(request, 405)
            # the Allow header: the accepted methods
            page["Allow"] = response["Allow"]
            return page
        return response

    def process_exception(self, request, exception):
        if isinstance(exception, InvalidSession):
            messages.error(request, _("Your session has expired: please log in again."))
            return auth.clear_token(redirect("login"))
        for cls, code in self.CODES.items():
            if isinstance(exception, cls):
                return error_page(request, code)
        return None

The two middleware components of the web layer (Example 24). Recall their order in the list [MIDDLEWARE] from [config/settings.py]: [SetLanguage] first, [ErrorPage] last.

  • Lines 25–39: the request language; if it matches the language of the [rdvmedecins_language] cookie, that language is used; otherwise, English is used. This is the [SetLanguage] middleware from Example 16, not [LocaleMiddleware] (Example 22): [LocaleMiddleware] would select the browser’s preferred language if no cookie is present; the other versions of the application always start in English, and this one does the same. The supported languages are read from the [LANGUAGES] setting (line 27, a read-only list executed once when the class is loaded). [translation.activate] (line 36) sets the active language (example 16): the language used for translations, dates, and the [LANGUAGE_CODE] variable in the templates (context processor [i18n], example 22). The language is also stored in [request.LANGUAGE_CODE] (line 38), as is the case with [LocaleMiddleware], for views that need to access it. Placed at the top, this middleware applies to all requests before any other processing: all pages, including error pages, are in the correct language;
  • Lines 62–69: A rejected HTTP method (a GET call to [/logout], which only accepts POST) does not throw an exception: the decorators [require_GET], [require_POST]... return a 405 response with no content. [__call__] replaces it with the error page, retaining the [Allow] header (the accepted methods), which is required in a 405 response;
  • Lines 71–78: Exceptions thrown by views ([process_exception], Example 24). A [InvalidSession] (the account has been deleted): the “session expired” message, deletion of the token cookie, and the login page. A HTTP error thrown by a view ([BadRequest], [PermissionDenied], [Http404]): the error page, with its code, in both production and development. Any other exception is a true anomaly: the method returns [None], and [Django] handles it itself; it logs it, along with its call stack, and then displays its debug page in development and the 500 error page ([handler500]) in production. The user never sees the call stack of an application in production.
$ curl -si http://localhost:8081/logout
HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Allow: POST
...
<!doctype html>
...

Code 405 (Method Not Allowed) is presented to the user as a page not found (the error page message, discussed below). A URL that does not match any route does not go through [ErrorPage]: [Django] directly calls the [handler404] view in production and displays its detailed 404 page in development (Example 24).

docs.title: 11.14. Dictionaries
docs.text:
The interface text is the same as in other versions of the application, which stored it in JSON files under keys ([LOGIN.TITLE] referred to the text [Sign in]). [Django] works differently (example 22): the original text, in English, is written directly in the code ([_("Sign in")]) and in the templates ([{% translate "Sign in" %}]); it serves as the key in the French dictionary, the file [locale/fr/LC_MESSAGES/django.po]:

#: web/views/schedule.py:202 web/views/area.py:75
msgid "Appointment cancelled."
msgstr "Rendez-vous annulé."

#: web/views/auth.py:62 web/views/area.py:142
#, python-format
msgid "Too many failed attempts. Try again in %(minutes)d minute."
msgid_plural "Too many failed attempts. Try again in %(minutes)d minutes."
msgstr[0] "Trop de tentatives infructueuses. Réessayez dans %(minutes)d minute."
msgstr[1] ""
"Trop de tentatives infructueuses. Réessayez dans %(minutes)d minutes."

This file, containing approximately 140 texts, is not reproduced here. It was generated by the command [python manage.py makemessages -l fr], which retrieves all texts marked with the code and templates, then completed manually, and compiled into [django.mo] by [python manage.py compilemessages] (example 22). The compiled [django.mo] file is delivered with the code: the application runs without the [gettext] tools. There is no English dictionary: text without a translation is displayed as-is, that is, in English.

The [#:] lines indicate where each text is used; [#, python-format] identifies a text with parameters ([%(minutes)d]), whose translation [makemessages] will verify. [gettext] enables something the other versions could not do: the plural (“1 minute,” “15 minutes”), with [ngettext] in the code (see below) and [msgid_plural] in the dictionary (example 22). Some text has been added: the message on page 419, which the other versions do not have.

Form error messages are translated in the same way (see below). The messages that [Django] generates itself (number too large, invalid email address, etc.) are translated using the dictionaries from [Django].

docs.title: 11.15. Forms
docs.text: “Person” forms are [Django] forms (examples 18 and 19): a class describes the fields and their constraints; the view builds the form with the user’s input ([PersonForm(request.POST)]), then checks whether it is valid ([is_valid]). An invalid form is redisplayed, showing the user’s input and error messages below the fields (excluding passwords: a [PasswordInput] field is never redisplayed). The anti-CSRF token is verified for all forms by the [CsrfViewMiddleware] middleware.

docs.title: 11.15.1. web/forms.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# web/forms.py: the "person" forms and their constraints (see
# examples 18 and 19). Three forms share the same identity fields
# (title, first name, last name):
#
#   PersonFieldsForm            title, first name, last name
#    ├─ PersonForm              + OPTIONAL login / password, version
#    │                            (the ADMIN adds or updates a doctor / client)
#    ├─ RegistrationForm        + REQUIRED login / password / confirmation
#    │                            (a patient creates their account)
#    └─ MyAccountForm           + login, optional new password, REQUIRED
#                                 CURRENT password, version
#                                 (a patient updates their account)
#
# The child classes INHERIT from PersonFieldsForm: they have its fields, plus
# their own. The validated input (cleaned_data) is turned into PersonData
# for the business layer by the person_data() method.
#
# The labels, the help texts and the error messages are translated (gettext_lazy,
# see business/errors.py). The maximum lengths are those of the SQL columns.
# =========================================================================

from django import forms
from django.core.exceptions import ValidationError
from django.core.validators import RegexValidator
from django.utils.translation import gettext_lazy as _

from business.person_data import PersonData
from security import passwords

TITLES = ["Mr", "Mme", "Melle"]
# minimum length of a password CHOSEN by a patient
PASSWORD_MIN = 6

# login: lower-case letters, digits, dot, hyphen, underscore - 30 characters at most
LOGIN_FORMAT = RegexValidator(r"^[a-z0-9._-]{1,30}$", message=_(
    "At most 30 characters: unaccented lower-case letters, digits, dot, hyphen, underscore."))


# bcrypt only takes into account the first 72 bytes of a password (see
# security/passwords.py); an accented letter takes two bytes in UTF-8
def bcrypt_length(value: str) -> None:
    if len(value.encode()) > passwords.MAX_BYTES:
        raise ValidationError(_("The password must not exceed 72 characters."))


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# a login is always in lower case: the field converts the input BEFORE its
# validation (to_python is called before the validators)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
class LoginField(forms.CharField):
    def to_python(self, value):
        text = super().to_python(value)
        return text.lower() if text else text


# a password field: never redisplayed, and without stripping spaces
# (strip=False: a space is part of the password)
def password_field(label, required, help_text="", min_length=None):
    messages = {
        "required": _("The password is required."),
        # %(limit_value)d: the minimum length, put in the message by Django
        "min_length": _("The password must be at least %(limit_value)d characters long."),
    }
    return forms.CharField(label=label, required=required, help_text=help_text, strip=False,
                           min_length=min_length, validators=[bcrypt_length],
                           error_messages=messages,
                           widget=forms.PasswordInput(attrs={"maxlength": 72,
                                                             "autocomplete": "new-password"}))


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# the parent class of our forms (see example 18): each input zone receives
# the Bootstrap CSS class that suits it; flag() frames in red (class
# is-invalid) the fields that have an input error, and those that a BUSINESS error
# designates (a login already taken...), the message then being at the bottom of the page
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
class BootstrapForm(forms.Form):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        for field in self.fields.values():
            css_class = "form-select" if isinstance(field.widget, forms.Select) else "form-control"
            field.widget.attrs["class"] = css_class

    def flag(self, fields=()):
        # errors: the input errors; |: the union of two sets
        for name in set(self.errors) | set(fields):
            if name in self.fields:
                self.fields[name].widget.attrs["class"] += " is-invalid"
        return self


class PersonFieldsForm(BootstrapForm):
    title = forms.ChoiceField(label=_("Title"), choices=[(t, t) for t in TITLES], error_messages={
        "required": _("Choose a title from the list."),
        "invalid_choice": _("Choose a title from the list.")})
    first_name = forms.CharField(label=_("First name"), max_length=20, error_messages={
        "required": _("The first name is required."),
        "max_length": _("The first name must not exceed 20 characters.")})
    last_name = forms.CharField(label=_("Last name"), max_length=20, error_messages={
        "required": _("The last name is required."),
        "max_length": _("The last name must not exceed 20 characters.")})

    # the validated input -> the data expected by the business layer. An empty
    # field is None (or None: an empty string is "falsy")
    def person_data(self) -> PersonData:
        d = self.cleaned_data
        return PersonData(d["title"], d["last_name"], d["first_name"], d.get("login") or None,
                          d.get("password") or None, d.get("version"))


# the form of a doctor or a client (ADMIN): OPTIONAL login and
# password; creation=False: the update form, with the version
class PersonForm(PersonFieldsForm):
    def __init__(self, *args, creation=True, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        # an empty field is accepted: the validators only apply to an entered value
        self.fields["login"] = LoginField(
            label=_("Login"), required=False, max_length=30, validators=[LOGIN_FORMAT],
            help_text=_("Optional: defaults to the last name in lower case.") if creation
            else _("Leave empty to keep it unchanged."),
            widget=forms.TextInput(attrs={"class": "form-control", "autocomplete": "off"}))
        self.fields["password"] = password_field(
            _("Password"), False,
            _("Optional: defaults to the login.") if creation
            else _("Leave empty to keep it unchanged."))
