        self.fields["password"].widget.attrs["class"] = "form-control"
        # update: the version of the displayed record, in a hidden field (the
        # optimistic lock)
        if not creation:
            self.fields["version"] = forms.IntegerField(widget=forms.HiddenInput)


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# the password and its confirmation: two fields, compared by clean (see
# example 19). Common to registration (required) and to the patient's account
# (optional: empty = password unchanged)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
class WithConfirmation(PersonFieldsForm):
    def add_passwords(self, required: bool):
        self.fields["login"] = LoginField(
            label=_("Login"), max_length=30, validators=[LOGIN_FORMAT],
            help_text=_("Unaccented lower-case letters, digits, dot, hyphen, underscore.")
            if required else "",
            error_messages={"required": _("The login is required.")},
            widget=forms.TextInput(attrs={"class": "form-control", "autocomplete": "username"}))
        self.fields["password"] = password_field(
            _("Password") if required else _("New password"), required,
            _("At least 6 characters.") if required else _("Leave empty to keep it unchanged."),
            min_length=PASSWORD_MIN)
        self.fields["confirmation"] = password_field(_("Confirm password"), required)
        self.fields["confirmation"].error_messages["required"] = _("Please confirm the password.")
        for name in ("password", "confirmation"):
            self.fields[name].widget.attrs["class"] = "form-control"

    # the validation of the whole form, after that of each field
    def clean(self):
        data = super().clean()
        password = data.get("password")
        confirmation = data.get("confirmation")
        if password and password != confirmation and "confirmation" not in self.errors:
            self.add_error("confirmation", _("The confirmation does not match the password."))
        return data


# "Create a patient account": REQUIRED login, password and confirmation
class RegistrationForm(WithConfirmation):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.add_passwords(required=True)


# "Manage my account" (a patient): required login, optional new password,
# REQUIRED CURRENT password, version
class MyAccountForm(WithConfirmation):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.add_passwords(required=False)
        # the CURRENT password, required for any update of the account
        self.fields["current_password"] = forms.CharField(
            label=_("Current password"), strip=False,
            help_text=_("Required to save any change."),
            error_messages={"required": _("Enter your current password.")},
            widget=forms.PasswordInput(attrs={"class": "form-control", "maxlength": 72,
                                              "autocomplete": "current-password"}))
        self.fields["version"] = forms.IntegerField(widget=forms.HiddenInput)

Three forms share the identity fields (title, first name, last name): the administrator form (for a doctor or a client), the patient account creation form, and “Manage my account.” The header comment outlines their inheritance hierarchy: their common parent class, [PersonFieldsForm], defines the identity fields; each child adds its own. The labels, tooltips, and messages are translated lazily ([gettext_lazy]): they are defined when the module loads and translated each time the page is displayed, into the language of the request (the business layer, mentioned above).

  • Lines 36–37: a login form, a validator ([RegexValidator]) that checks for a regular expression. A validator is a callable object that raises [ValidationError] for an incorrect value (Example 19); it is assigned to a field via its parameter [validators];
  • lines 42–44: a validator written as a simple function. [bcrypt] considers only the first 72 bytes of a password (the security layer, discussed above): the limit applies to bytes, not characters ([encode()]: an accented letter takes up two bytes in [UTF-8]);
  • lines 51–54: a username is always in lowercase. A custom field, a child of [CharField], redefines [to_python], the method that converts the input into a Python value: it is called before the validators, which therefore check the input after it has already been converted. [super().to_python(value)] first performs the standard processing of [CharField] (removing spaces surrounding the input);
  • Lines 59–69: a function that creates a password field. [strip=False]: spaces are not removed; they can be part of a password. [min_length]: the minimum length, which [Django] checks itself; its message contains [%(limit_value)d], the parameter that [Django] places there. The [PasswordInput] widget is never redrawn; the HTML attribute [maxlength] prevents users from typing more than 72 characters; [autocomplete="new-password"] instructs the browser to prompt for a new password, rather than filling the field with the saved password;
  • lines 78–90: the parent class of our forms (Example 18). Its constructor assigns each input field the appropriate subclass of CSS ([form-select] for a list, [form-control] for the others). The [flag] method adds the [is-invalid] class (a red border) to fields with input errors and to those flagged by a business rule error (a username that is already in use): [set(a) | set(b)] is the union of two sets. It returns the form itself: the views call it when passing the form to the template;
  • lines 93–102: the title, a list ([ChoiceField], example 18); the first and last names, 20 characters maximum, the column widths SQL (the [maxlength] field in the input area is added by [Django] itself). Each error message is replaced with our own ([error_messages], example 19). [invalid_choice] is the message for a value not included in the list (a manually crafted query). The spaces surrounding an entry are removed by [CharField];
  • lines 106–109: the validated input ([cleaned_data]), converted to [PersonData] for the business layer: the business layer is not familiar with forms. [d.get(key)] returns [None] for a field that the form does not have; [x or None] converts an empty string to [None] (unchanged, or the default value);
  • lines 114–131: the administrator’s form. The parameter [creation], which we have created, distinguishes between creation and modification; it is placed after [*args]: it is a required parameter ([PersonForm(request.POST, creation=False)]). The fields specific to this form are added by the builder in the [self.fields] dictionary: their options depend on [creation] (the tooltips differ: “Optional: defaults to the last name in lower case.”, “Leave empty to keep it unchanged.”). The username and password are optional ([required=False]): a validator applies only to an entered value, so an empty field is accepted. Only the “modify” field has the hidden “version” field (the optimistic lock, business layer);
  • lines 139–163: the password and its confirmation, which are common to both registration and the patient’s account. The two fields are compared using the form’s [clean] method (Example 19), which is called after each field is validated. [add_error] attaches the message to the confirmation field, unless that field already contains an error (“Please confirm the password.”): only one message per field. The minimum length requirement applies only to a password chosen by a patient (6 characters);
  • lines 167–170: creating a patient account: login, password, and confirmation are required;
  • lines 175–186: “Manage my account”: the new password is optional (blank: unchanged), the current password is required. It is not validated by the form, but by the view: an incorrect password must be counted by the attempt limiter as a failed login. [autocomplete="current-password"]: Here, the browser may suggest the saved password.

# =========================================================================
# web/view_models.py: the "view models": objects built
# in one go by a view, which the template merely reads. Rule followed by
# all the pages: no logic in the templates. The views prepare
# ALREADY formatted data ("Mme Marie PELISSIER", "8:00 - 8:20",
# selected = True...) already filtered according to the role of the user; the
# templates merely put them in the HTML.
# =========================================================================

from dataclasses import dataclass


# an option of a drop-down list (doctor, patient)
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class OptionView:
    id: int
    label: str
    selected: bool


# a row of the displayed schedule (a slot)
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ScheduleRow:
    slot_id: int
    time_range: str         # "8:00 - 8:20"
    free: bool
    # name displayed for a taken slot; None = "Booked"
    patient: str | None
    me: bool                # the appointment of the logged-in patient
    bookable: bool          # display the "Book" button?
    book_url: str
    # set only if the "Cancel" button is displayed
    appointment_id: int | None


# the displayed schedule: the doctor, the day, the rows
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ScheduleView:
    doctor: str             # "Mme Marie PELISSIER"
    day: str                # "Wednesday 23 September 2026"
    rows: list[ScheduleRow]


# the booking dialog of a slot
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class BookingView:
    slot_id: int
    time_range: str
    # ADMIN / DOCTOR: the patients to choose from
    clients: list[OptionView]
    # USER: the patient is themselves
    patient: str | None


# an upcoming appointment, in the patient's area
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AppointmentView:
    id: int
    day: str                # "Wednesday 23 September 2026"
    time_range: str         # "8:00 - 8:20"
    doctor: str             # "Mme Marie PELISSIER"
    schedule_url: str       # the schedule of the doctor that day

The file [web/view_models.py] contains the view templates: objects constructed by a view, which the template simply reads. The rule, followed by all pages: no logic in the templates. The views prepare data that is already formatted (“Ms. Marie PELISSIER,” “8:00 – 8:20”) and already filtered according to the user’s role; the templates place them in the HTML. These are fixed data classes ([frozen=True], example 08): once constructed, a view template never changes.

  • Lines 14–18: An option from a drop-down list: the ID, the label, and whether the option is selected?
  • Lines 22–33: A calendar entry: a time slot, and what the logged-in user is authorized to view and do with it. [patient] is populated only if the user is authorized to see the patient’s name; [bookable] indicates whether to display the “Book” button; [appointment_id] indicates whether to display the “Cancel” button;
  • lines 37–52: the displayed calendar and the booking window: for the administrator and doctors, the list of patients to choose from; for a patient, their own name;
  • lines 56–62: an upcoming appointment in the patient’s section.

# =========================================================================
# web/urls.py: the routes of the application. Their protection is not written here,
# but in security/access.py (one rule per URL prefix).
# =========================================================================

from django.urls import path, re_path

from .views import area, auth, language, registration, schedule
from .views.persons import clients, doctors

urlpatterns = [
    # login
    path("", auth.home, name="home"),
    path("login", auth.login, name="login"),
    path("logout", auth.logout, name="logout"),
    # the language: fr or en only
    re_path(r"^language/(?P<code>fr|en)$", language.change, name="language"),
    # the schedule
    path("schedule", schedule.show, name="schedule"),
    path("schedule/book", schedule.book, name="schedule_book"),
    path("schedule/cancel", schedule.cancel, name="schedule_cancel"),
    # the creation of a client account
    path("register/access", registration.access, name="registration_access"),
    path("register", registration.registration, name="registration"),
    # the patient's area
    path("my-area", area.area, name="area"),
    path("my-area/cancel", area.cancel_appointment, name="area_cancel"),
    path("my-account", area.account, name="account"),
    path("my-account/delete", area.delete_account, name="account_delete"),
    # the management of doctors and clients: the routes built by the two
    # PersonManagement objects; * "unpacks" the list they return
    *doctors.urls(),
    *clients.urls(),
]

The application’s routes, mounted at the root of the site by [config/urls.py]. The routes for managing doctors and clients are generated by two objects (discussed later); [*list] places the elements of one list into another list (lines 32–33). The command [show_urls] does not exist in [Django] (it comes from an extension); a short script, launched by [python manage.py shell], lists them all, along with their names:

$ python manage.py shell -v 0 -c "from django.urls import get_resolver; [print(f'{str(p.pattern):32} {p.name}') for p in get_resolver().url_patterns[0].url_patterns]"
                                 home
login                            login
logout                           logout
^language/(?P<code>fr|en)$       language
schedule                         schedule
schedule/book                    schedule_book
schedule/cancel                  schedule_cancel
register/access                  registration_access
register                         registration
my-area                          area
my-area/cancel                   area_cancel
my-account                       account
my-account/delete                account_delete
doctors                          doctors_list
doctors/add                      doctors_add
doctors/<int:id>/edit            doctors_edit
doctors/<int:id>/delete          doctors_delete
clients                          clients_list
clients/add                      clients_add
clients/<int:id>/edit            clients_edit
clients/<int:id>/delete          clients_delete

The URL files are those from other versions of the application: they do not have a trailing slash ([/schedule], not [/schedule/]), and editing and deleting a doctor are POST requests ([/doctors/{id}/edit], [/doctors/{id}/delete]), not PUT and DELETE as in Example 28. The code always generates the URL codes based on the route names ([redirect("login")], [reverse("schedule")], [{% url 'schedule' %}] in the templates, Example 04): changing a URL requires modifying only its route.

The methods accepted by each route are declared by the [require_GET], [require_POST], and [require_http_methods] decorators in the views (example 02). Access rules are not in the views, but in the [security/access.py] file, as seen above: one rule per URL prefix ([^/(doctors|clients)] for the administrator, [^/my-] for patients...), and a final rule requiring an authenticated user for all other URL files. The URL URLs in the application were chosen for this purpose: all pages within the same role begin the same way.

docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# web/views/errors.py: the error page (400, 403, 404, 405, 419, 500), and the views
# that Django calls for the errors it detects itself (see config/urls.py:
# handler400, handler403, handler404, handler500, and the CSRF_FAILURE_VIEW setting).
# =========================================================================

from django.shortcuts import render
from django.utils.translation import gettext_lazy as _

# the message of each code
MESSAGES = {
    400: _("The request is invalid."),
    403: _("Your role does not allow you to access this page."),
    404: _("This page does not exist."),
    405: _("This page does not exist."),
    419: _("The page has expired: reload it, then try again."),
    500: _("An unexpected error occurred. Please try again later."),
}


def error_page(request, code: int):
    return render(request, "error.html", {
        "page_title": _("Error"), "code": code, "message": MESSAGES.get(code, MESSAGES[500]),
    }, status=code)


# the views of the errors detected by Django (exception: the exception that caused
# the error; the 500 view does not receive it)
def error_400(request, exception):
    return error_page(request, 400)


def error_403(request, exception):
    return error_page(request, 403)


def error_404(request, exception):
    return error_page(request, 404)


def error_500(request):
    return error_page(request, 500)


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# a missing or wrong anti-CSRF token: the page has probably been displayed a
# long time ago, in another tab, before a change of the token cookie... Error
# 419, the (unofficial, but widespread) code of an expired page. reason: the reason
# for the refusal, given by CsrfViewMiddleware (in English)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
def csrf_rejected(request, reason=""):
    return error_page(request, 419)

The error page and the error views that [Django] detects itself:

  • lines 11–18: the message for each code. Code 405 is displayed as a “page not found” error;
  • lines 21–24: the error page, template [error.html], with response code HTTP ([status=code]). An unknown code receives the 500 error message ([dict.get(key, default)]);
  • lines 29–42: the four views [handler400]... [handler500], referred to as [config/urls.py] (example 24). Their signature is determined by [Django]: the request and the exception that caused the error (except for error 500);
  • lines 51–52: a missing or invalid anti-CSRF token. The [CsrfViewMiddleware] middleware rejects the request before calling the view (Example 21), and instead calls the view associated with the [CSRF_FAILURE_VIEW] setting (see [config/settings.py]): the 419 error page, the (unofficial but widely used) code for an expired page. This occurs when a page has remained open in a tab for a long time, even though the token cookie has since changed. The page then displays: “The page has expired: reload it, then try again.” Its parameter [reason] is the reason for the rejection, in English, intended for the log rather than the user.
