A named fragment ([{% partialdef %}], example 15), used by the three pages that display a “person” form: the identification fields, the title, then the first name and last name side by side (the grid from [Bootstrap]: [row], [col-sm-6]). docs.title: 11.18.3.1. templates/login.html
docs.text:
{% extends "layout.html" %}
{% comment %}
  =========================================================================
  templates/login.html - the login form (see web/views/auth.py).
  An ordinary HTML <form>, written by hand: the browser itself sends login,
  password and captcha answer in POST /login, without JavaScript. In case
  of failure, the server sends back THIS page, with the login already entered, a NEW
  captcha and the error, displayed at the bottom of the page by the parent template.
  =========================================================================
{% endcomment %}
{% load i18n %}

{% block content %}
<div class="row justify-content-center">
  <div class="col-sm-8 col-md-6 col-lg-5">
    <div class="card p-4">
      <h5 class="card-title mb-3">{% translate "Sign in" %}</h5>

      <form method="post" action="{% url 'login' %}">
        {% csrf_token %}
        <div class="mb-3">
          <label class="form-label" for="login">{% translate "Login" %}</label>
          {# autofocus: a boolean attribute, written if the condition is true. The cursor goes to the first field to fill in #}
          <input id="login" name="login" type="text" class="form-control" autocomplete="username"
                 value="{{ login }}" required{% if not login %} autofocus{% endif %}>
        </div>
        <div class="mb-3">
          <label class="form-label" for="password">{% translate "Password" %}</label>
          <input id="password" name="password" type="password" class="form-control"
                 autocomplete="current-password" required{% if login %} autofocus{% endif %}>
        </div>

        {% include "fragments/captcha.html" %}

        <button type="submit" class="btn btn-primary w-100">{% translate "Log in" %}</button>

        {% comment %}
          no account yet: a patient can create one themselves. It is NOT
          a simple link: it is a second submit button of THIS form, which goes
          to another address (formaction). The server checks there the captcha
          above before opening the account creation page (see
          web/views/registration.py). formnovalidate: the browser does not require
          login and password (useless to create an account). Enter in a
          field always triggers the FIRST button of the form, "Log in".
        {% endcomment %}
        <button type="submit" class="btn btn-outline-primary w-100 mt-3"
                formaction="{% url 'registration_access' %}" formnovalidate>{% translate "Create a patient account" %}</button>
        <div class="form-text text-center">{% translate "To create an account, first type the characters shown in the image." %}</div>
      </form>

      <div class="text-muted small mt-3">
        <span>{% translate "Demo accounts (password = login):" %}</span>
        <ul class="mb-0 mt-1">
          <li><code>admin</code> - <span>{% translate "ADMIN role: appointments + doctor and patient management" %}</span></li>
          <li><code>pelissier</code>, <code>tatou</code>, <code>dupont</code> - <span>{% translate "DOCTOR role: booking and cancelling appointments" %}</span></li>
          <li><code>martin</code>, <code>durand</code>, <code>bistrou</code>, <code>german</code> - <span>{% translate "USER role (patients): booking for themselves, managing their account" %}</span></li>
        </ul>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
{% endblock %}

The login form, a hand-coded [<form>], is sent via POST to [/login]. The [{% extends %}] tag is the first in the template (line 1), as required by DTL; the comment follows.

  • Lines 24–30: The entered login is redisplayed after a failed attempt ([login]). The attribute [autofocus] places the cursor in the first field to be filled in: the username if it is empty, the password otherwise (after a failed login attempt or after creating an account). A Boolean attribute is either present or absent: [{% if not login %} autofocus{% endif %}];
  • line 33: the CAPTCHA;
  • lines 46–47: the “Create a patient account” button is not a link; it is a second button that submits the same form to a different address (button attribute [formaction]). The server verifies the CAPTCHA there before opening the account creation page ([registration.access]). [formnovalidate]: The browser does not require a username and password (attributes [required]), as they are not needed to create an account. Pressing the Enter key in a field always triggers the first form submission button: Log in;
  • lines 51–58: demo accounts, for testing.

docs.title: 11.18.3.2. templates/schedule.html
docs.text:
{% extends "layout.html" %}
{% comment %}
  =========================================================================
  templates/schedule.html - the main page (see web/views/schedule.py).
  Three blocks:
    1. the choice of the doctor and the day;
    2. the schedule;
    3. the booking dialog (booking fragment).
  A possible error (invalid date, unknown doctor) is displayed at the bottom of
  the page by the parent template (error_zone tag).
  =========================================================================
{% endcomment %}
{% load i18n %}

{% block content %}
  {# 1. choice of the doctor and the day: a GET form, which simply reloads this page with ?doctorId=...&day=... #}
  <form method="get" action="{% url 'schedule' %}" class="card p-3 mb-3">
    <div class="row g-2 align-items-end">
      <div class="col-sm-5">
        <label class="form-label" for="doctorId">{% translate "Doctor" %}</label>
        <select id="doctorId" name="doctorId" class="form-select" required>
          <option value="">{% translate "-- choose a doctor --" %}</option>
          {% for doctor in doctors %}
          <option value="{{ doctor.id }}"{% if doctor.selected %} selected{% endif %}>{{ doctor.label }}</option>
          {% endfor %}
        </select>
      </div>
      <div class="col-sm-4">
        <label class="form-label" for="day">{% translate "Day" %}</label>
        <input id="day" name="day" type="date" class="form-control" value="{{ day }}" required>
      </div>
      <div class="col-sm-3">
        <button type="submit" class="btn btn-primary w-100">{% translate "View schedule" %}</button>
      </div>
    </div>
  </form>

  {# patient who already has an upcoming appointment: why there is no "Book" button #}
  {% if info %}
  <div class="alert alert-info">
    <span>{{ info }}</span>
    <a href="{% url 'area' %}" class="alert-link">{% translate "My area" %}</a>
  </div>
  {% endif %}

  {# 2. the schedule #}
  {% if schedule %}
  <div class="card p-3">
    <h5>{% translate "Schedule for" %} {{ schedule.day }} - {{ schedule.doctor }}</h5>

    {% if schedule.rows %}
    <table class="table table-hover align-middle">
      <thead>
        <tr>
          <th>{% translate "Slot" %}</th>
          <th>{% translate "Status" %}</th>
          <th></th>
        </tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        {% for row in schedule.rows %}
        <tr{% if row.bookable %} class="free-slot"{% endif %}>
          <td>{{ row.time_range }}</td>
          <td>
            {% comment %}
              [patient] is only set if the user is allowed to see this
              name (ADMIN, DOCTOR, or the patient for THEIR appointment) - otherwise,
              simply "Booked"
            {% endcomment %}
            {% if row.free %}
            <span class="badge text-bg-success">{% translate "Free" %}</span>
            {% elif row.patient %}
            <span class="badge {% if row.me %}text-bg-primary{% else %}text-bg-secondary{% endif %}">{{ row.patient }}</span>
            {% else %}
            <span class="badge text-bg-secondary">{% translate "Booked" %}</span>
            {% endif %}
          </td>
          <td>
            {% comment %}
              the displayed buttons have been decided by the view (bookable, appointment_id)
              according to the role of the user. "Book" is a simple link: it
              reopens this page with the booking dialog of this slot
            {% endcomment %}
            {% if row.bookable %}
            <a class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-success" href="{{ row.book_url }}">{% translate "Book" %}</a>
            {% endif %}
            {# "Cancel" MODIFIES data: it is therefore a POST #}
            {% if row.appointment_id %}
            <form method="post" action="{% url 'schedule_cancel' %}" class="m-0"
                  data-confirmation="{% translate 'Cancel this appointment?' %}">
              {% csrf_token %}
              <input type="hidden" name="appointmentId" value="{{ row.appointment_id }}">
              <input type="hidden" name="doctorId" value="{{ doctor_id }}">
              <input type="hidden" name="day" value="{{ day }}">
              <button type="submit" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-danger">{% translate "Cancel" %}</button>
            </form>
            {% endif %}
          </td>
        </tr>
        {% endfor %}
      </tbody>
    </table>
    {% else %}
    <p class="text-muted mb-0">{% translate "This doctor has no time slots." %}</p>
    {% endif %}
  </div>
  {% else %}
  <p class="text-muted">{% translate 'Choose a doctor and a day, then click "View schedule".' %}</p>
  {% endif %}

  {# 3. the booking dialog, only if the URL contains &book=... #}
  {% if booking %}
  {% include "fragments/booking.html" %}
  {% endif %}
{% endblock %}

The main page. Three sections: selecting a doctor and a day, the calendar, and the booking window.

  • Lines 17–36: Selecting a doctor and a day: a GET form (example 17), which reloads the page with [?doctorId=...&day=...] in the URL. The day is a [type="date"] field: the browser displays a calendar and sends the date in [yyyy-mm-dd] format, regardless of how it displays it ([30/09/2026] in French); the initial value ([value]) is written in this same format;
  • lines 39–44: for a patient who already has an upcoming appointment, why there is no “Book” button, with a link to “My area”;
  • Lines 70–76: The slot status: Free (in green), the patient’s name (in blue for an appointment booked by the logged-in patient, in gray otherwise), or “Booked.” The template does not determine anything: [row.patient] is only displayed if the user has permission to view that name;
  • lines 84–86: “Book” is a simple link: it reopens the page with the reservation window for that time slot ([row.book_url]). It does not modify anything: a GET is sufficient;
  • lines 88–97: “Cancel” modifies data: it is a POST form (example 21), with its anti-CSRF token, the appointment to be canceled, and information to return to the same page (the doctor, the day). The [data-confirmation] attribute causes the page’s script to request confirmation; its text is represented by [{% translate %}], enclosed in single quotes within the attribute, which is itself enclosed in double quotes;
  • lines 112–114: the booking window, if URL requests it (and if the time slot is bookable).

docs.title: 11.18.3.3. templates/persons/list.html
docs.text:
{% extends "layout.html" %}
{% comment %}
  =========================================================================
  templates/persons/list.html - the list of the doctors OR of the clients (ADMIN).
  A single template for both: the texts specific to each one arrive in
  [texts], and [section] ("doctors" or "clients") gives the start of the names of the
  routes (see web/views/persons.py).
  =========================================================================
{% endcomment %}
{% load i18n %}

{% block content %}
  <div class="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center mb-3">
    <h4 class="mb-0">{{ texts.title }}</h4>
    <a class="btn btn-primary" href="{{ add_url }}">{{ texts.add }}</a>
  </div>

  <div class="card p-3">
    {% if persons %}
    <table class="table table-hover align-middle mb-0">
      <thead>
        <tr>
          <th>{% translate "Title" %}</th>
          <th>{% translate "First name" %}</th>
          <th>{% translate "Last name" %}</th>
          <th>{% translate "Login" %}</th>
          <th></th>
        </tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        {# person.account.login: the account, loaded by the same query (select_related) #}
        {% for person in persons %}
        <tr>
          <td>{{ person.title }}</td>
          <td>{{ person.first_name }}</td>
          <td>{{ person.last_name }}</td>
          <td><code>{{ person.account.login }}</code></td>
          <td class="text-end">
            <div class="d-inline-flex gap-2">
              {# section|add:"_edit": "doctors_edit", the name of the route #}
              <a class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-primary"
                 href="{% url section|add:'_edit' person.id %}">{% translate "Edit" %}</a>
              {# data-confirmation: a confirmation dialog will open before the form is sent (see static/js/app.js) #}
              <form method="post" action="{% url section|add:'_delete' person.id %}" class="m-0"
                    data-confirmation="{{ texts.confirm_delete }}">
                {% csrf_token %}
                <button type="submit" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-danger">{% translate "Delete" %}</button>
              </form>
            </div>
          </td>
        </tr>
        {% endfor %}
      </tbody>
    </table>
    {% else %}
    <p class="text-muted mb-0">{{ texts.empty }}</p>
    {% endif %}
  </div>
{% endblock %}

The list of doctors or clients: the text specific to each one is stored in the variable [texts], and the route names are generated from the section name: [section|add:'_edit'] yields [doctors_edit] or [clients_edit] (the filter [add] adds two numbers or, as in this case, concatenates two strings). [{% url %}] thus accepts, as a route name, a calculated expression followed by the route parameters ([person.id]). [person.account.login]: the account login, loaded along with the list (layer DAO), and stored with it in the cache. The Delete button is a POST form, with confirmation.

docs.title: 11.18.3.4. templates/persons/form.html
docs.text:
{% extends "layout.html" %}
{% comment %}
  =========================================================================
  templates/persons/form.html - creation OR update of a doctor or
  a client (ADMIN), with the PersonForm form.

  When the input is refused (empty field, login already taken...), the view displays
  THIS page again, and the template shows:
    - the values already entered (except the password);
    - the faulty fields framed in red (Bootstrap class "is-invalid");
    - under a field refused by the validation, its message;
    - the error message of the page, AT THE BOTTOM of the page (error_zone tag).
  The form is sent to the URL of the page itself (no action attribute).
  =========================================================================
{% endcomment %}
{% load i18n %}

{% block content %}
<div class="row justify-content-center">
  <div class="col-md-8 col-lg-6">
    <div class="card p-4">
      <h5 class="card-title mb-3">{{ page_title }}</h5>

      <form method="post" novalidate>
        {% csrf_token %}
        {# title, first name, last name: a fragment common to three forms #}
        {% include "macros.html#identity" %}

        <h6 class="mt-4 text-muted">{% translate "User account" %}</h6>
        {{ form.login.as_field_group }}
        {# never pre-filled: the password never goes back to the browser #}
        {{ form.password.as_field_group }}
        {# in update mode only: the version of the record, in a hidden field (the optimistic lock) #}
        {% if form.version %}{{ form.version }}{% endif %}

        <div class="d-flex gap-2 mt-4">
          <button type="submit" class="btn btn-primary">{% translate "Save" %}</button>
          <a class="btn btn-secondary" href="{{ list_url }}">{% translate "Back to the list" %}</a>
        </div>
      </form>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
{% endblock %}

Creating or modifying a doctor or a client using the [PersonForm] form.

  • Line 24: a POST form without the [action] attribute: it is sent to the URL of the page itself ([/doctors/add] or [/doctors/3/edit]). [novalidate] disables browser validation ([required], [maxlength]...) when the form is submitted: the server performs the validation, and its result is authoritative (example 19);
  • line 27: title, first name, and last name, via the fragment [identity];
  • lines 30–32: the username and password, which are never pre-filled. Their tooltips differ between creation and modification (depending on the form builder);
  • line 34: for editing only, the hidden version field (the optimistic lock). [{{ form.version }}] populates the input field alone, without a label: [<input type="hidden" name="version" value="1" id="id_version">]. When creating a record, the form does not have a [version] field: the variable is empty, and the test evaluates to false.

Errors in the form itself that do not involve any fields ([non_field_errors], example 19) do not need to be displayed: the form does not generate any, and an invalid anti-CSRF token is rejected before the view (the 419 page).

docs.text:
{% extends "layout.html" %}
{% comment %}
  =========================================================================
  templates/registration.html - "Create a patient account" (public page, see
  web/views/registration.py), with the RegistrationForm form. Same identity
  fields as the ADMIN form (identity fragment), but the login and the
  password are required, with confirmation. No captcha HERE: this page
  is only reached after typing the one of the
  authentication page ("Create a patient account" button).
  =========================================================================
{% endcomment %}
{% load i18n %}

{% block content %}
<div class="row justify-content-center">
  <div class="col-md-8 col-lg-6">
    <div class="card p-4">
      <h5 class="card-title mb-1">{% translate "Create a patient account" %}</h5>
      <p class="text-muted small mb-3">{% translate "With this account you can book your own appointments." %}</p>

      <form method="post" action="{% url 'registration' %}" novalidate>
        {% csrf_token %}
        {% include "macros.html#identity" %}

        <h6 class="mt-4 text-muted">{% translate "User account" %}</h6>
        {{ form.login.as_field_group }}
        {# the password and its confirmation, side by side #}
        <div class="row g-3">
          <div class="col-sm-6">{{ form.password.as_field_group }}</div>
          <div class="col-sm-6">{{ form.confirmation.as_field_group }}</div>
        </div>

        <div class="d-flex gap-2 mt-3">
          <button type="submit" class="btn btn-primary">{% translate "Create my account" %}</button>
          <a class="btn btn-secondary" href="{% url 'login' %}">{% translate "Back to login" %}</a>
        </div>
      </form>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
{% endblock %}

Creating a patient account: the identity fields, followed by the username, password, and password confirmation—all required fields—side by side (lines 28–31). The password help text specifies the minimum length: “At least 6 characters.” There is no CAPTCHA here: you can only reach this page after entering the CAPTCHA from the login page.

docs.title: 11.18.3.6. templates/area.html
docs.text:
{% extends "layout.html" %}
{% comment %}
  =========================================================================
  templates/area.html - "My area": the home page of the patient (USER role),
  displayed just after they log in.
    - two options: [Manage my account] and [View a schedule];
    - their upcoming appointment, if they have one, with the means to cancel it.
  =========================================================================
{% endcomment %}
{% load i18n %}

{% block content %}
  <h4 class="mb-3">{% blocktranslate %}Hello {{ patient }}{% endblocktranslate %}</h4>

  <div class="row g-3 mb-4">
    <div class="col-sm-6">
      <a class="card p-4 h-100 text-decoration-none option-card" href="{% url 'account' %}">
        <h5 class="mb-1">{% translate "Manage my account" %}</h5>
        <span class="text-muted">{% translate "Change my details or password, or delete my account." %}</span>
      </a>
    </div>
    <div class="col-sm-6">
      <a class="card p-4 h-100 text-decoration-none option-card" href="{% url 'schedule' %}">
        <h5 class="mb-1">{% translate "View a schedule" %}</h5>
        <span class="text-muted">{% translate "See a doctor's schedule and book a slot." %}</span>
      </a>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="card p-3">
    <h5>{% translate "My appointment" %}</h5>
    {% comment %}
      normally only one (rule "one upcoming appointment at a time"), but the page
      can display several. {% for %} ... {% empty %}: a loop, and what
      is displayed if the list is empty; forloop.last: last element?
    {% endcomment %}
    {% for appointment in appointments %}
    <div class="d-flex flex-wrap justify-content-between align-items-center gap-2 py-2{% if not forloop.last %} border-bottom{% endif %}">
      <div>
        <div class="fw-semibold">{{ appointment.day }}, {{ appointment.time_range }}</div>
        <div class="text-muted">
          <span>{{ appointment.doctor }}</span> -
          <a href="{{ appointment.schedule_url }}">{% translate "see in the schedule" %}</a>
        </div>
      </div>
      <form method="post" action="{% url 'area_cancel' %}" class="m-0"
            data-confirmation="{% translate 'Cancel this appointment?' %}">
        {% csrf_token %}
        <input type="hidden" name="appointmentId" value="{{ appointment.id }}">
        <button type="submit" class="btn btn-outline-danger">{% translate "Cancel this appointment" %}</button>
      </form>
    </div>
    {% empty %}
    <p class="text-muted mb-0">{% translate "You have no upcoming appointment." %}</p>
    {% endfor %}
  </div>
{% endblock %}

“My area,” the patient’s home page: two large cards (“Manage my account,” “View a schedule”), and their upcoming appointment.

  • line 13: [{% blocktranslate %}Hello {{ patient }}{% endblocktranslate %}]: a translated text containing a variable ([Bonjour %(patient)s] in the French dictionary);
  • lines 37–55: [{% for %}] ... [{% empty %}] (Example 14) is a loop, followed by what to display if the list is empty. Normally, a patient has at most one upcoming appointment; however, the page is capable of displaying multiple appointments. [forloop.last] (Example 14): the last item has no separator;
  • lines 46–51: each appointment has a cancellation form (POST, with confirmation), which sends only its ID: the server will verify that it belongs to the logged-in patient.

docs.title: 11.18.3.7. templates/account.html
docs.text:
{% extends "layout.html" %}
{% comment %}
  =========================================================================
  templates/account.html - "Manage my account" (USER role). Two independent
  forms on the same page:
    1. the update (identity, login, optional new password), with
       the MyAccountForm form;
    2. the deletion of the account - which also cancels its appointments: a
       form written by hand.
  Both require the CURRENT password (current_password field).
  =========================================================================
{% endcomment %}
{% load i18n %}

{% block content %}
<div class="row justify-content-center">
  <div class="col-md-8 col-lg-6">

    {# 1. update; novalidate: it is the SERVER that validates (see example 19) #}
    <div class="card p-4 mb-4">
      <h5 class="card-title mb-3">{% translate "Manage my account" %}</h5>

      <form method="post" action="{% url 'account' %}" novalidate>
        {% csrf_token %}
        {% include "macros.html#identity" %}

        <h6 class="mt-4 text-muted">{% translate "User account" %}</h6>
        {{ form.login.as_field_group }}
        <div class="row g-3">
          <div class="col-sm-6">{{ form.password.as_field_group }}</div>
          <div class="col-sm-6">{{ form.confirmation.as_field_group }}</div>
        </div>
        {{ form.current_password.as_field_group }}
        {# the version of the record: a hidden field (the optimistic lock) #}
        {{ form.version }}

        <div class="d-flex gap-2 mt-4">
          <button type="submit" class="btn btn-primary">{% translate "Save" %}</button>
          <a class="btn btn-secondary" href="{% url 'area' %}">{% translate "Back to my area" %}</a>
        </div>
      </form>
    </div>

    {% comment %}
      2. deletion. The password field has the same NAME as that of the first
      form (current_password), but another id: two elements of the same
      page cannot have the same id
    {% endcomment %}
    <div class="card p-4 border-danger">
      <h5 class="card-title text-danger mb-1">{% translate "Delete my account" %}</h5>
      <p class="text-muted small">{% translate "Your account will be permanently deleted, together with all your appointments." %}</p>
      <form method="post" action="{% url 'account_delete' %}" class="d-flex flex-wrap gap-2 align-items-end"
            data-confirmation="{% translate 'Permanently delete your account? Any appointment you have will be cancelled.' %}">
        {% csrf_token %}
        <div class="flex-grow-1">
          <label class="form-label" for="delete_password">{% translate "Current password" %}</label>
          <input id="delete_password" name="current_password" type="password" maxlength="72"
                 autocomplete="current-password" required class="form-control">
        </div>
        <button type="submit" class="btn btn-danger">{% translate "Delete my account" %}</button>
      </form>
    </div>

  </div>
</div>
{% endblock %}

“Manage my account”: two independent forms on the same page.

  • Lines 20–42: the update, using the [MyAccountForm] form: the identity fields, the login, the new password and its confirmation (optional), the current password (required), and the hidden version field;
  • Lines 49–62: Account deletion, a handwritten form with its own field for the current password and a confirmation field. The field has the same name as the one on the first form ([current_password]), but a different ID: two elements on a page cannot have the same ID, as indicated by the attribute [for] for a label. The two forms are independent: the browser sends only the fields from the form whose button was clicked.

docs.text: The [static] folder contains the files that the server sends as-is (example 15): [Bootstrap] ([lib/bootstrap], the stylesheet alone, and its license), a stylesheet, and a script. docs.title: 11.19.2. static/js/app.js
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// static/js/app.js - the ONLY JavaScript of the application.
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The whole application works without JavaScript. This script adds a
// convenience: before sending a form that carries the attribute
// data-confirmation="...", a modal dialog asks "Are you sure?"
// (the dialog itself is in the page: templates/fragments/confirmation.html).
// If JavaScript is disabled, the form is simply sent without
// confirmation - nothing breaks ("progressive enhancement" principle).
//
// Why not window.confirm()? Its box cannot be styled, and its
// buttons stay in the language of the browser, not in that of the page.
// =========================================================================

(() => {
  const modal = document.getElementById('confirmation-modal');
  if (!modal) {
    return;
  }
  const message = document.getElementById('confirmation-modal-message');
  const noButton = modal.querySelector('.modal-footer [data-action="no"]');

  let pendingForm = null; // the form to send if the user confirms
  let previousFocus = null; // the element to give the focus back to on closing

  function open(form) {
    pendingForm = form;
    previousFocus = document.activeElement;
    // textContent (and not innerHTML): the message is displayed as TEXT,
    // never interpreted as HTML
    message.textContent = form.dataset.confirmation;
    modal.classList.remove('d-none');
    // the focus goes on "No": an absent-minded press on Enter deletes nothing
    noButton.focus();
  }

  function close() {
    modal.classList.add('d-none');
    pendingForm = null;
    if (previousFocus) {
      previousFocus.focus();
    }
  }

  // 1. we intercept the sending of the forms to confirm
  document.querySelectorAll('form[data-confirmation]').forEach((form) => {
    form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
      event.preventDefault();
      open(form);
    });
  });

  // 2. the buttons of the dialog (Yes / No / close cross)
  modal.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
    const action = event.target.closest('[data-action]')?.dataset.action;
    if (action === 'yes') {
      const form = pendingForm;
      close();
      // form.submit() sends the form WITHOUT triggering the
      // 'submit' event again: no new confirmation request
      form.submit();
    } else if (action === 'no') {
      close();
    } else if (event.target.classList.contains('modal')) {
      close(); // click on the grey background, outside the dialog
    }
  });

  // 3. keyboard: Escape closes the dialog; Tab stays INSIDE the dialog
  //    (otherwise the focus would go to the greyed-out page, behind)
  modal.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
    if (event.key === 'Escape') {
      close();
    } else if (event.key === 'Tab') {
      const buttons = [...modal.querySelectorAll('button')];
      const first = buttons[0];
      const last = buttons[buttons.length - 1];
      if (event.shiftKey && document.activeElement === first) {
        event.preventDefault();
        last.focus();
      } else if (!event.shiftKey && document.activeElement === last) {
        event.preventDefault();
        first.focus();
      }
    }
  });
})();

The only [JavaScript] in the application—the one from Example 21—with a few additions. The entire application works without [JavaScript]: this script adds convenience by providing a confirmation before submitting a form that carries the [data-confirmation] attribute. If [JavaScript] is disabled, the form submits without confirmation: nothing breaks (principle of progressive enhancement).

  • Lines 15–19: The script is a function called as soon as it is defined ([(() => { ... })()]); its variables are not visible to the rest of the page. Without a confirmation window on the page, it does nothing;
  • Lines 26–35: Opening the window: the form to be submitted if the user confirms is stored, and the form’s message is displayed in the window. [textContent], not [innerHTML]: the message is displayed as text and is never interpreted as HTML. Focus moves to the “No” button: accidentally pressing Enter does not delete anything;
  • lines 37–43: closing the window; focus returns to the element that had it previously;
  • lines 46–51: the submission of each form to be confirmed is intercepted ([preventDefault] prevents it), and the window opens. The [submit] event occurs only after the browser’s validations: the current password, which is required ([required]) in the account deletion form, is required before the prompt;
  • lines 54–67: the buttons in the window. A single handler for the entire window: [closest('[data-action]')] finds the clicked button or the element containing it; [?.] ensures [undefined] returns no error if none match. “Yes” submits the form via [form.submit()], which does not trigger the [submit] event: no new confirmation prompt appears. Clicking on the grayed-out background outside the window closes it;
  • lines 71–86: the keyboard. Esc closes the window; the Tab key moves the focus from one button to another without leaving the window (otherwise, it would move to the grayed-out page behind it): this is what users who navigate with the keyboard and screen readers expect.

docs.title: 12. Conclusion
docs.text:
This document described the development of a MVC web application using the [Django] framework: an application whose HTML pages are generated by the server using [Django] templates, without a browser-side [JavaScript] framework. He followed the [Symfony] course step by step, which itself builds upon the courses [Laravel], [Flask], [Spring MVC], [ASP.NET Core MVC], and [NestJS]: views and routing to templates, forms, internationalization, security, and data access, followed by a comprehensive case study.

The same 28 examples and the same application were thus written using seven frameworks: in [TypeScript], in [C#], in [Java], twice in [PHP], and twice in [Python]. The concepts are the same; only the names and mechanisms differ. The correspondences between [Symfony] and [Django]:

[Symfony][Django]core ([src/Kernel.php]), bundles, service container, dependency injectionsettings ([config/settings.py]), applications ([INSTALLED_APPS]), imported modules, providers ([functools.cache])[composer.json], folder [vendor], [php bin/console][requirements.txt], virtual environment ([.venv]), [python manage.py]file [.env], folder [config/packages] (files YAML), [%env(...)%]file [config/settings.py] (from [Python]), environment variables ([os.environ]), file [.env] read by us[#[Route]] attributes of the controllerslists [urlpatterns] ([path], [re_path], [include]), named routes, [app_name][render], [redirectToRoute], [generateUrl]; [path] in the views[render], [redirect], [reverse]; [{% url %}] in the templatesobject [Request], [requirements] ([{id<\d+>}]), argument resolvers, [#[MapQueryString]]object [HttpRequest] ([GET], [POST], [headers], [COOKIES]), converters ([<int:id>]), forms as validatorsValidator component (attribute constraints), Form component (types, [handleRequest], [isValid])[django.forms] forms (fields, validators, [clean], [error_messages], [is_valid], [cleaned_data])form theme [Bootstrap] 5rendering engine ([FORM_RENDERER]), field template, [as_field_group]views [Twig], [{{ }}], [{% for %}], [{% if %}]Templates for DTL, [{{ }}], [{% for %}] ... [{% empty %}], [{% if %}][{% extends %}] and blocks, [{% include %}], macros[{% extends %}] and blocks, [{% include %}], named fragments ([{% partialdef %}])global variables, extensions [Twig] (functions, filters)context processors, tag libraries ([templatetags]: filters, simple tags, inclusion tags)flash messages ([addFlash], [app.flashes]), file-based sessions[messages] application (signed cookie), sessions (files, signed cookie, database...)kernel event listeners ([kernel.request], [kernel.controller], [kernel.response]...)middleware ([__call__], [process_view], [process_exception]), signals ([request_started], [request_finished])headphones: [kernel.exception], [HttpException], [createNotFoundException][Http404], [PermissionDenied], [BadRequest], views [handler404]..., [process_exception]firewalls, authenticators, [access_control], [#[IsGranted]], votersauthentication and access control middleware written by us, decorators; or the [django.contrib.auth] applicationanti-CSRF token for the Form component, [csrf_token()], [isCsrfTokenValid][CsrfViewMiddleware] middleware, [{% csrf_token %}] tag, [CSRF_FAILURE_VIEW] (403 response, or 419 in our application)component [RateLimiter]a limiter written to the cacheFile [translations] (YAML, ICU), filter [trans], [TranslatorInterface]file [locale] ([gettext]: [.po], [.mo]), [gettext], [gettext_lazy], [ngettext], [{% translate %}], [{% blocktranslate %}][intl] extension: [IntlDateFormatter], [NumberFormatter]Formatting based on the active language (filter [date], [floatformat]), [Babel]Cache component (PSR-6 and contracts), Lock componentcache for [Django] ([LocMemCache], [FileBasedCache]...), [get_or_set][Doctrine]: Data Mapper entities, entity manager, DQL, and QueryBuilderORM from [Django]: Active Record models, managers ([objects]), [QuerySet], [select_related], [F()][wrapInTransaction(...)], [flush][transaction.atomic()], [select_for_update()][#[ORM\Version]], managed by [Doctrine] ([OptimisticLockException])[update()], version-dependent ([filter(version=...)]), written to the DAO layer[php -S localhost:8000 -t public], or [symfony server:start][python manage.py runserver]

Regarding [Symfony], the key points to note are:

  • the [Django] application is loaded once, when the server starts up, then remains in memory and processes all requests (example 01): the objects created at startup (settings, routes, middleware, services) are shared by all requests. It’s simple and fast, but it requires distinguishing between what belongs to the application (shared, and therefore without state specific to a request) and what belongs to a request (the [request] object, the local variables of the views), and to remember that a production server runs multiple processes, which share only what is stored outside of them (the database, the file cache);
  • no service container: services are [Python] modules that are imported, and provider functions that create a unique object on the first request. A module’s dependencies are visible in its [import] files; replacing them for testing purposes is done via a setting (example 06);
  • The configuration is a [Python] or [config/settings.py] file: a sequence of assignments that can be calculated, commented on, or split up. The [python manage.py diffsettings] command displays what differs from the default values;
  • The processing of a request passes through a list of middleware components in the order specified in the [MIDDLEWARE] list, and then in reverse order for the response: this is where language settings, anti-CSRF protection, authentication, access control, and error pages are handled. The mechanism is simpler than the kernel events in [Symfony]: the order of the list is the order of execution;
  • Views are simple functions that receive a request and return a response; decorators ([@require_POST], [@registration_pass_required]) wrap them to add control. We have written several of them, and even a class whose methods are views ([PersonManagement]), without requiring anything specific from [Django];
  • Forms are objects, described by classes: fields, value conversion, validators, input redisply, and error messages. They are rendered using templates that can be replaced (a rendering engine, a field template): fields throughout the application are rendered in the same way, using the classes from [Bootstrap] and accessibility attributes;
  • [Django] comes “ready to use”: sessions, messages, translations, cache, anti-CSRF protection, static files, ORM—everything is included, documented in one place, with no additional installation required. We’ve added only three libraries: the [MySQL] driver, [PyJWT], and [bcrypt]. The very comprehensive [django.contrib.auth] authentication application was left out: the case study database has its own users, and we wanted JWT tokens, just like the other versions of the application. Writing the authentication code from scratch, in about a hundred lines, demonstrated exactly what it does;
  • the ORM from [Django] follows the Active Record pattern: a model is a class linked to a table, where each object knows how to save itself. More straightforward than the Data Mapper in [Doctrine], it also works very well with an existing database ([managed = False], where table and column names are predefined). Its lazy [QuerySet], [select_related], [F()] expressions, and the conditional [update()] statements allow you to write efficient and safe queries, and the development mode console displays every SQL command sent to the database;
  • DTL templates use a deliberately limited language: no arithmetic, no function calls with parameters. A template can only display the data provided to it: this is both a constraint and a guarantee that drives logic into views and view models. Any missing information is added via filters and tags written in [Python]. Templates automatically escape whatever they display.

The case study shows that a classic HTML application, without the essential [JavaScript], remains a simple and robust solution: each page is a URL, the browser’s “Back” button works, and the server controls everything. The minimal use of [JavaScript] (confirmation windows) enhances the user experience without being necessary for functionality. [Django] can also support more interactive applications without straying from its templates (using the [htmx] library, for example, the named fragments from [Django] 6 work very well) or with a browser-side [JavaScript] framework, to which it provides a API JSON ([Django REST framework], [Django Ninja]): this will be covered in other documents.

For further information, please refer to the documentation for [Django] (docs.djangoproject.com, translated into French), particularly the pages dedicated to views and URL, forms, templates, middleware, internationalization, ORM, and security, its tutorial (which covers the administration interface and migrations, which are not covered here), the [Python] tutorial (docs.python.org/fr), and compare this application to its sister applications [Symfony], [Laravel], [Flask], [Spring MVC], [ASP.NET Core MVC], and [NestJS].

docs.title: 6. Data Scopes
docs.text:
A web application serves many users at once, and each user makes numerous requests. Data can therefore be shared at several levels, known as its scope:

  • application scope: the data is shared by all users throughout the application’s lifetime (the list of doctors, for example);
  • request scope: the data exists only for the duration of a request (a template’s model, the logged-in user as identified for that request);
  • session scope: the data is specific to a user and must persist from one request to the next (the selected language, a shopping cart);
  • client scope: data stored in the browser itself, in a cookie.

In [Python], these scopes take on a different nature than what readers of the [Symfony] course are familiar with, because the application remains in memory from one request to the next (Example 01). Data stored in a module variable (examples 06, 20, and 21) naturally has application scope: this is convenient and very fast. But this scope has two limitations. First, it lasts only for the duration of the process: a server restart clears it. Second, it is process-specific: in production, multiple application processes are typically launched (several “workers” of [gunicorn], for example), or even multiple servers behind a load balancer, and each would have its own copy of the data. Data that truly needs to be shared and persist over time is therefore stored in a database or in a shared cache ([Redis], [Memcached], which [Django] knows how to use via its [CACHES] setting). In exchange for speed, sharing requires strict discipline: a process handles multiple requests at once, across multiple threads, and shared data modified by one process is visible to all; it must be protected by a lock (example 20), and data belonging to a specific user must never be stored there.

In [Django], each scope has its own container:

ScopeContainerLifetimeapplicationa module variable (a single process), the [Django] cache ([CACHES] setting), or the databasethe one for the process; the duration selected for the cache; no limit for the databasequerythe [HttpRequest] object, to which a middleware component can add attributes (Example 12); the view’s local variablesthe processing of a querysessionthe session ([request.session], application [django.contrib.sessions]), maintained by the server, retrieved via a cookietwo weeks by default (setting [SESSION_COOKIE_AGE])clienta cookie ([set_cookie], example 22), either in plain text or signed ([set_signed_cookie])the cookie’s specified duration

The session for [Django] is, by default, a server-side session, like those for [Java] ([JSESSIONID]) or [PHP] ([PHPSESSID]): its data is stored on the server, and the browser only holds the identifier—a random number that is impossible to guess—in the [sessionid] cookie. The [SESSION_ENGINE] setting determines where the data is stored: in the database (the default option, in a table named [django_session]), in the cache, in files (the option used in our example), or even, as in the case of [Flask], entirely in a signed cookie on the client’s device.

[SessionMiddleware] retrieves the browser session at the start of the request using the [sessionid] cookie and stores it in [request.session]; at the end of the request, it saves the session if it has been modified and sends the cookie. It only actually reads the data upon the first access to [request.session]: a view that doesn’t use it incurs no cost. The second middleware is ours (see below);

docs.title: 6.1.2. The objects: scopes/counters.py and scopes/middleware.py
docs.text:
# scopes/counters.py: APPLICATION scope, counters shared by all the
# requests of all the users

import threading
from collections import Counter

# a Counter: a dictionary {key: number}, whose absent keys are worth 0. It is
# created when the module is loaded, and lives as long as the server process
_counters = Counter()
_lock = threading.Lock()


# one more number under the [key] key; += is not an atomic operation: two
# simultaneous requests could read the same value. The lock prevents it
def next_value(key: str) -> int:
    with _lock:
        _counters[key] += 1
        return _counters[key]
  • Line 5: the class [Counter] from the module [collections]: a dictionary whose values are numbers, and whose missing keys are set to 0;
  • Lines 9–10: the counters and their lock, created when the module is loaded; they exist for as long as the server process runs. This is the application scope;
  • lines 15–18: one more number under a key. The operation [+=] is not atomic: it reads the value, increments it, then writes it, and two simultaneous requests could read the same value—a visit would be lost. The lock (example 20) prevents this.
# scopes/middleware.py: REQUEST scope, the information of a request

from dataclasses import dataclass

from django.utils import timezone

from . import counters


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RequestInfo:
    number: int
    start: str


# the middleware creates ONE RequestInfo object per request, and stores it in the request:
# the view and the template find it through request.info. It disappears with it
class RequestInfoMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        request.info = RequestInfo(
            # one number per created OBJECT, taken from a counter common to all the requests
            number=counters.next_value("instances"),
            # the time, with its milliseconds
            start=timezone.localtime().strftime("%H:%M:%S.%f")[:-3])
        return self.get_response(request)
  • lines 10–13: request scope information: a number and the request time;
  • lines 18–28: the middleware creates a [RequestInfo] object for each request and stores it in the request (Example 12). The number is taken from a counter shared by all requests (the previous module, under a different key); therefore, each object has a different number. The time is written including milliseconds: [%f] represents the microseconds (six digits), from which [[:-3]] removes the last three (a string slice: all characters except the last three). The object is deleted along with the request.

[Django] has no service container, and therefore no “request-scope service”: it is the request itself that carries the objects in this scope. Readers of the [Symfony] course will recall that it was the opposite: in [PHP], every service was request-scoped, and a cache was required to obtain application scope.

docs.title: 6.1.3. Signed Cookies
docs.text:
A cookie is a piece of data entrusted to the client, which can read and modify it. For a cookie to be trustworthy, it simply needs to be signed: its value travels in plaintext, but it is followed by a signature that only the server knows how to calculate, because it depends on a secret key. A value modified by the client no longer has the correct signature, and the server rejects it. [Django] handles this for us: [response.set_signed_cookie(name, value)] sets a signed cookie, and [request.get_signed_cookie(name, default=...)] returns its value if the signature is correct; otherwise, it returns the default value. The signature is a HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code): a hash of the value (SHA-256), calculated using the application’s secret key ([SECRET_KEY], example 01), and a “salt” specific to the cookie’s name. [Django] adds the signature date, which allows an outdated cookie to be rejected ([get_signed_cookie(..., max_age=3600)]). The verification process compares the signatures in a time that does not depend on the number of identical characters: a standard comparison would stop at the first differing character, and an attacker could, by measuring the response time, guess the signature character by character. The [django.core.signing] module offers the same functions for signing any data ([signing.dumps], [signing.loads]): it is this module that signs the flash messages in Example 20.

This is the principle behind the JWT token, which the next chapter will use for authentication.

docs.title: 6.1.4. The view: scopes/views.py
docs.text:
# scopes/views.py: the four scopes of data

from django.shortcuts import render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET

from . import counters


@require_GET
def scopes(request):
    # APPLICATION: the shared counter
    total = counters.next_value("visits")
    # SESSION: data specific to THIS browser, kept by the SERVER (a
    # file of var/sessions), found thanks to the session cookie; the session
    # is used like a dictionary
    request.session["visits"] = request.session.get("visits", 0) + 1
    # CLIENT: data kept by the BROWSER in cookies, sent back to the
    # server with each request; one in plain text, the other signed
    my_visits = int(request.COOKIES.get("myVisits", 0)) + 1
    # get_signed_cookie: the value if the signature is the right one; default otherwise
    my_visits_signed = int(request.get_signed_cookie("myVisitsSigned", default=0)) + 1
    response = render(request, "scopes/scopes.html", {
        "total": total,
        "instance": request.info.number,
        "session_visits": request.session["visits"],
        "my_visits": my_visits,
        "my_visits_signed": my_visits_signed,
    })
    response.set_cookie("myVisits", str(my_visits))
    # set_signed_cookie: the value, followed by a signature computed with SECRET_KEY
    response.set_signed_cookie("myVisitsSigned", str(my_visits_signed))
    return response
  • line 12: the application scope;
  • line 16: the session scope. [request.session] is used like a dictionary: [get(key, default)] reads a value, and the assignment writes it. [Django] saves the session at the end of the request. Values must be convertible to JSON (strings, numbers, lists, dictionaries): this is how they are stored;
  • Lines 19–21: the client scope, with two cookies. [request.COOKIES] is the dictionary of cookies sent by the browser. Their values are strings provided by the browser and may therefore be missing or invalid: [int] converts them (a cookie named [myVisits=abc] would throw a [ValueError] exception here and result in a 500 error; a real application would verify the value; see example 07). The value of the signed cookie is accepted only if its signature is correct;
  • lines 22–28: the template context;
  • lines 29–31: To set a cookie, you need the response object: [render] constructs it (example 13), then [set_cookie] and [set_signed_cookie] add the cookies to it. Without an expiration time ([max_age]), a cookie lasts until the browser is closed (this is a “session” cookie, as defined by browsers).

docs.text:
<!doctype html>
{% load static %}
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Scopes</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css' %}">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3">
    <h1 class="h3">The scopes of data</h1>
    {# request.info: the object stored in the request by the middleware; it is the same as the view's one #}
    <ul>
      <li>application: {{ total }} visit(s) to the site, all browsers combined</li>
      <li>request: object no. {{ instance }} (no. {{ request.info.number }} in the template),
        request received at {{ request.info.start }}</li>
      {# request.session: the session, also accessible in the templates #}
      <li>session: {{ session_visits }} visit(s) from this browser ({{ request.session.visits }} in the template)</li>
      <li>client: {{ my_visits }} visit(s) from this browser (plain cookie),
        {{ my_visits_signed }} (signed cookie)</li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</body>
</html>
  • line 16: [request.info], the object stored in the request by the middleware: this is the same [RequestInfo] object as the one in the view; the template displays its number, which must be the one received from the view;
  • line 19: the session is also accessible in the templates, via [request.session].

docs.title: 6.1.6. Execution
docs.text:
After three visits in a browser:

The request object number is greater than the number of visits: on the first visit, the browser also requested the site icon ([/favicon.ico]), which does not exist. This request, which resulted in a 404 error, passed through the middleware and therefore had its own object, [RequestInfo].

Let’s track the requests with [curl], which acts as a first browser by storing its cookies in the file [a.txt] (the server has just been started):

curl -i -c a.txt -b a.txt http://localhost:8000/

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Vary: Cookie
Set-Cookie: myVisits=1; Path=/
Set-Cookie: myVisitsSigned=1:1xAspT:iu2OlkhoUcBt0QBGkt_Gkjm2PoYfUeS6WSsO5KEHt0k; Path=/
Set-Cookie: sessionid=ij72qd9hyuhwoqlplawuxycwg6ggccsq; expires=Sun, 11 Oct 2026 17:38:23 GMT; HttpOnly; Max-Age=1209600; Path=/; SameSite=Lax
...
      <li>application: 1 visit(s) to the site, all browsers combined</li>
      <li>request: object no. 1 (no. 1 in the template),
        request received at 19:38:23.123</li>
      <li>session: 1 visit(s) from this browser (1 in the template)</li>
      <li>client: 1 visit(s) from this browser (plain cookie),
        1 (signed cookie)</li>
...

The response sets three cookies. The first, [myVisits], contains the value in plain text. The second, [myVisitsSigned], contains the same value, followed by a colon, the signature date (in base 62), and the signature itself. The third, [sessionid], is the session ID, valid for two weeks ([Max-Age=1209600] seconds), [HttpOnly], and [SameSite=Lax] (example 20). The session data is stored in a file on the server, [var/sessions/sessionidij72qd9hyuhwoqlplawuxycwg6ggccsq], whose name is derived from the identifier:

eyJ2aXNpdHMiOjF9:1xAspT:mYytMt_81vJlDI_gaKudIqPgoxAvrGUZbnk578MZr3I

Here we can recognize the format of the signed data from [Django]: the data, the date, and the signature. The data is from JSON, encoded in Base64: [eyJ2aXNpdHMiOjF9] decodes to [{"visits":1}]. The server even signs its own session files: a file modified by a third party would be rejected. A second visit, with the same cookies:

curl -i -c a.txt -b a.txt http://localhost:8000/

...
Set-Cookie: myVisits=2; Path=/
Set-Cookie: myVisitsSigned=2:1xAspT:E9lE-GK-yE7WfT5Ak58h2tufzXQ5vLWcWz5UBAS-dLA; Path=/
Set-Cookie: sessionid=ij72qd9hyuhwoqlplawuxycwg6ggccsq; expires=Sun, 11 Oct 2026 17:38:23 GMT; HttpOnly; Max-Age=1209600; Path=/; SameSite=Lax
...
      <li>application: 2 visit(s) to the site, all browsers combined</li>
      <li>request: object no. 2 (no. 2 in the template),
        request received at 19:38:23.150</li>
      <li>session: 2 visit(s) from this browser (2 in the template)</li>
      <li>client: 2 visit(s) from this browser (plain cookie),
        2 (signed cookie)</li>
...

The session is the same (same ID); its cookie is sent back because the session has been modified, which extends its lifetime. A second “browser,” with its own cookie file, initially empty:

curl -c b.txt -b b.txt http://localhost:8000/

      <li>application: 3 visit(s) to the site, all browsers combined</li>
      <li>request: object no. 3 (no. 3 in the template),
        request received at 19:38:23.167</li>
      <li>session: 1 visit(s) from this browser (1 in the template)</li>
      <li>client: 1 visit(s) from this browser (plain cookie),
        1 (signed cookie)</li>

The application counter has continued; the session and cookies for the second browser start over at 1. Each request had its own [RequestInfo] object, and in each one, the view and template were the same. Finally, a malicious user forges their own cookies: 1,000 visits in [myVisits], 999 in [myVisitsSigned] (with a fabricated signature), and a session ID of their own invention:

curl -i -b "myVisits=1000;myVisitsSigned=999:abc;sessionid=abc" http://localhost:8000/

...
Set-Cookie: myVisits=1001; Path=/
Set-Cookie: myVisitsSigned=1:1xAspT:iu2OlkhoUcBt0QBGkt_Gkjm2PoYfUeS6WSsO5KEHt0k; Path=/
Set-Cookie: sessionid=l4316xnwacgz81f7yemjar89cfe05jm3; expires=Sun, 11 Oct 2026 17:38:23 GMT; HttpOnly; Max-Age=1209600; Path=/; SameSite=Lax
...
      <li>session: 1 visit(s) from this browser (1 in the template)</li>
      <li>client: 1001 visit(s) from this browser (plain cookie),
        1 (signed cookie)</li>
...

The plaintext cookie was accepted as-is: 1,001 visits. The cookie [myVisitsSigned], however, did not have the correct signature: it was ignored, as if it were missing. Copying the signature from another value (that of [1], for example, next to the value [999]) doesn’t work any better: the signature depends on the value. As for the made-up session ID, it does not refer to any existing session: [Django] ignores it and creates a new session with a new ID that it chooses itself. The user therefore cannot select another user’s session.

Let’s remember the rule: data coming from the client is trustworthy only if it is protected by the server (signed, as here or as with the token in the chapter on authentication, or encrypted); data that has nothing to hide, and whose value is verified by the server (the language in Example 22), can remain in plaintext. A signature guarantees that a value has not been altered, but it does not hide it: a secret must never be entrusted to the client, even if it is signed.

The case study brings them together into a complete, realistic-sized application (nearly 90 files, approximately 5,500 lines, including comments). It was written with the same care as the examples: each file begins with a comment explaining its role, and tricky sections are annotated in the code. Each main folder also contains a file named [README.md] that lists its files. The document’s comments highlight what the examples did not show and refer to them for the rest.

docs.title: 5. Internationalization
docs.text:
An internationalized application displays its text in the user’s language. The case study is in French and English. The principle is simple: the templates contain text marked as “to be translated,” and a dictionary for each language associates each text with its translation. The selected language is stored in a cookie.

[Django] uses [gettext] for this purpose, the translation system from the GNU project, which [Python] also recognizes (the [gettext] module from the standard library), and which is found in many open-source software programs. With [gettext], the key for a text is the text itself, written in the original language: a template written in [{% translate "Home" %}], and the French dictionary associates “Home” with “Accueil.” A page thus remains readable and functional even without a dictionary: the text is displayed in the original language. This differs from versions [Symfony], [Laravel], [Flask], [Spring MVC], [ASP.NET Core MVC], and [NestJS] from the case study, which used abstract keys ([MENU.HOME]). Dictionaries are text files in the [.po] (Portable Object) format, which tools can extract from the code and which translation software can edit; [Django] reads their compiled version, the [.mo] (Machine Object) files. [gettext] can also inflect text into the plural form according to the rules of each language. [Django] is itself translated in this way: it is thanks to its dictionaries that it can display its error messages in French (since Example 08, they have been in English, the default language). The formatting of dates and amounts remains the same as in Example 16.
