docs.title: 9.1.3. The Person model: persons/models.py
docs.text:
# persons/models.py: a row of the [persons] table, a Django MODEL

from django.db import models


# a Django model: a class that inherits from models.Model; each class attribute
# that is a FIELD (models.XxxField) corresponds to a column of the table
class Person(models.Model):
    # the primary key, generated by the database (AUTO_INCREMENT)
    id = models.AutoField(primary_key=True)
    # the VERSION of the row, increased at each modification (see the DAO layer)
    version = models.IntegerField(default=0)
    # the VARCHAR(30) and INT columns
    first_name = models.CharField(max_length=30)
    last_name = models.CharField(max_length=30)
    age = models.IntegerField()

    # Meta: the information about the model itself
    class Meta:
        # the name of the table (by default: persons_person, application_model)
        db_table = "persons"
        # the table already exists (script database/dbpersons.sql): Django does not create it
        managed = False
        # the order of the rows when the query does not specify one
        ordering = ["last_name", "first_name"]

    # the text that represents the object (in the console, the messages...)
    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.first_name} {self.last_name}"

The file is named [models.py]: this is where [Django] looks for the models of an application declared in [INSTALLED_APPS].

  • Line 8: A template is a class that inherits from [models.Model];
  • Line 10: The primary key, generated by the database ([AutoField]: the [AUTO_INCREMENT] of [MySQL]). [Django] would add it automatically if it were not declared (a field [id], of the type chosen by the setting [DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD]); we include it here for clarity. It is equal to [None] until the object has been inserted;
  • line 12: the row version. The ORM from [Django] does not have a built-in optimistic lock: it is written by the DAO layer (see below);
  • lines 14–16: the columns. Each class attribute that is a field in the model ([models.XxxField]) corresponds to the column of the same name; the column type is inferred from the field type ([CharField]: [VARCHAR], of length [max_length]; [IntegerField]: [INT]). As in a form (example 08), the fields are declared as attributes of the class, but they are not the same fields: those in [django.db.models] describe columns, while those in [django.forms] describe form fields;
  • lines 19–25: the inner class [Meta] provides information about the template itself. [db_table]: the table name (otherwise, [Django] would take the application name followed by the model name, [persons_person]). [managed = False]: The table already exists, and [Django] does not manage it: [makemigrations] will not generate any creation or modification migrations for it. [ordering]: the order of rows when a query does not specify one;
  • lines 28–29: the method [__str__] (Example 12) returns the text representing the object: [str(p)], or [{p}] in an f-string, returns [Marie Pélissier].

A model is an ordinary class to which methods and properties can be added. The ORM, on the other hand, populates the attributes based on the lines read and generates the commands SQL from the attributes.

docs.title: 9.1.4. The DAO layer: persons/dao.py
docs.text:
# persons/dao.py: the DAO layer, queries, no business rule

from django.db.models import F

from .models import Person


# SELECT ... FROM persons ORDER BY last_name, first_name. objects: the MANAGER of the model,
# where all the queries start from; all() returns a QuerySet, a query that is only
# executed when its results are read (here, by list)
def list_all() -> list[Person]:
    return list(Person.objects.all())


# SELECT ... FROM persons WHERE id = ?; None if the person does not exist
def read(id: int) -> Person | None:
    return Person.objects.filter(id=id).first()


# a person with the same first and last names, other than [except_id]. filter: the WHERE
# conditions; exclude: the WHERE NOT conditions
def namesake(first_name: str, last_name: str, except_id: int = 0) -> Person | None:
    return Person.objects.filter(first_name=first_name, last_name=last_name).exclude(id=except_id).first()


# INSERT INTO persons ...: create builds the object and saves it
def insert(first_name: str, last_name: str, age: int) -> Person:
    return Person.objects.create(first_name=first_name, last_name=last_name, age=age)


# UPDATE persons SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?: the
# row is modified only if its version has not changed since it was read (OPTIMISTIC
# LOCK). F("version") designates the column itself, in the SQL statement. update
# returns the number of modified rows: 0 if the version has changed
def update(id: int, version: int, first_name: str, last_name: str, age: int) -> bool:
    rows = Person.objects.filter(id=id, version=version).update(
        first_name=first_name, last_name=last_name, age=age, version=F("version") + 1)
    return rows == 1


# DELETE FROM persons WHERE id = ?
def delete(person: Person) -> None:
    person.delete()

The DAO layer contains only queries, with no business rules. Each function begins with [Person.objects], the model manager, from which all queries originate.

  • Lines 11–12: [all()] returns a [QuerySet]: an object that describes a query without executing it. The query is sent to the database only when its results are needed (here, when [list] iterates through them): a [QuerySet] is said to be lazy. It can thus be populated before execution ([filter], [exclude], [order_by]...), with each method returning a new [QuerySet]. The order is that of [Meta.ordering];
  • Lines 16–17: [filter(id=id)] adds the condition [WHERE id = ...]; [first()] executes the query, limited to one row ([LIMIT 1]), and returns the first object, or [None]. ([Person.objects.get(id=id)] would return the object, but would throw the exception [Person.DoesNotExist] if it did not exist, and the shortcut [get_object_or_404], example 03, would return a 404 error);
  • Lines 22–23: Several conditions in [filter] are combined by [AND]; [exclude] adds a condition [NOT]. The named parameters refer to the fields ([first_name=...]); suffixes specify the comparison: [age__gte=18] ([>=]), [last_name__startswith="P"], [last_name__iexact=...] (case-insensitive)... The values are transmitted to the database separately and are never copied into the text of the order SQL, which makes injection impossible SQL;
  • lines 27–28: [create] constructs the object and saves it ([INSERT]); after insertion, ORM stores the ID generated by the database in the object. This is equivalent to [p = Person(first_name=..., ...)] followed by [p.save()];
  • lines 35–38: the update, with its optimistic lock. [update] updates all rows specified by [QuerySet] in a single operation using a single [UPDATE] command, and returns the number of updated rows. The filter has two conditions: the ID and the read version. If another query has modified the row in the meantime—causing its version to change—[UPDATE] does not modify any rows, and the function returns [False]. This is the principle of optimistic locking: nothing is locked, but concurrent modifications are detected. The expression [F("version") + 1] refers to the column itself, in the order SQL ([version = version + 1]): the calculation is performed by the database, not in [Python] based on a value read earlier;
  • Lines 42–43: the deletion: [delete()] sends the [DELETE] from the object’s line.

Unlike [Doctrine], ORM from [Django] does not have a handler that compares each read object to its original state in order to save only the modified columns: [save()] rewrites all columns of the object (or those of its parameter [update_fields]). This is simpler and more predictable; [update] allows you to write exactly in the desired order.

docs.title: 9.1.5. The business layer: persons/business.py
docs.text:
# persons/business.py: the BUSINESS layer, the business rules, and only them.
# Each operation that writes is a TRANSACTION: committed (COMMIT) if the function
# ends normally, cancelled (ROLLBACK) if an exception leaves it

from dataclasses import dataclass

from django.db import IntegrityError, transaction

from . import dao
from .models import Person

NAMESAKE = "A person already has these first and last names."
MODIFIED = "This record has been modified meanwhile: reload it."
UNKNOWN = "This person does not exist (anymore)."


# a business rule refuses the operation; the message is intended for the user
class BusinessError(Exception):
    pass


# the data of a person, as the web layer passes them
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PersonData:
    first_name: str
    last_name: str
    age: int


def list_all() -> list[Person]:
    return dao.list_all()


def read(id: int) -> Person:
    person = dao.read(id)
    if person is None:
        raise BusinessError(UNKNOWN)
    return person


# with transaction.atomic(): the block is executed in a transaction. The uniqueness
# constraint of the database (two simultaneous additions) raises IntegrityError, which becomes a
# business error
def add(data: PersonData) -> Person:
    try:
        with transaction.atomic():
            # rule 1: no two persons with the same first and last names
            if dao.namesake(data.first_name, data.last_name):
                raise BusinessError(NAMESAKE)
            return dao.insert(data.first_name, data.last_name, data.age)
    except IntegrityError as e:
        raise BusinessError(NAMESAKE) from e


def update(id: int, version: int, data: PersonData) -> Person:
    try:
        with transaction.atomic():
            person = read(id)
            # rule 2: a record modified meanwhile by someone else is not modified
            if person.version != version:
                raise BusinessError(MODIFIED)
            if dao.namesake(data.first_name, data.last_name, id):
                raise BusinessError(NAMESAKE)
            # the UPDATE ... WHERE version = ... modifies nothing if another request has
            # modified the row since our reading
            if not dao.update(id, version, data.first_name, data.last_name, data.age):
                raise BusinessError(MODIFIED)
            return read(id)
    except IntegrityError as e:
        raise BusinessError(NAMESAKE) from e


def delete(id: int) -> Person:
    with transaction.atomic():
        person = read(id)
        dao.delete(person)
        return person
  • lines 12–14: messages from business rules;
  • lines 18–19: an exception class specific to the business layer: a business rule rejects the operation, and the exception message is intended for the user. It inherits from [Exception] without adding anything to it; only its name matters;
  • lines 23–27: a person’s data, as transmitted by the web layer to the business layer: a simple object, unrelated to [Django];
  • lines 34–38: a nonexistent person is a business error;
  • lines 44–52: Rule No. 1: No two people may have the same first and last names. The rule is verified before writing to the database, and a [BusinessError] exception is thrown if it is not followed. But this verification is not sufficient: two simultaneous requests could both verify that there is no namesake, and then both proceed to insert the record. The database’s uniqueness constraint then rejects the second [INSERT], and the ORM raises a [IntegrityError], which is transformed into the same [BusinessError]. The database is the last line of defense. [raise ... from e] links the original exception to the new one: the log will show both;
  • lines 55–70: Rule No. 2: Do not modify a record that has been modified in the meantime by someone else. The update form carries the version of the record that was read (in a hidden field); if it differs from the current version, the record has changed since it was displayed. There remains the case where the concurrent modification occurs between reading line 58 and saving line 66: this is detected by the optimistic lock in layer DAO. The function then re-reads the person record to return the new version;
  • lines 73–77: the deletion sets the person to “deleted” for the confirmation message.

Every operation that writes data is executed within a transaction: [transaction.atomic()], used by [with] (a context manager, example 20), opens a transaction ([BEGIN]) at the beginning of the block; if the block ends normally (even with a [return]), the transaction is committed ([COMMIT]); if an exception occurs within the block, the transaction is rolled back ([ROLLBACK]): none of the changes made within the block are retained, and the exception continues on its path. [transaction.atomic] can also be used as a decorator for an entire function ([@transaction.atomic]). The business layer thus determines the scope of transactions: one business operation equals one transaction. Outside a [atomic] block, ORM operates in “autocommit” mode: each SQL command is committed immediately. A [IntegrityError] is intercepted outside the [with] block: inside the block, the transaction would no longer be usable after the error. Other exceptions (such as a database failure or a programming error) are not business errors: they continue to be processed.

docs.title: 9.1.6. The Web Layer
docs.text:
The data entry is described by a form (Example 19):

# persons/forms.py: the form of a person (see examples 18 and 19)

from django import forms

from .business import PersonData


class PersonForm(forms.Form):
    first_name = forms.CharField(label="First name", max_length=30, error_messages={
        "required": "The first name is required.", "max_length": "30 characters at most."})
    last_name = forms.CharField(label="Last name", max_length=30, error_messages={
        "required": "The last name is required.", "max_length": "30 characters at most."})
    age = forms.IntegerField(label="Age", min_value=0, max_value=150, error_messages={
        "required": "The age is required.",
        "invalid": "The age must be an integer.",
        "min_value": "The age must be between 0 and 150.",
        "max_value": "The age must be between 0 and 150."})

    # edit=True: the edit form, which has one more field
    def __init__(self, *args, edit=False, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        for field in self.fields.values():
            field.widget.attrs["class"] = "form-control"
        # the version: a hidden field, in the edit form only
        if edit:
            self.fields["version"] = forms.IntegerField(widget=forms.HiddenInput)

    # the validated data, for the business layer; CharField has already removed the
    # spaces at the start and end of the input (strip option, true by default)
    def data_for_business(self) -> PersonData:
        d = self.cleaned_data
        return PersonData(d["first_name"], d["last_name"], d["age"])
  • lines 9–17: the fields and their constraints, with messages in English;
  • lines 20–26: an additional parameter for the constructor, [edit], specified by name ([PersonForm(request.POST, edit=True)]): a parameter written after [*args] can only be passed by name. The update form receives one additional field, “version,” in a hidden field: [self.fields] is a dictionary to which a field can be added;
  • Lines 30–32: the validated data, in the format expected by the business layer.

[Django] can also generate a form from a template (the [forms.ModelForm] class): its fields and their constraints are derived from the columns, and its [save()] method saves the object. This is very common. However, the form would then modify the model before the business layer has verified its rules. A separate form keeps the layers distinct: the web layer transmits only validated data to the business layer.

# persons/views.py: the WEB layer; it only knows the business layer

from django.contrib import messages
from django.shortcuts import redirect, render
from django.urls import reverse
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET, require_http_methods

from . import business
from .business import BusinessError
from .forms import PersonForm


@require_GET
def home(request):
    return redirect("persons_list")


@require_GET
def list_persons(request):
    return render(request, "persons/list.html", {"persons": business.list_all()})


# GET: the empty form; POST: the sent form
@require_http_methods(["GET", "POST"])
def add(request):
    title = "Add a person"
    action = reverse("persons_add")
    if request.method == "GET":
        return form_page(request, title, PersonForm(), action)
    form = PersonForm(request.POST)
    if not form.is_valid():
        return form_page(request, title, form, action, status=422)
    try:
        p = business.add(form.data_for_business())
    except BusinessError as e:
        # a business rule refuses: the form is displayed again, with the input, and
        # the message, at the bottom of the page
        return form_page(request, title, form, action, error=str(e))
    messages.success(request, f"{p} has been added.")
    return redirect("persons_list")


# GET: the edit form, pre-filled
@require_GET
def edit(request, id):
    try:
        p = business.read(id)
    except BusinessError as e:
        messages.error(request, str(e))
        return redirect("persons_list")
    form = PersonForm(edit=True, initial={
        "first_name": p.first_name, "last_name": p.last_name, "age": p.age, "version": p.version})
    return form_page(request, "Edit a person", form,
                     reverse("persons_person", args=[id]), method="PUT")


# PUT: the sent edit form; DELETE: the deletion
@require_http_methods(["PUT", "DELETE"])
def person(request, id):
    if request.method == "DELETE":
        try:
            p = business.delete(id)
            messages.success(request, f"{p} has been deleted.")
        except BusinessError as e:
            # no form to display again: the error also travels as a flash message
            messages.error(request, str(e))
        return redirect("persons_list")
    title = "Edit a person"
    action = reverse("persons_person", args=[id])
    form = PersonForm(request.POST, edit=True)
    if not form.is_valid():
        return form_page(request, title, form, action, method="PUT", status=422)
    try:
        p = business.update(id, form.cleaned_data["version"], form.data_for_business())
    except BusinessError as e:
        return form_page(request, title, form, action, method="PUT", error=str(e))
    messages.success(request, f"{p} has been edited.")
    return redirect("persons_list")


# the page of the form; a business error: the 422 code, as for an invalid form
# (see example 19)
def form_page(request, title, form, action, method=None, error=None, status=200):
    return render(request, "persons/form.html", {
        "title": title, "form": form, "action": action, "method": method,
        "error": error}, status=422 if error else status)
  • line 8: the business layer, the only layer known to the web layer;
  • lines 25–40: the addition, in three steps: form validation (input errors, example 19); the call to the business layer (business rules); then the PRG schema, with a success flash message (example 20). A [BusinessError] re-displays the form, along with the entered data and the exception message ([str(e)]), which the template will display at the bottom of the page. Input errors and business logic errors are thus handled in the same way;
  • lines 44–54: the edit form, pre-filled with the retrieved person (parameter [initial], example 18). If the person does not exist, the form redirects to the list with a flash error message ([messages.error]). The form is submitted using method PUT (the hidden field [_method], Example 21), to URL [/persons/<id>] ([reverse], with the route parameters in [args]);
  • lines 58–78: the view from [/persons/<id>], for the methods PUT (update, following the same pattern as the add operation) and DELETE (delete, protected by the anti-CSRF token, Example 21). For deletion, there is no form to redisplay: any error is also conveyed in a flash message;
  • lines 83–86: the form page. A business error is returned with code 422, as for an invalid form.

The web layer contains neither SQL nor any business rules: it translates the request into a call to the business layer and the result into a page. The routes ([persons/urls.py]): [/persons] (the list), [/persons/add], [/persons/<id>/edit], and [/persons/<id>] (PUT and DELETE).

The templates:

<!doctype html>
{% load static %}
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Persons</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css' %}">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'css/styles.css' %}">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3" style="max-width: 44rem">
    {# the flash messages; tags: their level (success, error) #}
    {% for message in messages %}
      <div class="alert {% if message.tags == 'error' %}alert-danger{% else %}alert-success{% endif %}" role="status">{{ message }}</div>
    {% endfor %}
    <main>
      {% block content %}{% endblock %}
    </main>
    {% block page_bottom %}{% endblock %}
  </div>
  {% include "fragments/confirmation.html" %}
  <script src="{% static 'js/app.js' %}"></script>
</body>
</html>
  • lines 14–16: the flash messages at the top of the page (example 20). Their label ([message.tags]: [success], [error]) determines their color;
  • line 20: the footer block, where pages display their errors (example 19);
  • lines 22–23: the confirmation window and its script (example 21).
{% extends "layout.html" %}

{% block content %}
  <div class="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center mb-2">
    <h1 class="h3 mb-0">Persons</h1>
    <a class="btn btn-primary btn-sm" href="{% url 'persons_add' %}">Add</a>
  </div>
  <table class="table align-middle">
    <thead><tr><th>First name</th><th>Last name</th><th>Age</th><th></th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      {% for p in persons %}
        <tr>
          <td>{{ p.first_name }}</td>
          <td>{{ p.last_name }}</td>
          <td>{{ p.age }}</td>
          <td class="text-end">
            <a class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-primary" href="{% url 'persons_edit' p.id %}">Edit</a>
            <form method="post" class="d-inline" action="{% url 'persons_person' p.id %}"
                  data-confirmation="Delete {{ p.first_name }} {{ p.last_name }}?">
              {% csrf_token %}
              <input type="hidden" name="_method" value="DELETE">
              <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-danger" type="submit">Delete</button>
            </form>
          </td>
        </tr>
      {% empty %}
        <tr><td colspan="4">No persons.</td></tr>
      {% endfor %}
    </tbody>
  </table>
{% endblock %}

The list includes the links and buttons from Example 21, along with its confirmation window (the files [fragments/confirmation.html] and [static/js/app.js] are those from Example 21). The attributes [p.first_name], [p.last_name]... are those of the [Person] objects read by ORM. The block [{% empty %}] (Example 14) processes the empty list.

{% extends "layout.html" %}

{% block content %}
  <h1 class="h3">{{ title }}</h1>
  <form method="post" action="{{ action }}" novalidate style="max-width: 24rem">
    {% csrf_token %}
    {# the modification is sent with the PUT method (see example 21) #}
    {% if method %}<input type="hidden" name="_method" value="{{ method }}">{% endif %}
    {{ form.first_name.as_field_group }}
    {{ form.last_name.as_field_group }}
    {{ form.age.as_field_group }}
    {# the version: a hidden field, in the edit form only #}
    {% if form.version %}{{ form.version }}{% endif %}
    <div class="d-flex gap-2">
      <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Save</button>
      <a class="btn btn-link" href="{% url 'persons_list' %}">Cancel</a>
    </div>
  </form>
{% endblock %}

{% block page_bottom %}
  {% if error %}
    <div class="error-area" role="alert">{{ error }}</div>
  {% endif %}
{% endblock %}

A template common to both adding and modifying:

  • line 8: the hidden field [_method], for modification only;
  • line 13: the hidden version field, if it exists in the form;
  • lines 21–25: the business error, at the bottom of the page.

docs.title: 9.1.8. The SQL commands
docs.text:
Let’s track the SQL commands for a modification in the console (the server was restarted, and the database was recreated). The display of the modification form for person #1:

(0.000)
                SELECT VERSION(),
                       @@sql_mode,
                       @@default_storage_engine,
                       @@sql_auto_is_null,
                       @@lower_case_table_names,
                       CONVERT_TZ('2001-01-01 01:00:00', 'UTC', 'UTC') IS NOT NULL
            ; args=None; alias=default
(0.000) SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED; args=None; alias=default
(0.000) SELECT `persons`.`id`, `persons`.`version`, `persons`.`first_name`, `persons`.`last_name`, `persons`.`age` FROM `persons` WHERE `persons`.`id` = 1 ORDER BY `persons`.`last_name` ASC, `persons`.`first_name` ASC LIMIT 1; args=(1,); alias=default
[27/Sep/2026 19:45:19] "GET /persons/1/edit HTTP/1.1" 200 2460

Each line shows the command’s duration (in seconds), the command SQL, its parameters ([args]), and the database name ([alias]). The first two commands are used to establish the connection: [Django] queries the server (its version, its settings), then sets the transaction isolation level ([READ COMMITTED]: a transaction sees the changes committed by others). Next comes the read by primary key, with its [ORDER BY] (corresponding to [Meta.ordering]) and its [LIMIT 1] (corresponding to [first()]). In the log, the parameters are copied in order so that they can be read; originally, they are sent separately ([args]). There is no transaction: an isolated read does not require one. The master record is saved with a new age:

(0.000) BEGIN; args=None; alias=default
(0.001) SELECT `persons`.`id`, `persons`.`version`, `persons`.`first_name`, `persons`.`last_name`, `persons`.`age` FROM `persons` WHERE `persons`.`id` = 1 ORDER BY `persons`.`last_name` ASC, `persons`.`first_name` ASC LIMIT 1; args=(1,); alias=default
(0.001) SELECT `persons`.`id`, `persons`.`version`, `persons`.`first_name`, `persons`.`last_name`, `persons`.`age` FROM `persons` WHERE (`persons`.`first_name` = 'Marie' AND `persons`.`last_name` = 'Pélissier' AND NOT (`persons`.`id` = 1)) ORDER BY `persons`.`last_name` ASC, `persons`.`first_name` ASC LIMIT 1; args=('Marie', 'Pélissier', 1); alias=default
(0.000) UPDATE `persons` SET `first_name` = 'Marie', `last_name` = 'Pélissier', `age` = 43, `version` = (`persons`.`version` + 1) WHERE (`persons`.`id` = 1 AND `persons`.`version` = 0); args=('Marie', 'Pélissier', 43, 1, 1, 0); alias=default
(0.000) SELECT `persons`.`id`, `persons`.`version`, `persons`.`first_name`, `persons`.`last_name`, `persons`.`age` FROM `persons` WHERE `persons`.`id` = 1 ORDER BY `persons`.`last_name` ASC, `persons`.`first_name` ASC LIMIT 1; args=(1,); alias=default
(0.001) COMMIT; args=None; alias=default
[27/Sep/2026 19:45:19] "POST /persons/1 HTTP/1.1" 302 0

(the connection was opened, as in the previous request). Within a single transaction ([BEGIN] ... [COMMIT]), we can see: the read of the record, the search for a namesake, the [UPDATE], and then the re-read of the record. The [UPDATE] increments the version ([version + 1]) and sets the optimistic lock condition ([AND version = 0]). The development server logs the request as a POST: this is how it arrived, before the middleware converted it to a PUT. Now let’s submit the same form a second time, still using the old version:

(0.000) BEGIN; args=None; alias=default
(0.000) SELECT `persons`.`id`, `persons`.`version`, `persons`.`first_name`, `persons`.`last_name`, `persons`.`age` FROM `persons` WHERE `persons`.`id` = 1 ORDER BY `persons`.`last_name` ASC, `persons`.`first_name` ASC LIMIT 1; args=(1,); alias=default
(0.000) ROLLBACK; args=None; alias=default
Unprocessable Content: /persons/1
[27/Sep/2026 19:45:19] "POST /persons/1 HTTP/1.1" 422 2562

The version being read is not the one from the form: the business layer raised a [BusinessError], which rolled back the transaction ([ROLLBACK]), and the page displays “This record has been modified meanwhile: reload it.” Similarly, adding a namesake stops after the namesake search, without a [INSERT].

docs.title: 4. Templates and Forms
docs.text:
Until now, views generated their own responses: text, JSON, and a few HTML tags written as a string. In a MVC application, generating the page is the role of the V, which [Django] calls a template: a file that describes the page, with placesholders for the data passed to it by the view—the template context (the M model of MVC; see introduction).

[Django] has its own template engine and its own template language, DTL (Django Template Language). It can also use other engines, such as [Jinja2], the one used by [Flask] (setting [TEMPLATES]); this document focuses on DTL, which all [Django] applications use. A template is a text file, in this case HTML (given the extension [.html]), stored in a folder named [templates], in which three types of tags are interpreted on the server:

  • [{{ variable }}]: the value of a context variable, inserted into the page;
  • [{% tag %}]: a tag that controls the engine: condition ([{% if %}]), loop ([{% for %}]), template inheritance ([{% extends %}], [{% block %}]), inclusion ([{% include %}]), creation of a URL ([{% url %}])...;
  • [{# comment #}]: a comment that does not appear on the generated page. It fits on a single line; a multi-line comment is written between the [{% comment %}] and [{% endcomment %}] tags.

Everything else is copied verbatim. The expressions are not written in [Python], but in the deliberately limited language of DTL: [model.title] refers to the key [title] in a dictionary, or the attribute [title] of an object, or the element [title] in a list ([Django] tries them in that order), and, if it is a method, [Django] calls it without any parameters; filters transform a value ([name|upper] capitalizes a name); tags perform actions. That’s it: DTL has no arithmetic operators, no function calls with parameters, and no assignments. This is by design: the creators of [Django] wanted templates to be written by graphic designers, without the risk of application logic creeping into the pages. A calculation is therefore performed in [Python]—either in the view or in a method of a context object—and the template simply displays the result. The languages of [Twig] ([Symfony]) and [Jinja2] ([Flask]), which were inspired by it, are more permissive: they perform calculations ([total / count]) and call functions with parameters. Finally, a template is not re-parsed with every request: upon its first use, [Django] parses it and transforms it into a list of nodes—a [Python] object—which it keeps in memory and reuses thereafter (in debug mode, it re-parses it if it has been modified). We’ll see what this list looks like.

docs.title: 4.1.1. The configuration: config/settings.py
docs.text:
The template engine is configured via the setting [TEMPLATES]:

# config/settings.py: the configuration of example 13

from pathlib import Path

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
DEBUG = True
SECRET_KEY = "django-insecure-_ph!-_ox*o_&n8o2i=ykjwic(j9!mwf!cc2(()%nzdrs9ssai_"
ALLOWED_HOSTS = []
LANGUAGE_CODE = "en"
TIME_ZONE = "Europe/Paris"
ROOT_URLCONF = "config.urls"
WSGI_APPLICATION = "config.wsgi.application"

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    "pages",
]

# the TEMPLATE ENGINES: here a single one, Django's (the DTL, Django Template
# Language), which looks for the templates in the project's templates folder
TEMPLATES = [
    {
        "BACKEND": "django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates",
        "DIRS": [BASE_DIR / "templates"],
    },
]
  • Lines 19–24: [TEMPLATES] is a list of template engines, each described by a dictionary. Here, there is only one: [BACKEND] refers to the engine [Django] (DTL); [DIRS] is the list of folders where it searches for templates: the [templates] folder of the project. The configuration can also instruct the engine to look for templates in the [templates] folder of each application within the [INSTALLED_APPS] configuration ([APP_DIRS: True], example 18): this is how a reusable application provides its own templates.

The templates are stored in a subfolder named [pages], which is named after the application: this is standard practice, which prevents two applications from each having a [index.html] template and one from overwriting the other.

docs.title: 4.1.2. The template context: pages/viewmodels.py
docs.text:
# pages/viewmodels.py: the view's model, the data the Python view passes to the template

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PageModel:
    title: str
    message: str
    time: str

A template’s context is a [Python] dictionary. Here, it will have only one entry, [model], an immutable object of the class [PageModel] (see Example 03), which contains the three pieces of information that the template will display. There is no requirement to define a template’s context using a class: one could pass three separate variables to the template. However, a class documents what the template expects and allows the editor to verify the view’s code. This is the approach that the case study will follow, where each important page has its own template class.

docs.title: 4.1.3. Views: pages/views.py
docs.text:
# pages/views.py: views that return a page built by a TEMPLATE

from django.shortcuts import render
from django.utils import timezone
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET

from .viewmodels import PageModel


# render: the template engine builds the page from the template
# templates/pages/index.html and from the CONTEXT, a dictionary of the variables made
# available to the template (here a single one, model); the produced page is the body
# of the response
@require_GET
def index(request):
    model = PageModel(
        "My first template",
        "This page was built by Django, on the server.",
        # the time, in the application's time zone (TIME_ZONE setting)
        timezone.localtime().strftime("%H:%M:%S"))
    return render(request, "pages/index.html", {"model": model})


# the same template with another model; or another template, with the 404 code
@require_GET
def hello(request, name):
    if name == "unknown":
        # status: the code of the response
        return render(request, "pages/unknown.html", {"name": name}, status=404)
    model = PageModel(
        f"Hello {name}",
        "This time, the title of the page comes from the URL.",
        timezone.localtime().strftime("%H:%M:%S"))
    return render(request, "pages/index.html", {"model": model})
  • Lines 16–20: The view constructs the model. [timezone.localtime()], from the [django.utils.timezone] module, returns the current time in the application’s time zone (settings [TIME_ZONE], [Europe/Paris]); [strftime] formats it: [%H] for hours, [%M] for minutes, [%S] for seconds;
  • Line 21: The shortcut [render] (from the [django.shortcuts] module, example 04) causes the template engine to generate the page. It receives the request, the template name (the file path, relative to one of the template folders), and the context: a dictionary, where each key becomes a template variable—in this case, a single one: [model]. [render] returns a [HttpResponse] object, whose body is the rendered page (of type [text/html]);
  • lines 27–29: another template, with a different variable ([name]). The parameter [status] of [render] specifies the response code: in this case, 404, for a custom error page;
  • lines 30–34: the same template as the view [index], with a different model. This is the benefit of separating views from templates: a single template can be used for multiple views.

The routes ([pages/urls.py]) associate [/] with the view [index], and [/hello/<str:name>] with the view [hello].

docs.title: 4.1.4. The template: templates/pages/index.html
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  {# {{ ... }}: the value of a variable, inserted into the page #}
  <title>{{ model.title }}</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>{{ model.title }}</h1>
  <p>{{ model.message }}</p>
  <p>Page built at {{ model.time }}.</p>
</body>
</html>
  • line 5: a comment from DTL;
  • line 6: [{{ model.title }}] inserts the value of the [title] attribute of the [model] variable. The dot is the access operator for DTL, whereas [Python] would write [model.title] or [model["title"]], as appropriate.

Everything inserted by [{{ }}] is escaped: the characters [<], [>], [&], ["], and ['] are replaced by their entities HTML. This is the role that function [format_html] played in Example 09, but this time it is automatic: a template therefore cannot inadvertently insert the HTML provided by a user into the page.

docs.title: 4.1.5. The template: templates/pages/unknown.html
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Unknown</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Nobody is called [{{ name }}] here.</h1>
</body>
</html>

A template does not have to accept an object: the variable [name] is a string.

docs.title: 4.1.6. Execution
docs.text:
The time displayed is that of the application's time zone. The raw response shows how the engine works: the [{{ }}] tags have been replaced with their values, and the comment has disappeared (leaving behind an empty line with its indentation).

curl -i http://localhost:8000/

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">

  <title>My first template</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>My first template</h1>
  <p>This page was built by Django, on the server.</p>
  <p>Page built at 19:28:44.</p>
</body>
</html>

The “custom” error page, followed by a name containing HTML and an apostrophe ([<b>martin'], encoded as URL):

curl -i http://localhost:8000/hello/unknown
curl "http://localhost:8000/hello/%3Cb%3Emartin'"

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Unknown</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Nobody is called [unknown] here.</h1>
</body>
</html>
<!doctype html>
...
  <title>Hello <b>martin'</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Hello <b>martin'</h1>
  <p>This time, the title of the page comes from the URL.</p>
...

The tag [<b>] was escaped, without the view or the template having to do anything (the apostrophe was also escaped: [']). Here, finally, is the template as [Django] stores it in memory. The command [python manage.py shell] opens a console [Python] where [Django] is ready; the option [-c] causes it to execute a few instructions:

python manage.py shell -c "from django.template.loader import get_template; print(*get_template('pages/index.html').template.nodelist, sep='\n')"

<TextNode: '<!doctype html>\n<html lan'>
<TextNode: '\n  <title>'>
<Variable Node: model.title>
<TextNode: '</title>\n</head>\n<body>\n '>
<Variable Node: model.title>
<TextNode: '</h1>\n  <p>'>
<Variable Node: model.message>
<TextNode: '</p>\n  <p>Page built at '>
<Variable Node: model.time>
<TextNode: '.</p>\n</body>\n</html>\n'>

The template has become a list of nodes: pieces of text ([TextNode], whose display is truncated), copied as-is, and variables ([VariableNode]), whose values are looked up in the context and then escaped. The comment left no nodes. Generating the page involves iterating through this list and reassembling the text fragments. A template is therefore simply a safer and more readable way to write a function [Python] that generates HTML.

docs.title: 4.2. Example 14: The Template Language
docs.text: This example combines the main constructs of DTL into a single template.

docs.title: 4.2.1. The Model and the View
docs.text:
The template model is described by three immutable data classes:

# basics/viewmodels.py: the model of the template of example 14

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Address:
    street: str
    city: str


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Product:
    name: str
    price: float
    in_stock: bool


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class BasicsModel:
    title: str
    name: str
    # str | None: a string, or None
    nickname: str | None
    html: str
    logged_in: bool
    currency: str
    products: list[Product]
    cart: list[Product]
    address: Address

    # @property: a method that is read like an attribute (model.total). The
    # template language cannot compute: the calculations are done in Python
    @property
    def total(self) -> float:
        return sum(p.price for p in self.products)

    @property
    def average_price(self) -> float:
        return self.total / len(self.products)
  • line 24: [str | None]: a string, or [None] (example 06);
  • lines 28–29: lists of [Product] objects;
  • lines 34–40: Since DTL cannot perform calculations, the calculations required by the template (total price, average price) are methods of the model. The decorator [@property] turns a method into a property: it is read as an attribute, without parentheses ([model.total]), and this is how DTL will see it. For simplicity, the prices here are of type [float] (Example 06 showed why we prefer whole cents).

The model contains values of various types: strings, [None], Booleans, lists of objects, empty lists, and objects containing other objects.

# basics/views.py: a template that uses the main constructs of Django's language

from django.shortcuts import render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET

from .viewmodels import Address, BasicsModel, Product


@require_GET
def index(request):
    # NAMED arguments: each value is associated with an attribute by its name
    model = BasicsModel(
        title="Template basics",
        name="Martin",
        nickname=None,
        html="<b>this is HTML</b>",
        logged_in=True,
        currency="€",
        products=[
            Product("Keyboard", 25, True),
            Product("Mouse", 12.5, False),
            Product("Screen", 149, True),
        ],
        cart=[],
        address=Address("12 rue des Lilas", "Angers"))
    return render(request, "basics/index.html", {"model": model})

The view constructs the model using named parameters (see Example 02): each value is preceded by the name of the attribute it is intended for, which makes the call readable despite the number of parameters.

docs.title: 4.2.2. The template: templates/basics/index.html
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>{{ model.title }}</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>{{ model.title }}</h1>
  {% comment %}
    1. display a value of the model; None is displayed... None; the default filter
    replaces an empty value (None, "", 0, empty list...). A {# #} comment fits
    on a single line; this one, on several, is written between comment and endcomment
  {% endcomment %}
  <p>1. Name: {{ model.name }} - nickname: [{{ model.nickname }}] [{{ model.nickname|default:"none" }}]</p>
  {# 2. {{ }} escapes the HTML; the safe filter inserts it as is #}
  <p>2a. {{ model.html }}</p>
  <p>2b. {{ model.html|safe }}</p>
  {# 3. a condition #}
  {% if model.logged_in %}
    <p>3. You are logged in.</p>
  {% else %}
    <p>3. You are not logged in.</p>
  {% endif %}
  {# 4. a loop: the forloop variable describes the state of the loop #}
  <p>4. Our products:</p>
  <ul>
    {% for product in model.products %}
      <li>no. {{ forloop.counter0 }}: {{ product.name }}, {{ product.price }} {{ model.currency }}
        {{ product.in_stock|yesno:"(in stock),(sold out)" }}
        {% if forloop.first %} - the first{% endif %}
        {% if forloop.last %} - the last, seen by {{ model.name }}{% endif %}
      </li>
    {% endfor %}
  </ul>
  {# 5. the empty list: the empty block of a for loop #}
  <p>5. Your cart:
    {% for p in model.cart %}<span>{{ p.name }}</span>{% empty %} it is empty.{% endfor %}
  </p>
  {% comment %}
    6. with: a template variable; the length filter counts the products;
    floatformat rounds, and writes the number according to the language (LANGUAGE_CODE setting)
  {% endcomment %}
  {% with count=model.products|length %}
    <p>6. {{ count }} products, for a total of {{ model.total }} {{ model.currency }};
      average price: {{ model.average_price|floatformat:2 }} {{ model.currency }}</p>
  {% endwith %}
  {# 7. an object within an object, and a filter that converts to uppercase #}
  <p>7. Address: {{ model.address.street }}, {{ model.address.city|upper }}</p>
  {# 8. verbatim: a text Django copies without interpreting it #}
  <p>8. Braces displayed as they are: {% verbatim %}{{ model.name }}{% endverbatim %}</p>
</body>
</html>
  • Lines 9–13: a multi-line comment;
  • line 14: a value [None] is displayed... [None]: this is the text representation of [None]. The filter [default] replaces an “empty” value ([None], empty string, 0, empty list...) with a default value. A filter is applied using a vertical bar and may take an optional parameter following a colon: [value|filter:"parameter"]. A variable that does not exist at all in the context ([model.unknown]) would be displayed as an empty string, without an error;
  • lines 16–17: [{{ }}] escapes HTML (2a); the filter [safe], on the other hand, inserts the value as-is, without escaping (2b). [safe] is reserved for HTML generated by the application itself, never for user input. The [{% autoescape off %}] tag disables escaping for an entire section of the template;
  • lines 19–23: a condition: [{% if %}], [{% elif %}], [{% else %}], [{% endif %}]. Each block is closed by a [{% end... %}] tag. A condition can use the operators [==], [!=], [<], [>], [<=], [>=], [in], [not], [and], [or];
  • lines 27–33: a loop [{% for ... in ... %}] ... [{% endfor %}]. Within the loop, the special variable [forloop] describes the loop’s state: [forloop.counter0] (the iteration number, starting at 0), [forloop.counter] (starting at 1), [forloop.first], [forloop.last] (true on the first and last iterations), [forloop.revcounter] (the number of remaining iterations). The variables outside the loop ([model.name], [model.currency]) remain accessible;
  • Line 29: The [yesno] filter selects a text based on whether a value is true or false: its two texts (a third, optional text would be used for [None]) are separated by a comma. This is the equivalent, in DTL, of a conditional expression;
  • line 37: a [for] loop can have a [{% empty %}] block, which is executed if the list is empty. This is simpler than a [{% if %}] that would test the length of the list;
  • Lines 43–46: the [{% with %}] tag creates a variable that is valid until [{% endwith %}]: in this case, the number of products, calculated by the [length] filter (the number of elements in a list or characters in a string);
  • Lines 44–45: the calculated properties of the model. The filter [floatformat] rounds a number—[floatformat:2]—to two decimal places. It formats the number according to the conventions of the application’s language ([LANGUAGE_CODE]): the decimal point is formatted for English. All numbers inserted into a page are formatted this way: [Django] formats numbers and dates according to the active language (in French, [12.5] would become [12,5]);
  • line 48: the period passes through objects ([model.address.city]), and the filter [upper] capitalizes a string (while correctly handling accented characters);
  • line 50: the [{% verbatim %}] tag copies its content without interpreting it: this is useful when a page contains curly braces intended for a [JavaScript] framework.

The DTL has about sixty filters ([lower], [capfirst], [title], [truncatechars], [join], [slice], [first], [last], [date], [time], [linebreaks], [urlize], [pluralize], [add], [divisibleby], [escape], [json_script]...) and about thirty tags ([if], [for], [with], [url], [now], [cycle], [firstof], [include], [extends], [block], [load], [csrf_token], [spaceless]...); The applications for [Django] add more ([static], [translate]...), and the application can write its own (Example 16).

docs.title: 4.2.3. Execution
docs.text:
The generated page:

curl http://localhost:8000/

<html lang="en">
<head>

  <title>Template basics</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Template basics</h1>

  <p>1. Name: Martin - nickname: [None] [none]</p>

  <p>2a. <b>this is HTML</b></p>
  <p>2b. <b>this is HTML</b></p>


    <p>3. You are logged in.</p>


  <p>4. Our products:</p>
  <ul>

      <li>no. 0: Keyboard, 25 €
        (in stock)
         - the first

      </li>

      <li>no. 1: Mouse, 12.5 €
        (sold out)
...
  <p>5. Your cart:
     it is empty.
  </p>


    <p>6. 3 products, for a total of 186.5 €;
      average price: 62.17 €</p>


  <p>7. Address: 12 rue des Lilas, ANGERS</p>

The comments and tags have disappeared, but they leave behind their spaces and line breaks: [Django] does not remove any whitespace. This has no effect: the browser ignores this whitespace. (The [{% spaceless %}] tag would remove the whitespace between the HTML tags in a template section.) The numbers have been written in the English style ([12.5], [186.5]), even though the template did not require it.

docs.title: 4.3. Example 15: Parent template, fragments, static files
docs.text:
The pages of a website usually share the same structure: a header, a navigation bar, a footer, and the same style sheets. Rather than repeating this structure in every template, it is written once in a parent template (also called a layout), which the pages extend. This example also uses [Bootstrap], the most widely used CSS framework, for the layout.

15-layout/
├── config/
│   ├── contexts.py
│   ├── settings.py
│   └── ...
├── pages/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── viewmodels.py
│   └── views.py
├── static/
│   └── css/
│       └── styles.css
├── templates/
│   ├── fragments/
│   │   └── navbar.html
│   ├── pages/
│   │   ├── home.html
│   │   ├── raw.html
│   │   └── team.html
│   ├── layout.html
│   └── macros.html
└── manage.py

docs.title: 4.3.1. Static Files
docs.text:
A HTML page references other files: style sheets, [JavaScript] scripts, and images. These files, which the server sends as-is, are called static files. With [Django], they are stored in [static] folders (the project folder and the application folders), and the [django.contrib.staticfiles] application manages them. The configuration:

# config/settings.py: the configuration of example 15

from pathlib import Path

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
DEBUG = True
SECRET_KEY = "django-insecure-u0g1t-=6%v^*y#i*czmc@ge#-yk6m!jj13lte=0yw_pa6y+2m4"
ALLOWED_HOSTS = []
LANGUAGE_CODE = "en"
TIME_ZONE = "Europe/Paris"
ROOT_URLCONF = "config.urls"
WSGI_APPLICATION = "config.wsgi.application"

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    # Django's application that manages the STATIC files (style sheets,
    # images, scripts): the {% static %} tag, and their serving by runserver
    "django.contrib.staticfiles",
    "pages",
]

TEMPLATES = [
    {
        "BACKEND": "django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates",
        "DIRS": [BASE_DIR / "templates"],
        "OPTIONS": {
            # the CONTEXT PROCESSORS: functions that add variables to the
            # context of ALL the templates; request: the current request
            "context_processors": [
                "django.template.context_processors.request",
                "config.contexts.site",
            ],
        },
    },
]

# the URL of the static files: {% static 'css/styles.css' %} -> /static/css/styles.css
STATIC_URL = "static/"
# the folders where Django looks for the static files: the example's one, and
# Bootstrap's one, shared by examples 15 to 28
STATICFILES_DIRS = [
    BASE_DIR / "static",
    BASE_DIR.parent / "common" / "static",
]
  • lines 14–19: the [django.contrib.staticfiles] application, one of the applications included with [Django];
  • lines 21–34: the template engine, with two context processors, described later;
  • line 37: [STATIC_URL], the prefix for the URL static files: the file [css/styles.css] will be available in URL and [/static/css/styles.css];
  • Lines 40–43: [STATICFILES_DIRS], the list of static file folders for the project (in addition to the [static] folders for the applications). The first one is the one from the example. The second is the [examples/common/static] folder, which contains [Bootstrap]: rather than including a copy in each example, examples 15 through 28 share it (see introduction). [Django] searches for a file in all these folders, in order, and returns the first one found.

In debug mode, the development server serves the static files itself, using the [staticfiles] application: a URL that begins with [/static/] is not handled by the application’s routes, but by the static file handler. In production ([DEBUG = False]), it no longer does this: that is not the role of a [Python] application. The command [python manage.py collectstatic] then copies all static files from the project and applications into a single folder (the setting [STATIC_ROOT]), which the web server ([nginx], [Apache]...) serves directly, or that is served by a library such as [WhiteNoise] (see case study).

/* a few settings in addition to Bootstrap */
body {
  background-color: #f5f7fa;
}

/* the footer of the layout */
.footer {
  margin-top: 2rem;
  font-size: 0.85rem;
  color: #6c757d;
}

/* the error messages, at the bottom of the page, on a light pink background */
.error-area {
  margin-top: 1.5rem;
  padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
  background-color: #fdecef;
  border: 1px solid #f5c2c7;
  border-radius: 0.375rem;
  color: #842029;
}

A few additional CSS rules in addition to [Bootstrap]: a light gray background, the footer style, and the style for an error area that will be used in the following examples.

docs.title: 4.3.2. The parent template: templates/layout.html
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
{# the PARENT template of the pages: the pages EXTEND it, and fill its blocks #}
{% load static %}
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  {# block: a slot that the page can fill; here with a default content #}
  <title>{% block title %}Home{% endblock %} - {{ site_name }}</title>
  {# static: the URL of a static file #}
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css' %}">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'css/styles.css' %}">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3">
    {# insertion of the fragments/navbar.html template #}
    {% include "fragments/navbar.html" %}
    <main>
      {# the content of the page requested by the view is inserted here #}
      {% block content %}{% endblock %}
    </main>
    {# request: the current request; site_name: a global variable (see config/contexts.py) #}
    <footer class="footer">Page [{{ request.path }}] - © {% now "Y" %} {{ site_name }}</footer>
  </div>
</body>
</html>
  • Line 3: [{% load static %}] loads a tag library: that of the [staticfiles] application, which provides the [{% static %}] tag. Tags and filters that are not part of the core of DTL are stored in libraries, which a template must load before using them;
  • line 7: the [viewport] tag instructs mobile browsers to display the page at the screen’s width, which is what [Bootstrap] expects;
  • line 9: the [{% block %}] tag marks a named slot, which pages that extend the template can fill by defining a block with the same name. The content written between [{% block title %}] and [{% endblock %}] is the default content for the placeholder, used by a page that does not define this block. [site_name] is a global variable present in all templates (see [config/contexts.py], below);
  • Lines 11–12: [{% static 'path' %}] generates URL from a static file: [STATIC_URL] followed by the path. Writing the URL files by hand ([/static/css/styles.css]) would also work, but [{% static %}] adapts if you change [STATIC_URL] (to serve the files from another site, for example), or if you add a hash of their content to the filenames for caching purposes (case study);
  • line 17: [{% include %}] inserts the content of another template, in this case the navigation bar. The included template sees the variables from the template that includes it;
  • line 20: the placeholder that each page fills with its own content;
  • line 23: the variable [request] is the current request ([request.path]: the path of the requested URL). It is present in all templates thanks to the context processor [request] (see below). The tag [{% now "Y" %}] writes the current date in the following format: [Y], with the year as four digits.

The [container] class of [Bootstrap] centers the content and limits its width; [py-3] adds vertical padding: [Bootstrap] provides hundreds of classes of this type, which are combined in the [class] attribute.

docs.title: 4.3.3. Global variables: config/contexts.py
docs.text:
# config/contexts.py: a context processor

# Django calls it for each template rendered with the request (render(request, ...));
# the dictionary it returns is added to the context: site_name is a GLOBAL variable,
# present in all the templates
def site(request):
    return {"site_name": "My site"}

A context processor is a function that receives the request and returns a dictionary of variables to be added to the context of all templates. [Django] calls the processors from the [context_processors] setting (lines 28–31 of the file [config/settings.py]) every time a template is generated using the request (as is the case with [render(request, ...)]). The [django.template.context_processors.request] processor, included with [Django], adds the variable [request]; ours adds [site_name]. Other applications of [Django] provide their own: messages (example 20), language (example 22)... A processor is called for each template generated: it must be fast.

docs.title: 4.3.4. The navigation bar: templates/fragments/navbar.html
docs.text:
{# a fragment: a piece of page, inserted by include #}
<nav class="navbar navbar-expand bg-light rounded mb-3 px-3">
  <span class="navbar-brand">{{ site_name }}</span>
  <div class="navbar-nav">
    {# url: the URL of a route, designated by its name #}
    <a class="nav-link" href="{% url 'home' %}">Home</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="{% url 'team' %}">Team</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="{% url 'raw' %}">Page without parent template</a>
  </div>
</nav>

A fragment: a piece of a page that has no meaning on its own. The classes [navbar], [navbar-brand], and [nav-link] are those of the navigation bar in [Bootstrap]. The links are generated by the [{% url %}] tag (line 6), based on the route names (example 04): [{% url 'team' %}] yields [/team]. The route parameters follow the name: [{% url 'contacts_details' contact.id %}] (example 21).

docs.title: 4.3.5. Named fragments: templates/macros.html
docs.text:
{# NAMED FRAGMENTS (partialdef): reusable pieces of page, stored in a same file #}

{# a Bootstrap card, with a name and a role #}
{% partialdef card %}
  <div class="card">
    <div class="card-body">
      <h5 class="card-title">{{ name }}</h5>
      <p class="card-text">{{ role }}</p>
    </div>
  </div>
{% endpartialdef %}
  • lines 4–11: The [{% partialdef %}] tag, introduced with [Django] 6.0, defines a named fragment (partial): a portion of a template, in this case a card ([card]) from [Bootstrap]. A file can contain several of these. Defined in this way, the fragment is not displayed where it is written: it is displayed elsewhere, using [{% include "macros.html#card" %}] (the file name, a hash symbol, the fragment name), or, within the same file, using [{% partial card %}]. The fragment displays two variables, [name] and [role], which will be provided to it upon inclusion.

Students of the [Symfony] course will recognize how this course used the macros from [Twig]. There is one difference: a macro from [Twig] could only see its own parameters; an included fragment can see all the variables in the template that includes it, in addition to the ones passed to it. The keyword [only] ([{% include "..." with name="..." only %}]) restricts it to the latter. For a more complex component that requires [Python] code, an inclusion tag is written (Example 16).

docs.title: 4.3.6. The pages
docs.text:
{# this page EXTENDS the parent template: it only provides the content of its blocks #}
{% extends "layout.html" %}

{% block content %}
  <h1>Welcome</h1>
  <p>This page only contains its own content: the header, the navigation
    bar and the footer come from the parent template <code>layout.html</code>.</p>
  {# the [card] fragment of the macros.html file, with two variables written in place #}
  {% include "macros.html#card" with name="A fragment" role="included with variables written in place" %}
{% endblock %}
  • Line 2: The page extends the parent template: [Django] generates the parent page, replacing its blocks with those defined by the page. [{% extends %}] must be the first tag in the template (only a comment [{# #}] may precede it). In a template that extends another template, all content must be within blocks: text written outside of blocks does not appear in the generated page;
  • lines 4–10: the [content] block, which fills the slot of the same name. The page does not define the [title] block: the slot retains its default content, “Home”;
  • line 9: the inclusion of the fragment [card], with two variables specified after the keyword [with]. The HTML in the fragment is not escaped a second time: [Django] knows it is already safe HTML (the variables, however, were escaped within the fragment).
{% extends "layout.html" %}

{% block title %}Our team{% endblock %}

{% block content %}
  <h1>Our team</h1>
  <div class="row g-3">
    {% for member in members %}
      <div class="col-md-4">
        {# the variables of the fragment are any expressions #}
        {% include "macros.html#card" with name=member.name role=member.role %}
      </div>
    {% endfor %}
  </div>
{% endblock %}
  • line 3: the block [title], on a single line;
  • lines 7–14: one card per team member, in a grid of [Bootstrap] ([row], [col-md-4]: three columns on a medium or large screen, one column on a narrow screen);
  • line 11: the variables passed to the fragment can be any expressions.

A block in the parent can also be supplemented rather than replaced: [{{ block.super }}], written in the page block, inserts the content that the block had in the parent. A template can extend a template that itself extends another: inheritance has as many levels as needed. The view contains no new features:

# pages/views.py: three pages

from django.shortcuts import render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET

from .viewmodels import Member


@require_GET
def home(request):
    return render(request, "pages/home.html")


@require_GET
def team(request):
    members = [
        Member("Marie Pélissier", "Director"),
        Member("Jacques Bromard", "Developer"),
        Member("Philippe Jandot", "Graphic designer"),
    ]
    return render(request, "pages/team.html", {"members": members})


@require_GET
def raw(request):
    return render(request, "pages/raw.html")

Finally, the third page does not use the parent template:

<!doctype html>
{# this template does not extend the parent template: it is a complete page #}
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Raw page</title>
</head>
<body>
  <p>This page does not use the parent template: neither Bootstrap, nor navigation bar.</p>
  <p><a href="{% url 'home' %}">Back to the home page</a></p>
</body>
</html>

The URL style sheets were calculated by [{% static %}]: these are URL specific to the site. curl -I http://localhost:8000/static/bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "http://localhost:8000/static/..%2F..%2Fconfig%2Fsettings.py"

500

(the [-s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n"] options display only the response code; under [Windows], it displays [-o NUL]). The URL option requests the [config/settings.py] file from the example, moving up two folders (the [/] files are encoded as [%2F], so that neither [curl] nor the browser simplifies the path on its own). docs.title: 4.4. Example 16: Extending the template language
docs.text:
A template often needs to format values: an amount with its currency, a date written out in full, or text in uppercase. This code does not belong in the view (which does not handle presentation), and DTL does not allow it to be written in the template (see the introduction to this chapter). Instead, it is written in [Python], in a library of tags and filters: a module that adds its own filters and tags to the template language. Components that generate pieces of HTML from data—the inclusion tags—are also written in [Python].

16-extensions/
├── config/
│   ├── middleware.py
│   ├── settings.py
│   └── ...
├── pages/
│   ├── templatetags/
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   └── formats.py
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── viewmodels.py
│   └── views.py
├── static/
│   └── css/
│       └── styles.css
├── templates/
│   ├── fragments/
│   │   └── navbar.html
│   ├── pages/
│   │   ├── home.html
│   │   └── products.html
│   ├── tags/
│   │   ├── badge.html
│   │   └── link.html
│   └── layout.html
└── manage.py

docs.title: 4.4.1. The library: pages/templatetags/formats.py
docs.text:
A tag library is a module contained in an application’s [templatetags] package (which must be declared in [INSTALLED_APPS]); the module name ([formats]) is the name that a template will assign to [{% load formats %}]:

# pages/templatetags/formats.py: a LIBRARY of extensions of the template
# language, loaded by {% load formats %}: two filters and two tags

from babel.dates import format_date
from babel.numbers import format_currency
from django import template
from django.utils.translation import get_language

# the object that registers the filters and tags of the library
register = template.Library()


# a FILTER: {{ product.price_cents|money }} or {{ ...|money:"USD" }}. An
# amount in cents, in a currency, in the format of the active language:
# 114990 -> "€1,149.90" in English, "1 149,90 €" in French. The Babel
# library knows the conventions of each country
@register.filter
def money(cents, currency="EUR"):
    return format_currency(cents / 100, currency, locale=get_language())


# a date in full words, in the active language: "Sunday, September 27, 2026"
@register.filter
def long_date(day):
    return format_date(day, format="full", locale=get_language())


# an INCLUSION TAG: {% link 'products' '/products' 'Products' %} displays the
# tags/link.html template, with the context the function returns.
# takes_context: the function also receives the context of the calling template
@register.inclusion_tag("tags/link.html", takes_context=True)
def link(context, route, path, text):
    # a link of the navigation bar, which receives the [active] class if the
    # current page is under the [path] path
    active = context["request"].path.startswith(path)
    return {"route": route, "text": text, "active": active}


# a Bootstrap badge: green if the product is in stock, red otherwise
@register.inclusion_tag("tags/badge.html")
def badge(stock):
    return {"stock": stock}
  • lines 4–5: two functions from the [Babel] library (see introduction), which knows the conventions for writing numbers, amounts, and dates for all countries (it uses data from the Unicode project CLDR);
  • line 7: [get_language] sets the active language for the current query ([fr], [en]); we’ll see who sets it;
  • line 10: the object [register], a [template.Library], stores the module’s filters and tags. The variable name is hard-coded: this is where [Django] looks for them;
  • Lines 17–19: A filter is a function, registered by the decorator [@register.filter] under its own name, [money]. Its first parameter is the filtered value; the second, optional parameter is the filter’s parameter in the template ([price|money:"USD"]): here, the currency, designated by its international code ([EUR], [USD]). The filter formats an amount received in cents (see example 06). The formatting depends on the language: in French, [1 149,90 €] (space to separate thousands, decimal comma, currency symbol after the amount); in English, [€1,149.90];
  • lines 23–25: date formatting: the format [full] writes the date in full, including the day of the week ([Sunday, September 27, 2026]);
  • lines 31–36: an inclusion tag, defined by [@register.inclusion_tag]: a function that calculates a context, and a template (here, [tags/link.html]) that displays it. In a template, [{% link 'products' '/products' 'Products' %}] calls the function with these three parameters, then inserts the template, built using the dictionary it returned. With [takes_context=True], the function receives the context of the calling template as its first parameter: it finds the query there and determines whether the link points to the current page ([startswith] checks the beginning of a string);
  • lines 40–42: a second inclusion tag, without the context: a badge.

A library can also provide “simple” tags ([@register.simple_tag]), which return a value, and complete tags, which parse their own content (such as [{% if %}]): this is less common. The templates for the two inclusion tags:

<a class="nav-link{% if active %} active{% endif %}" href="{% url route %}">{{ text }}</a>

{% if stock > 0 %}<span class="badge text-bg-success">{{ stock }} in stock</span>{% else %}<span class="badge text-bg-danger">sold out</span>{% endif %}

The link for the current page is assigned the class [active] by [Bootstrap], which highlights it. [{% url route %}] generates the URL for a route whose name is stored in a variable. The badge is green ([text-bg-success]) or red ([text-bg-danger]) depending on inventory. The package [templatetags] also has its file [__init__.py]; without it, it would not be a package.

docs.title: 4.4.2. The language of each request: config/middleware.py
docs.text:
# config/middleware.py: the language of each request

from django.utils import translation


class SetLanguage:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    # the ?lang=fr parameter of the URL, English otherwise
    def __call__(self, request):
        language = "fr" if request.GET.get("lang") == "fr" else "en"
        # activate: the ACTIVE language, which Django uses to format the
        # numbers and dates, and to translate its messages
        translation.activate(language)
        return self.get_response(request)

Each request has an active language, which, by default, is the same as the one specified in the [LANGUAGE_CODE] setting. Here, the [?lang=fr] parameter of URL selects French; English is the default language. A middleware component (example 03) sets it before each view using the [translation.activate] function: This is the language that [get_language] will return—the language in which [Django] formats numbers and dates and translates its own messages (such as form error messages). The active language is specific to the execution thread handling the request: two simultaneous requests may have different languages. It is not reset from one request to the next; this is why the middleware sets it for each request, even for English. The chapter on internationalization will replace this middleware with that of [Django] and [LocaleMiddleware], and will use this same language to translate the text.

docs.title: 4.4.4. The view: pages/views.py
docs.text:
# pages/views.py: two pages

from datetime import date

from django.shortcuts import render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET

from .viewmodels import Product


@require_GET
def home(request):
    return render(request, "pages/home.html", {"today": date.today()})


@require_GET
def products(request):
    items = [
        Product("keyboard", 2500, 12),
        Product("mouse", 1250, 0),
        Product("screen", 114990, 3),
    ]
    # the calculation is done here, in Python: the template only has to display it
    total = sum(p.price_cents * p.stock for p in items)
    return render(request, "pages/products.html", {"products": items, "stock_total": total})

Views pass raw values to templates: a date ([date.today()], today’s date) and amounts in cents. Formatting is handled by the templates. The total inventory, however, is a calculation: it is calculated in [Python] (line 24), since DTL cannot perform calculations. The [Product] class combines a name, a price (in cents; see example 06), and a stock quantity.

docs.title: 4.4.5. The templates
docs.text:
{% load formats %}
<nav class="navbar navbar-expand bg-light rounded mb-3 px-3">
  <span class="navbar-brand">Extensions</span>
  <div class="navbar-nav">
    {# 1. a condition written in the template; resolver_match: the route of the current request #}
    <a class="nav-link{% if request.resolver_match.url_name == 'home' %} active{% endif %}" href="{% url 'home' %}">Home</a>
    {# 2. our [link] tag #}
    {% link 'products' '/products' 'Products' %}
    {# 3. url builds the path of a route; the URL parameters are added by hand #}
    <a class="nav-link" href="{% url 'products' %}?lang=fr">Produits (fr)</a>
  </div>
</nav>
  • line 1: the fragment loads the library it needs on its own: [{% load %}] libraries are not passed on to included templates or to templates that extend a parent. Each template loads its own libraries;
  • line 6: the same as with the [link] tag, written directly in the template, with a condition. [request.resolver_match] describes the result of routing the current request: [url_name] is the name of the route. The tag avoids having to repeat the condition for each link;
  • line 8: the tag call, with its three parameters, separated by spaces;
  • line 10: [{% url %}] only generates the path: the parameters for URL are added manually ([?lang=fr]).
{% extends "layout.html" %}
{% load i18n formats %}
{% block title %}Home{% endblock %}

{% block content %}
  <h1>Home</h1>
  {# our long_date filter #}
  <p>Today is {{ today|long_date }}.</p>
  {# the active language, set by the SetLanguage middleware #}
  {% get_current_language as language %}
  <p>Formatting language: {{ language }}
    (<a href="{% url 'home' %}?lang=fr">in French</a>, <a href="{% url 'home' %}">in English</a>)</p>
{% endblock %}
  • Line 2: The page loads two libraries: [i18n], the internationalization library for [Django], and our own;
  • line 8: our filter [long_date];
  • Lines 10–11: The [{% get_current_language as language %}] tag, from the [i18n] library, stores the active language in a template variable.
{% extends "layout.html" %}
{% load formats %}
{% block title %}Products{% endblock %}

{% block content %}
  <h1>Products</h1>
  <table class="table table-sm w-auto">
    <thead><tr><th>Product</th><th>Price</th><th>Price in dollars</th><th>Stock</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      {% for product in products %}
        <tr>
          {# a Django filter (upper), then our money filter, without then with parameter #}
          <td>{{ product.name|upper }}</td>
          <td>{{ product.price_cents|money }}</td>
          <td>{{ product.price_cents|money:"USD" }}</td>
          {# our [badge] tag builds the HTML of the badge #}
          <td>{% badge product.stock %}</td>
        </tr>
      {% endfor %}
    </tbody>
  </table>
  <p>Stock total: {{ stock_total|money }}</p>
{% endblock %}
  • line 13: a [Django] filter;
  • lines 14–15: our [money] filter, first with its default currency, then with a parameter;
  • line 17: the call to the [badge] tag;
  • line 22: the total inventory, calculated by the view.

The parent template [layout.html] is a simplified version of the one in Example 15; its attribute [lang] receives the active language ([<html lang="{{ language }}">], after [{% get_current_language as language %}]).
