docs.title: 4.5. Example 17: a GET form
docs.text:
A HTML form sends its fields to the server in one of two ways, depending on its [method] attribute:

  • [method="get"]: The fields are added to the URL as parameters ([/search?keyword=le&genre=novel]). This is the method used by a form that performs a query: a search or a filter. The URL containing the results can be bookmarked, shared, or reloaded safely;
  • [method="post"]: The fields are included in the request body (see Example 11). This is the method used by a form that modifies data: a registration, an addition, or a deletion.

This first form is a book search. It is hand-coded in HTML within the template: the following examples will use the [Django] form templates.

docs.title: 4.5.1. The template: books/viewmodels.py
docs.text:
# books/viewmodels.py: a book, and the model of the search template

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Book:
    title: str
    author: str
    genre: str


# the model of the template: the input (to display it again), the genres, the results
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SearchModel:
    keyword: str
    genre: str
    genres: list[str]
    results: list[Book]
  • Lines 14–19: The template contains the user’s input, which the form will display, the list of suggested genres, and the results.

docs.title: 4.5.2. The view: books/views.py
docs.text:
# books/views.py: a search form, sent by GET

from django.shortcuts import render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET

from .viewmodels import Book, SearchModel

# CONSTANTS of the module: the data, written in the code for the example
GENRES = ["novel", "poetry", "drama"]
BOOKS = [
    Book("Le Rouge et le Noir", "Stendhal", "novel"),
    Book("Les Fleurs du mal", "Baudelaire", "poetry"),
    Book("Madame Bovary", "Flaubert", "novel"),
    Book("Alcools", "Apollinaire", "poetry"),
    Book("Le Cid", "Corneille", "drama"),
]


# GET / and GET /search?keyword=...&genre=...: the form AND its results
@require_GET
def search(request):
    keyword = request.GET.get("keyword", "")
    genre = request.GET.get("genre", "")
    word = keyword.lower()
    # a list COMPREHENSION: the books that satisfy the condition
    results = [book for book in BOOKS
               if (word == "" or word in book.title.lower() or word in book.author.lower())
               and (genre == "" or book.genre == genre)]
    return render(request, "books/search.html", {
        "model": SearchModel(keyword, genre, GENRES, results),
    })
  • lines 9–16: two module constants: the list of genres and the list of books. In a real application, these would come from a database;
  • lines 20–21: a single view referenced by two routes ([config/urls.py]: [""] and ["search"], named [books_home] and [books_search]). On the first visit ([/]), there are no parameters, and all books are displayed;
  • lines 22–23: the form fields are read as parameters for URL (example 07), with an empty string as the default value;
  • lines 24–28: filtering, using a list comprehension with a condition ([if]): a book is selected if the keyword is empty or appears in its title or author (in lowercase on both sides: [lower()] correctly handles accented characters), and if the genre is empty or matches the book’s genre. A condition can span multiple lines, enclosed in parentheses;
  • lines 29–31: the template.

docs.title: 4.5.3. The template: templates/books/search.html
docs.text:
{% extends "layout.html" %}

{% block content %}
  <h1 class="h3">Book search</h1>
  {# method="get": the fields are sent in the URL (?keyword=...&genre=...) #}
  <form method="get" action="{% url 'books_search' %}" class="row g-2 align-items-end mb-3">
    <div class="col-auto">
      <label class="form-label" for="keyword">Title or author</label>
      {# value: the field displays again what was typed (escaped by {{ }}) #}
      <input class="form-control" id="keyword" name="keyword" value="{{ model.keyword }}">
    </div>
    <div class="col-auto">
      <label class="form-label" for="genre">Genre</label>
      <select class="form-select" id="genre" name="genre">
        <option value="">(all)</option>
        {% for genre in model.genres %}
          {# the boolean attribute selected, written if the condition is true, omitted otherwise #}
          <option value="{{ genre }}"{% if genre == model.genre %} selected{% endif %}>{{ genre }}</option>
        {% endfor %}
      </select>
    </div>
    <div class="col-auto">
      <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Search</button>
    </div>
  </form>
  <p>{{ model.results|length }} book(s) found.</p>
  <ul>
    {% for book in model.results %}
      <li><i>{{ book.title }}</i>, {{ book.author }} ({{ book.genre }})</li>
    {% endfor %}
  </ul>
{% endblock %}
  • line 6: the [<form>] tag. The [action] attribute is the URL to which the form is submitted; [method="get"] places the fields in the URL. The classes of [Bootstrap] arrange the fields on a single line;
  • line 8: a label. Its [for] attribute specifies the identifier ([id]) of the field it describes: clicking the label places the cursor in the field, and screen readers read the label along with the field;
  • line 10: an input field. Its attribute [name] is the name of the parameter sent to the server: this is the link between the form and the view ([request.GET.get("keyword", "")]). The attribute [value] is the displayed value: the previous entry, redisplayed (and escaped by [{{ }}], which is essential in an attribute: an entry containing a quotation mark ["] would otherwise close the attribute);
  • lines 14–20: a drop-down list. Each [<option>] has a value ([value]), sent to the server, and text, displayed. The first option, with an empty value, means “all genres”;
  • line 18: the option selected in the previous request is assigned the attribute [selected]. This is a Boolean attribute: its presence alone is sufficient; it has no value. The condition sets it if true, and sets nothing otherwise;
  • line 23: the submit button;
  • line 26: the number of results.

docs.title: 4.6. Example 18: Form fields
docs.text:
This example shows all the field types in a HTML form, which was sent this time by POST. It demonstrates how to redisplay each field type along with its current value, how the browser sends the values for each field, and how the server verifies that a received value is indeed one of the available options. Writing all of this by hand, as in Example 17, would be time-consuming and repetitive. The forms from [Django], which we used in the previous chapter to validate parameters, can also be displayed: each field has a widget—an object that creates its input field in HTML, along with the current value—and the form redisplays the input and any errors. This is the complete version of what the [Symfony] course delegated to its Form component, and what the [Flask] course delegated to [WTForms].

18-fields/
├── config/
│   ├── rendering.py
│   ├── settings.py
│   └── ...
├── form/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── forms.py
│   ├── lists.py
│   └── views.py
├── static/
│   └── ...
├── templates/
│   ├── django/
│   │   └── forms/
│   │       └── widgets/
│   │           ├── input_option.html
│   │           └── multiple_input.html
│   ├── form/
│   │   └── form.html
│   ├── forms/
│   │   └── field.html
│   └── layout.html
└── manage.py

docs.title: 4.6.1. Lists: form/lists.py
docs.text:
# form/lists.py: the lists offered by the form. In a real
# application, they would come from a database

# each list: pairs (sent value, displayed text)
TITLES = [("Mr", "Mr"), ("Mme", "Mme"), ("Melle", "Melle")]
COUNTRIES = [("fr", "France"), ("be", "Belgium"), ("ch", "Switzerland"), ("ca", "Canada")]
HOBBIES = [("reading", "reading"), ("music", "music"), ("sport", "sport"), ("cinema", "cinema")]
LANGUAGES = [("French", "French"), ("English", "English"), ("Spanish", "Spanish"),
             ("German", "German")]

The form’s dropdown lists (titles, countries, hobbies, languages) are constants in a module: in a real application, they would come from a database. Each list consists of (value, text) pairs: the value is what is sent to the server, and the text is what is displayed (example 08). A pair is written in parentheses: it is a tuple, a sequence of values that cannot be modified.

docs.title: 4.6.2. The form: form/forms.py
docs.text:
# form/forms.py: the DESCRIPTION of the form: its fields, their type, their widget

from django import forms

from . import lists


# a parent class for our forms: it gives each input area the
# Bootstrap CSS class that suits it
class BootstrapForm(forms.Form):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        # fields: the fields of the form, in a dictionary {name: field}
        for field in self.fields.values():
            widget = field.widget
            if isinstance(widget, (forms.RadioSelect, forms.CheckboxSelectMultiple)):
                css_class = "form-check-input"
            elif isinstance(widget, forms.Select):
                css_class = "form-select"
            else:
                css_class = "form-control"
            # attrs: the HTML attributes of the input area
            widget.attrs["class"] = css_class


# the fields of the form, in their display order. The FIELD (forms.XxxField)
# converts and validates the value; the WIDGET (forms.XxxInput...) draws the input area
class FieldsForm(BootstrapForm):
    # radio buttons: a list of choices, drawn by the RadioSelect widget;
    # error_messages: the message of the "required field" error
    title = forms.ChoiceField(choices=lists.TITLES, widget=forms.RadioSelect,
                              error_messages={"required": "The title is required."})
    # an input area; required=False: the field is not required
    name = forms.CharField(required=False)
    # a password: never displayed again in the page
    password = forms.CharField(label="Password", required=False, widget=forms.PasswordInput)
    # a date: an <input type="date"> field; the value is a Python date
    birth_date = forms.DateField(label="Date of birth", required=False,
                                 widget=forms.DateInput(attrs={"type": "date"}))
    # checkboxes: a list of MULTIPLE choices
    hobbies = forms.MultipleChoiceField(choices=lists.HOBBIES, required=False,
                                        widget=forms.CheckboxSelectMultiple)
    # drop-down list: the default widget of a ChoiceField
    country = forms.ChoiceField(choices=lists.COUNTRIES)
    # multiple-selection list, displayed on four lines
    languages = forms.MultipleChoiceField(label="Spoken languages", choices=lists.LANGUAGES,
                                          required=False,
                                          widget=forms.SelectMultiple(attrs={"size": 4}))
    comment = forms.CharField(required=False, widget=forms.Textarea(attrs={"rows": 2}))
    # a hidden field
    token = forms.CharField(widget=forms.HiddenInput)
  • Lines 10–23: A parent class for our forms, which assigns each input field the appropriate class (CSS derived from [Bootstrap]). It redefines the constructor ([__init__]), which receives the same parameters as that of [forms.Form] ([*args], [**kwargs], example 08), and begins by calling it ([super().__init__(...)]). The form’s [fields] attribute is then a dictionary of its fields; each field has its own widget ([field.widget]), whose dictionary [attrs] contains the attributes HTML of the input field. [isinstance] accepts a tuple of classes: is the widget of one of these classes? Radio buttons and checkboxes take the class [form-check-input], lists take [form-select], and others take [form-control];
  • Lines 28–51: the fields, in the order they are displayed. Two objects must be distinguished: the field ([forms.XxxField]) converts and validates the value, as in the previous chapter; its widget ([forms.XxxInput], [forms.Select]...) draws the input field. Each field has a default widget, which is replaced by the parameter [widget]. By default, a field’s label is its name, formatted ([password] would become “Password,” [name] “Name”); the parameter [label] selects it;
  • Lines 31–32: A [ChoiceField] is a drop-down list. With the [RadioSelect] widget, it becomes a group of radio buttons (a single selection). The [error_messages] parameter (example 09) displays the “required field” error message;
  • line 34: a [CharField] (default widget: [TextInput], a [<input type="text">]), optional. A required field ([required=True], the default) generates the attribute HTML [required], which the browser checks (example 19);
  • line 36: a password (widget [PasswordInput], a [<input type="password">]), which is never returned to the page: its field is always empty when displayed;
  • lines 38–39: a date ([DateField]), whose value will be an object [date] of type [Python]. The [DateInput] widget receives the [type="date"] attribute: a [<input type="date">] field, for which the browser displays a calendar. Such a field exchanges its value with the server in the [yyyy-mm-dd] format, regardless of the format in which the browser displays it ([DateField] accepts this format);
  • lines 41–42: a [MultipleChoiceField] (example 10), drawn by the [CheckboxSelectMultiple] widget: checkboxes;
  • Line 44: a [ChoiceField] with its default widget, [Select]: a drop-down list;
  • Lines 46–48: a [MultipleChoiceField] with its default widget, [SelectMultiple]: a multi-select list, displayed across four lines (the HTML [size] attribute, specified by [attrs]);
  • line 49: a text box ([Textarea]), spanning two lines;
  • line 51: a hidden field ([HiddenInput]).

[Django] also provides [EmailField] (example 19), [IntegerField], [DecimalField], [URLField], [BooleanField] (a single checkbox), [FileField], [ImageField], [SlugField], [UUIDField], [JSONField]... and other widgets: [EmailInput], [NumberInput], [CheckboxInput], [ClearableFileInput], [SelectDateWidget] (three lists: day, month, year)...

docs.title: 4.6.3. Field layout: config/rendering.py and form templates
docs.text:
A [Django] form is automatically generated using templates: one template for the entire form, one for each complete field (label, input field, tooltip, error messages), and one for each type of widget. [Django] provides all these templates in the [django.forms] application, with a neutral layout. To achieve the layout of [Bootstrap], we replace a few of them. First, [Django] must search for the form templates, just like the others, in the folders defined by the [TEMPLATES] configuration: this is the role of a form renderer:

# config/rendering.py: the rendering engine of the forms

from django.forms.renderers import TemplatesSetting


# TemplatesSetting: a rendering engine that looks for its templates like the other
# templates of the project (TEMPLATES setting): a template of the project's templates folder
# can therefore replace Django's one
class BootstrapRenderer(TemplatesSetting):
    # the template of a complete field: label, input area, help, errors
    field_template_name = "forms/field.html"
  • line 9: [TemplatesSetting] is the form renderer that searches for its templates using the project’s template engine: a template from the project’s [templates] folder can therefore replace a template from [Django] with the same name. Our class inherits this behavior;
  • Line 11: The [field_template_name] attribute specifies the template for a complete field: ours, [forms/field.html].

The configuration:

# config/settings.py: the configuration of example 18

from pathlib import Path

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
DEBUG = True
SECRET_KEY = "django-insecure-b13ls-fk@*cj%i9(=5e1aa_eg(j0&*2cs)oc=j+qo&(!v06l^y"
ALLOWED_HOSTS = []
LANGUAGE_CODE = "en"
TIME_ZONE = "Europe/Paris"
ROOT_URLCONF = "config.urls"
WSGI_APPLICATION = "config.wsgi.application"

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    "django.contrib.staticfiles",
    # the templates of Django's forms (one template per kind of field)
    "django.forms",
    "form",
]

MIDDLEWARE = [
    # the anti-CSRF protection of ALL the POST requests (see further on)
    "django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware",
]

TEMPLATES = [
    {
        "BACKEND": "django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates",
        "DIRS": [BASE_DIR / "templates"],
        # APP_DIRS: Django also looks for the templates in the templates folder of
        # each application, including django.forms
        "APP_DIRS": True,
    },
]

# the RENDERING ENGINE of the forms: ours, which draws the fields with the
# Bootstrap 5 classes (see config/rendering.py)
FORM_RENDERER = "config.rendering.BootstrapRenderer"

STATIC_URL = "static/"
STATICFILES_DIRS = [
    BASE_DIR / "static",
    BASE_DIR.parent / "common" / "static",
]
  • line 17: the application [django.forms], which provides the form templates from [Django], in its folder [templates];
  • Lines 21–24: the anti-CSRF protection middleware (see below);
  • line 32: [APP_DIRS: True]: [Django] also searches for templates in the [templates] folder of each declared application, including [django.forms]. The [DIRS] folders are checked first: our templates take precedence over those in [Django];
  • line 38: the [FORM_RENDERER] setting specifies our rendering engine.

The template for a complete field:

{# a complete field, with the Bootstrap classes; field: the field to draw #}
{% if field.use_fieldset %}
  {# a group of radio buttons or checkboxes: a fieldset and its legend #}
  <fieldset class="mb-3">
    <legend class="form-label fs-6 mb-1">{{ field.label }}</legend>
    {{ field }}
{% else %}
  <div class="mb-3">
    <label class="form-label" for="{{ field.id_for_label }}">{{ field.label }}</label>
    {{ field }}
{% endif %}
    {% if field.help_text %}<div class="form-text" id="{{ field.auto_id }}_helptext">{{ field.help_text }}</div>{% endif %}
    {% if field.errors %}<div class="invalid-feedback d-block" id="{{ field.auto_id }}_error">{% for error in field.errors %}{{ error }}{% if not forloop.last %}<br>{% endif %}{% endfor %}</div>{% endif %}
{% if field.use_fieldset %}</fieldset>{% else %}</div>{% endif %}

The template receives the field to be rendered, [field] (a [BoundField] object: the field, linked to the form, and therefore to its value and errors):

  • Lines 2–6: A group of radio buttons or checkboxes ([field.use_fieldset] applies to these widgets) is surrounded by a [<fieldset>], whose caption ([<legend>]) is the group label: this is what screen readers expect;
  • lines 8–10: another field has a [<label>], linked to the input field by its identifier ([id_for_label]: [id_name], by default [id_] followed by the field name). [{{ field }}] defines the input field using its widget’s template;
  • line 12: the field’s help text (parameter [help_text] for a field), if it has one;
  • line 13: the field’s errors ([field.errors]), using the classes from [Bootstrap] ([invalid-feedback]: red text, [d-block]: always visible). Its identifier, [id_name_error], is the one specified by [Django] in the [aria-describedby] attribute of the input field, so that screen readers read the message along with the field;
  • Line 14: the closing tag for the tag opened in the first part.

Finally, two widget templates from [Django] are replaced so that the radio buttons and checkboxes are displayed in the same way as in [Bootstrap], side by side:

{# replaces Django's template: a group of radio buttons or checkboxes, side by side #}
<div id="{{ widget.attrs.id }}">{% for group, options, index in widget.optgroups %}{% for option in options %}
  <div class="form-check form-check-inline">{% include option.template_name with widget=option %}</div>{% endfor %}{% endfor %}
</div>

{# replaces Django's template: ONE radio button or ONE checkbox, followed by its label #}
{% include "django/forms/widgets/input.html" %}
<label class="form-check-label" for="{{ widget.attrs.id }}">{{ widget.label }}</label>

They have exactly the same names and paths as the templates in [Django] that they replace ([django/forms/widgets/...], found in the [django/forms/templates] folder of the library):

  • [multiple_input.html] draws the group: for each option ([widget.optgroups]: the options, grouped together; we have no subgroups), a [<div class="form-check form-check-inline">] that contains the option, drawn using its own template ([option.template_name]);
  • [input_option.html] renders an option: the input field ([<input type="radio">] or [<input type="checkbox">], using the template from [Django] and [input.html]), followed by its label.

All of this needs to be written only once: Examples 19, 21, and 28, as well as the case study, use these files. Ready-made libraries, such as [django-crispy-forms] and its package [crispy-bootstrap5], or [django-bootstrap5], do the same; we preferred to demonstrate the mechanism.

docs.title: 4.6.4. The view: form/views.py
docs.text:
# form/views.py: a form that uses all the kinds of fields

from django.shortcuts import render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_http_methods

from .forms import FieldsForm

# the initial values (one per field, a list for a multiple field)
INITIAL_VALUES = {"title": "Mme", "country": "fr", "languages": ["French"], "token": "A7X2"}


# GET: the form, with initial values; POST: the sent fields are
# read, validated, then displayed again by the same form
@require_http_methods(["GET", "POST"])
def form(request):
    if request.method == "GET":
        # initial: the values displayed as long as nothing has been sent
        return render(request, "form/form.html",
                      {"form": FieldsForm(initial=INITIAL_VALUES)})
    # a form BOUND to the sent data: it converts and validates them
    form = FieldsForm(request.POST)
    valid = form.is_valid()
    data = None
    if valid:
        # cleaned_data: the values converted by each field; a list (multiple
        # field) is written as text, its values separated by commas
        data = {key: ", ".join(value) if isinstance(value, list) else value
                for key, value in form.cleaned_data.items()}
    # what the browser actually sent, field by field; lists(): the
    # pairs (name, list of all the values of the field)
    received = "\n".join(f"{name} = [{', '.join(values)}]" for name, values in request.POST.lists())
    return render(request, "form/form.html", {
        "form": form,
        "received": received,
        "valid": valid,
        "data": data,
    })
  • line 9: the form’s initial values: a dictionary, one value per field (a list for a multi-value field);
  • line 14: a single view for both methods: GET displays the form, POST processes it;
  • lines 16–19: in GET, an unbound form (without data), with its initial values (parameter [initial]): it is not validated and does not display any errors;
  • lines 21–22: in POST, a form linked to the submitted fields ([request.POST]), then validated ([is_valid], previous chapter): each field converts its value (the date, the lists, etc.), verifies that a selection is among those that were offered, and applies its constraints;
  • lines 24–28: if the form is valid, its data is converted ([cleaned_data]) into a human-readable dictionary (using the [{key: value for ...}] syntax): a list is written as text, with its elements separated by commas ([", ".join(...)]);
  • Line 31: For this example, what the browser actually sent. The method [lists()] of a [QueryDict] (Example 10) iterates through the pairs (name, list of all values). The string [\n] is a line break;
  • lines 32–37: the linked form is passed to the template, which will display it, along with the user’s input and any errors.

docs.title: 4.6.5. The template: templates/form/form.html
docs.text:
{% extends "layout.html" %}

{% block content %}
  <h1 class="h3">A complete form</h1>
  <form method="post" action="{% url 'form' %}" style="max-width: 40rem">
    {# the anti-CSRF token: a hidden field, which the CsrfViewMiddleware middleware checks #}
    {% csrf_token %}
    {# as_field_group: a complete field (label, input area, errors) #}
    {{ form.title.as_field_group }}
    <div class="row g-2">
      <div class="col">{{ form.name.as_field_group }}</div>
      <div class="col">{{ form.password.as_field_group }}</div>
      <div class="col">{{ form.birth_date.as_field_group }}</div>
    </div>
    {{ form.hobbies.as_field_group }}
    <div class="row g-2">
      <div class="col">{{ form.country.as_field_group }}</div>
      <div class="col">{{ form.languages.as_field_group }}</div>
    </div>
    {{ form.comment.as_field_group }}
    {# a hidden field: the input area alone, without label #}
    {{ form.token }}
    <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Send</button>
  </form>
  {# received: present in the context if the form has been sent #}
  {% if received %}
    <h2 class="h5 mt-3">What the server received</h2>
    <pre class="bg-light p-2 border">{{ received }}</pre>
    <p>Valid form: {{ valid|yesno:"yes,no" }}</p>
    <ul>
      {# errors: a dictionary {field: list of errors}; items: its pairs #}
      {% for field, errors in form.errors.items %}
        {% for error in errors %}<li>{{ field }}: {{ error }}</li>{% endfor %}
      {% endfor %}
    </ul>
    {% if valid %}
      <p>The data of the form:</p>
      <ul>
        {% for key, value in data.items %}
          <li>{{ key }}: {{ value }}</li>
        {% endfor %}
      </ul>
    {% endif %}
  {% endif %}
{% endblock %}
  • Line 5: The [<form>] tag, entered manually: the [Django] form does not generate it;
  • line 7: the [{% csrf_token %}] tag creates a hidden field containing the anti-CSRF token (see below);
  • line 9: [{{ form.title }}] refers to the [title] field in the form (a [BoundField]); its method [as_field_group] renders it in full using the template [forms/field.html]: label, input field (with its current value), and error messages;
  • lines 10–20: the other fields, arranged according to the grid classes of [Bootstrap];
  • line 22: the hidden field, of which only the input field is rendered;
  • line 26: the variable [received] exists only after a submission; a missing variable is “false”;
  • lines 32–34: the errors. [form.errors] is a dictionary, which is iterated over using [items] (without parentheses, as in DTL): for each field, the list of its errors;
  • lines 39–41: a loop over a dictionary that iterates through both the keys and the values.

We could have written the entire form in a single line: [{{ form }}], which renders all the fields in order using the form template (rendering engine setting [form_template_name]). By processing the fields one by one, you can arrange them as you like.

docs.title: 4.6.6. CSRF Protection
docs.text:
A CSRF attack (Cross-Site Request Forgery) involves a malicious site tricking the victim’s browser into sending a form to our application. The browser includes our application’s cookies in the request—and thus the logged-in user’s session—so the request appears legitimate. The solution: every form in our application contains a random token that the malicious site cannot know.

[Django] applies this to the entire application via a middleware component, [CsrfViewMiddleware] (line 23 of the file [config/settings.py]). When a page is generated, the [{% csrf_token %}] tag writes to the hidden field [csrfmiddlewaretoken], and the middleware sends, along with the response, a cookie named [csrftoken], which contains a secret. For any request that modifies (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE), before rendering the view, the middleware verifies that the token sent (in the [csrfmiddlewaretoken] field, or in the [X-CSRFToken] header, for a request sent via [JavaScript]) matches the cookie’s secret. A malicious site cannot read our site’s cookie or view our pages: it cannot generate a valid token. If the verification fails, the view is not called: [Django] responds with a 403 error on its own. This is a significant difference from [Symfony], whose Form component verified the token for each form and let the action decide what to do next: With [Django], all POST requests are protected, and a view cannot forget to be protected. The [@csrf_exempt] decorator exempts a view from this verification (for a API called by other servers, for example).

docs.title: 4.6.7. Execution
docs.text:
The initial values are visible: the “Mme” radio button, the country “France,” and the language “French.” The HTML generates (excerpts):

<form method="post" action="/form" style="max-width: 40rem">
    <input type="hidden" name="csrfmiddlewaretoken" value="HuaIyQ2pbEWYQCG1mTPuWEDSd9zjBvCQhGfposguhAGFVRfIl5gRe39M2HPOHKnm">
    <fieldset class="mb-3">
    <legend class="form-label fs-6 mb-1">Title</legend>
    <div id="id_title">
  <div class="form-check form-check-inline">
<input type="radio" name="title" value="Mr" class="form-check-input" required id="id_title_0">
<label class="form-check-label" for="id_title_0">Mr</label>
</div>
  <div class="form-check form-check-inline">
<input type="radio" name="title" value="Mme" class="form-check-input" required id="id_title_1" checked>
<label class="form-check-label" for="id_title_1">Mme</label>
</div>
...
<input type="checkbox" name="hobbies" value="reading" class="form-check-input" id="id_hobbies_0">
...
    <select name="languages" size="4" class="form-select" id="id_languages" multiple>
  <option value="French" selected>French</option>
  <option value="English">English</option>
...
    <input type="hidden" name="token" value="A7X2" class="form-control" id="id_token">
    <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Send</button>
  </form>

[Django] has written everything: the identifiers ([id_title_1]), the labels associated with their fields, the field names (the checkboxes all have the name [hobbies]: the browser will send a repeated parameter, example 10), the attributes [checked] and [selected] for current values, the attribute [required] for required fields, and the classes of [Bootstrap]. The first hidden field contains the anti-CSRF token; it is different on every page (it is “masked” by a random number, so that a network eavesdropper cannot guess the secret by comparing multiple pages). Let’s fill out the form and submit it:

The page shows what the server received: one parameter per field, with multiple values for the checkboxes and the dropdown list; the password was sent but is not displayed again in its field. The browser displayed the date according to its own settings, but sent it in the format [yyyy-mm-dd]; the template formatted it in the English style, [May 14, 1990], just like any date it displays. The hidden field [token] was sent back exactly as is: this is how information that the user cannot see is sent back and forth (the case study uses this for a record’s version number). However, a hidden field is not a protected field: the user can modify it using their browser’s developer tools, and the server must validate it just like any other field. The anti-CSRF token is also included among the received fields; it is not part of the form data.

Now let's submit a form using [curl], without a token, and with a country that wasn't listed:

curl -i -d "name=Martin&country=xx" http://localhost:8000/form

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
...
  <title>403 Forbidden</title>
...

The request did not proceed beyond the middleware: the view was not called, and the server console indicates this:

Forbidden (CSRF cookie not set.): /form
[27/Sep/2026 19:30:21] "POST /form HTTP/1.1" 403 2908

In a browser, the error page for [Django] explains the reason for the rejection (in debug mode):

For the token to be accepted, [curl] must behave like a browser: first request the form, retaining the [csrftoken] cookie (option [-c], which saves received cookies to a file), then resend the cookie (option [-b]) and the token read from the page:

curl -c cookies.txt http://localhost:8000/form
curl -b cookies.txt -d "csrfmiddlewaretoken=k4ZfzHvE...yBD&name=Martin&country=xx&token=A7X2" http://localhost:8000/form

...
    <pre class="bg-light p-2 border">csrfmiddlewaretoken = [k4ZfzHvER4iJYcaDFRMsYh0OizTJGRMw2AtHYeGuGelfF3DZahfrxLcwUbVn0yBD]
name = [Martin]
country = [xx]
token = [A7X2]</pre>
    <p>Valid form: no</p>
    <ul>


        <li>title: The title is required.</li>

        <li>country: Select a valid choice. xx is not one of the available choices.</li>

    </ul>
...

(the token is the one from the page received by the first request). This time, the view was called, and the form is invalid for two reasons: no title was sent, and the country [xx] is not among the options. This final check is performed by the [ChoiceField] field itself, without us having requested it: a malicious user could send anything, not just what the page suggested. Here, the view returns the invalid form with a 200 status code; the following example will choose a more appropriate status code.

docs.title: 4.7. Example 19: Form Validation
docs.text:
A registration form, in which each field has its own constraints. If an error occurs, the form is redisplayed with the user’s input and a message below each invalid field. We add a rule that applies to two fields: the password and its confirmation must match.

19-form-validation/
├── config/
│   ├── rendering.py
│   ├── settings.py
│   └── ...
├── registration/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── forms.py
│   └── views.py
├── static/
│   └── ...

# registration/forms.py: the registration form, its fields and their constraints

from django import forms


# the parent class of example 18: the Bootstrap CSS classes
class BootstrapForm(forms.Form):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        for field in self.fields.values():
            field.widget.attrs["class"] = "form-control"


class RegistrationForm(BootstrapForm):
    # max_length: a constraint checked by the server, which Django also writes into
    # the page (maxlength attribute), for the browser
    name = forms.CharField(max_length=20, error_messages={
        "required": "The name is required.",
        "max_length": "The name must not exceed 20 characters."})
    # EmailField: a valid address, with a full domain name (example.com, and not example)
    email = forms.EmailField(label="Email address", error_messages={
        "required": "The email address is required.",
        "invalid": "Invalid email address."})
    # IntegerField: an integer; an input that is not one produces the invalid error
    age = forms.IntegerField(label="Age", min_value=18, max_value=120, error_messages={
        "required": "The age is required.",
        "invalid": "An integer is expected.",
        "min_value": "The age must be between 18 and 120 years.",
        "max_value": "The age must be between 18 and 120 years."})
    password = forms.CharField(label="Password", min_length=6, widget=forms.PasswordInput,
                               error_messages={
                                   "required": "The password is required.",
                                   "min_length": "The password must have at least 6 characters."})
    confirmation = forms.CharField(label="Confirmation", widget=forms.PasswordInput,
                                   error_messages={"required": "The confirmation is required."})

    # clean: the validation of the WHOLE form, after that of each field. It is
    # here that two fields are compared
    def clean(self):
        data = super().clean()
        password = data.get("password")
        confirmation = data.get("confirmation")
        # the two fields passed their own validation, but differ
        if password and confirmation and password != confirmation:
            # add_error: an error, attached to the confirmation field
            self.add_error("confirmation", "The confirmation does not match the password.")
        return data
  • lines 7–11: the parent class from Example 18, simplified: all fields are input fields;
  • lines 17–19: the name is required and must not exceed 20 characters. Each error is assigned its own message based on its code (example 09). The parameter [max_length] has two effects: the field checks the length (on the server), and its widget sets the attribute HTML [maxlength], which limits the input in the browser ([min_length] does the same, with the attribute [minlength]);
  • lines 21–23: a [EmailField] verifies that an address is valid and requires a fully qualified domain name ([example.com], not [example]). Its widget, [EmailInput], generates a [<input type="email">], which the browser can validate;
  • lines 25–29: a [IntegerField] produces a [<input type="number">], with the attributes [min] and [max] derived from [min_value] and [max_value], and converts the input to an integer. An entry that is not an integer produces the error [invalid];
  • lines 30–35: the password (at least 6 characters) and its confirmation, two [CharField] fields using the [PasswordInput] widget. A parameter can span multiple lines;
  • lines 39–47: the method [clean] validates the entire form after validating each field (and its methods [clean_<field>], example 12). [super().clean()] returns [cleaned_data], which contains only the valid fields: [data.get("password")] equals [None] if the password has already been rejected (too short). The comparison is performed only if both fields are valid; if they differ, [add_error] attaches an error to the [confirmation] field ([add_error(None, "...")] would attach it to the form itself: a “general” error, which is returned by [non_field_errors()]). This is the way to validate a rule that applies to multiple fields.

docs.text:
# registration/views.py: a form validated by the server

from django.shortcuts import render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_http_methods

from .forms import RegistrationForm


# GET /register: the form; ?html5=true: we let the browser validate it
# before sending. POST /register: the sent form
@require_http_methods(["GET", "POST"])
def register(request):
    html5 = request.GET.get("html5") == "true"
    if request.method == "POST":
        form = RegistrationForm(request.POST)
        # is_valid: each field could be converted and respects its constraints, and
        # the clean method did not report any error
        if form.is_valid():
            return render(request, "registration/welcome.html",
                          {"registration": form.cleaned_data})
        # an invalid form, displayed again with the input and the errors, with the
        # 422 code (Unprocessable Content)
        return render(request, "registration/registration.html",
                      {"form": form, "html5": html5}, status=422)
    # the first display: an empty form
    return render(request, "registration/registration.html",
                  {"form": RegistrationForm(), "html5": html5})
  • Line 13: The parameter [?html5=true] enables browser validation (see below);
  • lines 15–20: a form linked to the submitted fields. If it is valid, the welcome page receives its data (the following example will show that it is better to redirect after a successful POST);
  • lines 23–24: otherwise, the form is redisplayed, showing the input and any errors, along with code 422 (Unprocessable Content: “the request is well-formed, but its content is invalid”);
  • lines 26–27: on the first display, an empty, unbound form.

The invalid form is therefore redisplayed by the POST view itself, which retains the input and errors: this is the standard approach used by [Django], as well as by [Symfony]. Other frameworks, such as [Laravel], instead respond by redirecting to the form page, while preserving the input and errors in the session for the next request.

docs.title: 4.7.4. Execution
docs.text:
Let’s submit a form full of errors: a name consisting of spaces, an address without a full domain, an age of 12, a password that’s too short, and a different confirmation:

The input was retained (except for the passwords), and each error is flagged below its corresponding field. The name consisting of spaces is flagged as missing: a ***[CharField] removes the spaces surrounding each entry (parameter ***[strip]***, example 08), and redisplays the cleaned-up value. The confirmation, however, contains no errors, even though it differs from the password: since the password was rejected, the [clean]* method did not compare them. The URL is the form’s, [/register]: the page was displayed by the view in response to POST. With [curl], by providing the anti-CSRF token as in Example 18, you can also send something a browser would not send—a non-numeric age:

curl -i -b cookies.txt -d "csrfmiddlewaretoken=...&name=Martin&email=jean.martin@example.com&age=abc&password=secret123&confirmation=secret123" http://localhost:8000/register

HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
...
    <label class="form-label" for="id_age">Age</label>
    <input type="number" name="age" value="abc" min="18" max="120" class="form-control" required aria-invalid="true" aria-describedby="id_age_error" id="id_age">
    <div class="invalid-feedback d-block" id="id_age_error">An integer is expected.</div>
...

We see the input redisplayed, the attributes HTML5 ([required], [min], [max]), the error message [invalid], and the attributes [aria-invalid] and [aria-describedby]—which [Django] automatically adds to a field with an error—and which link the field to its message for screen readers.

docs.title: 4.7.5. Browser validation
docs.text:
Let's remove the [novalidate] attribute by clicking the "Enable" link (parameter [?html5=true]). The browser then checks the attributes [required], [type="email"], [min], [max], [maxlength]... before submitting the form, and displays its own messages in a tooltip below the first field with an error (“Please fill in this field,” “The value must be greater than or equal to 18,” etc.): the form is not submitted as long as there is an error. [Django] generated these attributes automatically based on the fields: [required] for any required field, [maxlength] and [minlength] based on [max_length] and [min_length], [min] and [max] based on [min_value] and [max_value], [type="email"] and [type="number"] based on the widgets. They therefore always comply with the server’s constraints. Only the rule for the [clean] method (confirmation) is not handled by the browser.

This validation is convenient for the user: it’s immediate, with no back-and-forth with the server. But it does not replace the server’s validation: a user can disable it, and a program like [curl] ignores it completely. The rule is absolute: the server always validates; browser validation is merely an added convenience.

A correct entry, at last. The name, entered with spaces on either side, was cleaned up by the form:

docs.title: 4.8. Example 20: The Post/Redirect/Get Pattern
docs.text:
When a POST view responds with a page, that page is the result of a POST. If the user reloads it (presses [F5]), the browser sends the POST, after a warning that few people read: the command is sent twice, and the message is posted twice. The Post/Redirect/Get pattern (PRG) avoids this problem: a successful POST view does not render a page; it responds with a redirect (example 04) to a page GET, which the browser requests immediately. Reloading this page simply re-executes the GET.

One problem remains: the GET page would like to display a message (“the task has been added”), but it is the POST view that knows this message, and it cannot pass a variable to a request that has not yet occurred. The solution: a flash message, posted by the POST view, which is retained until it is read, displayed, and then discarded. [Django] provides these through its [django.contrib.messages] application.

docs.title: 4.8.2. The service: tasks/service.py
docs.text:
# tasks/service.py: the list of tasks, shared by all the users

import threading

# the server process stays in memory from one request to the next: a variable of the
# MODULE lives as long as it does. The list is therefore shared by all the
# requests of all the users (and lost when the server stops)
_tasks = ["Read chapter 3"]

# the server handles several requests AT THE SAME TIME, in several threads of execution
# (threads): a lock guarantees that only one at a time modifies the list
_lock = threading.Lock()


def list_tasks() -> list[str]:
    # a copy: the caller cannot modify the service's list
    with _lock:
        return list(_tasks)


def add(label: str) -> None:
    # with: the lock is taken here, and released on leaving the block, even after an exception
    with _lock:
        _tasks.append(label)

The task list is shared by all users and must persist from one request to the next. We saw this in Examples 01 and 06: in [Python], the server remains in memory from one request to the next. A simple module variable is therefore sufficient. Readers of the [Symfony] course will recall that, in [PHP], the list had to be stored in a cache or a file.

  • Line 8: the list, a module variable. It exists for as long as the server process runs: it is lost when the server shuts down or restarts (after a code change, during development). And if the production server runs multiple processes (which is standard practice: one per processor, for example), each will have its own list. A real-world application would therefore store the list in a database (Chapter 7);
  • Line 12: The development server processes multiple requests at the same time, each in its own thread. Two simultaneous updates could conflict. A lock ([threading.Lock]) ensures that only one thread at a time executes the code it protects;
  • lines 15–18: The function returns a copy of the list, created under the protection of the lock;
  • lines 21–24: The statement [with] acquires the lock, executes the block, and then releases the lock—in all cases, even if an exception interrupts the block. An object that can be used by [with] is called a context manager; files are another example ([with open(...) as f:] closes the file at the end of the block).

The service is a module, not a class: its functions are called by [service.list_tasks()] and [service.add(...)]. This is the simplest way, in [Python], to have a single object shared by the entire application (Example 06).

docs.title: 4.8.3. Views: tasks/views.py
docs.text:
# tasks/views.py: the Post / Redirect / Get pattern

from django.contrib import messages
from django.shortcuts import redirect, render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_http_methods, require_POST

from . import service


# GET /tasks: the list and the add form; POST /tasks: the addition, according to the
# Post / Redirect / Get pattern
@require_http_methods(["GET", "POST"])
def tasks(request):
    if request.method == "GET":
        return render(request, "tasks/tasks.html", {"tasks": service.list_tasks()})
    label = request.POST.get("label", "").strip()
    if label == "" or len(label) > 40:
        # invalid input: we display the page again, without a redirect
        return render(request, "tasks/tasks.html", {
            "tasks": service.list_tasks(),
            "label": label,
            "error": "The label must have 1 to 40 characters."})
    service.add(label)
    # a "flash" message: it will survive the redirect, for the NEXT request
    messages.success(request, f"The task [{label}] has been added.")
    # no page: a redirect to the GET page
    return redirect("tasks")


# POST /tasks/without-prg: the counter-example (a page in response to the POST)
@require_POST
def add_without_prg(request):
    service.add(request.POST.get("label", "").strip() or "(untitled)")
    return render(request, "tasks/tasks.html", {"tasks": service.list_tasks(), "without_prg": True})
  • lines 16–22: The input is validated manually to keep the example concise ([strip] removes the surrounding spaces). An invalid entry is redisplayed without redirection: there is nothing to protect against a duplicate submission, since nothing has been modified;
  • line 25: [messages.success] displays a “success” level flash message " (there are also [debug], [info], [warning], and [error]: the level allows messages to be displayed differently);
  • line 27: the redirect to the page GET, named [tasks] (example 04);
  • lines 31–34: the counterexample: a page in response to POST. The operator [or] returns its left operand if it is “true” (here, a non-empty string), and the right operand otherwise.

docs.title: 4.8.5. Where are flash messages stored?
docs.text:
Between the POST request and the subsequent GET request, the message must be stored somewhere. We chose a cookie. Let’s examine it using [curl], by saving the cookies to a file (options [-c] and [-b], Example 18), after requesting the page to obtain the anti-CSRF token:

curl -i -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt -d "csrfmiddlewaretoken=...&label=Do%20the%20exercises" http://localhost:8000/tasks

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Location: /tasks
Set-Cookie: messages=W1siX19qc29uX21lc3NhZ2UiLDAsMjUsIlRoZSB0YXNrIFtEbyB0aGUgZXhlcmNpc2VzXSBoYXMgYmVlbiBhZGRlZC4iLCIiXV0:1xAsjI:xIWL3aUp2CbHdwZRyfv13cVIN1QG9baN2Ss020Pzyl0; HttpOnly; Path=/; SameSite=Lax

The response to POST is a redirect (status code 302, header [Location]), accompanied by the cookie [messages]. This cookie is [HttpOnly] (the [JavaScript] on the page cannot read it) and [SameSite=Lax] (the browser does not send it with a POST request originating from another site). Its value consists of three parts, separated by colons: the data, a date (encoded in base 62), and a signature. The data is the list of messages, in JSON, base-64-encoded (it is not compressed here: [Django] compresses the data only when that makes them shorter, and a compressed value begins with a period). When decoded, they yield:

[["__json_message",0,25,"The task [Do the exercises] has been added.",""]]

It shows the message level (25: success) and its text. The cookie’s content is therefore not secret: anyone can decode it. But it is signed: the signature is calculated based on the data and the application’s secret key ([SECRET_KEY], example 01). If the browser sends back a modified cookie, the signature no longer matches, and [Django] ignores it: a user cannot fabricate fake messages. Let’s follow the redirect by sending back the cookie:

curl -i -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt http://localhost:8000/tasks

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Vary: Cookie
Set-Cookie: messages=""; expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT; Max-Age=0; Path=/; SameSite=Lax
...
      <div class="alert alert-success" role="status">The task [Do the exercises] has been added.</div>
...
      <li>Read chapter 3</li>

      <li>Do the exercises</li>
...

The message is displayed; the middleware, seeing that it has been read, deletes the cookie (an empty cookie that expired in 1970). A new request, GET, would no longer display the message. The [Vary: Cookie] header alerts caches that the response depends on the request’s cookies. The task list, meanwhile, is stored in the server’s memory.

docs.text:
Adding a task: the browser followed the redirect; the URL header corresponds to the GET page, which can be safely reloaded.

An invalid entry, redisplayed with its error message:

The counterexample: the page is the response to POST, and its URL is [/tasks/without-prg]. If you click on [F5], the browser asks if you want to resubmit the form; if you agree, the task is added a second time.

docs.title: 4.9. Example 21: Links, Buttons, and Confirmation
docs.text:
A principle of the HTTP protocol: a GET request does not change anything. Browsers, search engines, and tools that preload pages freely follow links without asking the user for permission. A “delete” link ([<a href="/contacts/2/delete">]) would therefore be dangerous: a bot crawling the site would delete everything. In a web application:

  • viewing is done via a link ([<a href>]), which sends a GET request;
  • editing (save, duplicate, delete) is done via a button placed in a form, protected by an anti-CSRF token.

This example manages a contact list and displays a confirmation window before each deletion.

docs.title: 4.9.1. Method simulation: config/middleware.py
docs.text:
A HTML form can only send GET and POST requests. However, the HTTP protocol supports other methods: DELETE for deletion, and PUT and PATCH for updates. Many frameworks work around this limitation: a POST form that contains a hidden field [_method], with a value of [DELETE] (or [PUT], [PATCH]), is treated as a request for that method. This is known as method spoofing. [Symfony] offered this as an option; [Django] does not. Let’s implement it as middleware:

# config/middleware.py: the HTTP method of a form, replaced by its _method field

# an HTML form can only send GET and POST. A POST form that contains a
# hidden _method field (DELETE, PUT, PATCH) is handled as a request of that method
class MethodOverride:
    METHODS = {"DELETE", "PUT", "PATCH"}

    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        return self.get_response(request)

    # process_view: Django calls it AFTER the routing, just before the view (and after the
    # process_view of the middlewares that precede this one, including the one that checks the
    # anti-CSRF token of a POST). Returning None: the request continues on its way
    def process_view(self, request, view_func, view_args, view_kwargs):
        if request.method == "POST":
            method = request.POST.get("_method", "").upper()
            if method in self.METHODS:
                request.method = method
        return None
  • line 6: a class attribute: the set ([set], enclosed in curly braces) of accepted methods;
  • lines 11–12: [__call__] passes the request on without doing anything;
  • lines 17–22: the method [process_view]: [Django] calls it after routing, just before calling the view, with the selected view and its parameters (the chapter on the lifecycle will cover this in detail). If the request is a POST whose [_method] field points to one of the accepted methods, the middleware replaces the method in the request. Returning [None] allows the request to continue on its path.

Why [process_view], and not [__call__]? Because of anti-CSRF protection. The [CsrfViewMiddleware] middleware performs its validation within its own method, [process_view], which is called before ours, since it precedes it in the [MIDDLEWARE] configuration. The token is therefore validated on the POST request, before we transform it into DELETE. This is what the comment in the [config/settings.py] file states:

# contacts/service.py: the contacts, shared by everyone, in memory (see example 20)

import threading

from .viewmodels import Contact

_contacts = [
    Contact(1, "Marie Durand", "01 23 45 67 89"),
    Contact(2, "Paul Martin", "06 12 34 56 78"),
    Contact(3, "Philippe Jandot", "02 98 76 54 32"),
]
_last_id = 3
_lock = threading.Lock()


def list_contacts() -> list[Contact]:
    with _lock:
        return list(_contacts)


# the contact, or None if it does not exist
def read(id: int) -> Contact | None:
    with _lock:
        return next((c for c in _contacts if c.id == id), None)


def update(id: int, name: str, phone: str) -> Contact | None:
    with _lock:
        # enumerate: the pairs (position, element) of the list
        for i, contact in enumerate(_contacts):
            if contact.id == id:
                # a contact is immutable (frozen): we build a new one, which
                # replaces the old one in the list
                _contacts[i] = Contact(id, name, phone)
                return _contacts[i]
        return None


def add(name: str, phone: str) -> Contact:
    # global: the function modifies the module's _last_id variable (without this word,
    # the assignment would create a local variable)
    global _last_id
    with _lock:
        _last_id += 1
        contact = Contact(_last_id, name, phone)
        _contacts.append(contact)
        return contact


def delete(id: int) -> Contact | None:
    with _lock:
        for i, contact in enumerate(_contacts):
            if contact.id == id:
                # pop removes element i from the list, and returns it
                return _contacts.pop(i)
        return None

Contacts are stored in memory, just like the tasks in Example 20. Each contact is an immutable object [Contact] (an ID, a name, a phone number, file [contacts/viewmodels.py]). A few points about [Python]:

  • line 12: the last assigned identifier;
  • lines 27–36: a contact is immutable; we create a new one, which replaces the old one in the list. [enumerate] iterates through a list in pairs (position, element);
  • lines 39–47: a function that assigns a value to a module variable must declare it using [global] (line 42): without this keyword, the assignment [_last_id += 1] would create a local variable for the function (and would fail here, since it reads its value before assigning it). Reading a module variable, or modifying the list it refers to ([_contacts.append(...)]), does not require anything of the sort;
  • line 55: [pop(i)] removes the element at position [i] from the list and returns it;
  • The functions return [None] for a nonexistent contact: it is up to the view to decide on the response.

# contacts/views.py: links (GET) and buttons (POST, DELETE)

from django.contrib import messages
from django.http import Http404
from django.shortcuts import redirect, render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET, require_http_methods

from . import service
from .forms import ContactForm


# the contact, or a 404 response if it does not exist
def contact_or_404(contact):
    if contact is None:
        raise Http404("unknown contact")
    return contact


# a LINK (<a href>): a GET request, which modifies nothing
@require_GET
def list_contacts(request):
    return render(request, "contacts/list.html", {"contacts": service.list_contacts()})


# GET /contacts/2: the details page; POST /contacts/2: one of its two buttons;
# DELETE /contacts/2: the deletion (a POST and its _method field)
@require_http_methods(["GET", "POST", "DELETE"])
def contact(request, id):
    if request.method == "DELETE":
        return delete(request, id)
    contact = contact_or_404(service.read(id))
    if request.method == "GET":
        form = ContactForm(initial={"name": contact.name, "phone": contact.phone})
        return render(request, "contacts/details.html", {"contact": contact, "form": form})
    form = ContactForm(request.POST)
    if not form.is_valid():
        return render(request, "contacts/details.html", {"contact": contact, "form": form})
    name = form.cleaned_data["name"]
    phone = form.cleaned_data["phone"]
    # the clicked button is the only one to send its name: "duplicate" in request.POST
    # is true if it is the one that sent the form
    if "duplicate" in request.POST:
        copy = service.add(f"{name} (copy)", phone)
        messages.success(request, f"The contact [{copy.name}] has been created.")
    else:
        service.update(id, name, phone)
        messages.success(request, f"The contact [{name}] has been edited.")
    return redirect("contacts")


# the deletion; the anti-CSRF token has already been checked by CsrfViewMiddleware
def delete(request, id):
    contact = contact_or_404(service.delete(id))
    messages.success(request, f"The contact [{contact.name}] has been deleted.")
    return redirect("contacts")
  • lines 13–16: a utility function—a nonexistent contact returns a 404 response to terminate the view;
  • lines 20–22: the GET view of the list, which does not modify anything;
  • lines 27–48: a contact’s record. In GET, it displays the form, populated with the contact’s information; in POST, it processes the form; in DELETE, it deletes the contact. The same URL and [/contacts/2] are thus used to view, save, and delete. The decorator [require_http_methods] is checked when the view is called, i.e., after [process_view]: it does indeed see the method DELETE;
  • lines 35–37: an invalid form is redisplayed;
  • lines 42–47: A form can have multiple submit buttons. When the form is submitted, the browser sends, in addition to the fields, the name (attribute [name]) of the clicked button, and only that button’s name. [in] checks for the presence of a key in a dictionary: ["duplicate" in request.POST] is true if the form was submitted via the [duplicate] button. Depending on the button, the view either duplicates or saves the contact;
  • line 48: in both cases, the PRG flow (example 20), with a flash message;
  • lines 52–55: deletion. It does not need to verify the anti-CSRF token: [CsrfViewMiddleware] did so beforehand. A missing or invalid token would have stopped the request with a 403 error.

The browser can display a confirmation box (function [JavaScript] [confirm]), but it is not very attractive, and its appearance depends on the browser. Here we use a modal window from [Bootstrap], displayed by a few lines of [JavaScript]. The window is a fragment, included in the parent template, and is therefore present—though hidden—on all pages:

  • line 20: the window, included on all pages;
  • line 22: the script, placed at the bottom of the page: when it runs, the elements it searches for already exist. It is a static file, stored in the [static/js] folder.

The [static/js/app.js] script:

// confirmation of the forms that carry the data-confirmation="..." attribute
// Without JavaScript, these forms are simply sent without confirmation.
(() => {
  const modal = document.getElementById('confirmation-modal');
  const message = document.getElementById('confirmation-modal-message');
  let pending = null; // the form to send if the user confirms

  // 1. we intercept the submission of the forms to confirm
  document.querySelectorAll('form[data-confirmation]').forEach((form) => {
    form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
      event.preventDefault(); // the submission is suspended
      pending = form;
      message.textContent = form.dataset.confirmation;
      modal.classList.remove('d-none'); // the window appears
    });
  });

  // 2. the two buttons of the window
  modal.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
    const action = event.target.dataset.action;
    if (action === 'yes') {
      pending.submit(); // submission, WITHOUT firing the 'submit' event again
    } else if (action === 'no') {
      modal.classList.add('d-none');
      pending = null;
    }
  });
})();
  • line 3: the code is enclosed in an anonymous function that is executed immediately; its variables do not interfere with those of the other scripts on the page;
  • lines 4–6: the window, the message location, and the form awaiting confirmation;
  • Lines 9–16: For each form that has the [data-confirmation] attribute, the [submit] event—triggered when the form is submitted—is intercepted. [preventDefault()] suspends the submission; the form is put on hold, and its message ([dataset.confirmation], the value of the [data-confirmation] attribute) is displayed in the window that appears;
  • lines 19–27: a single handler for clicks in the window: [event.target] is the element clicked; its attribute [data-action] specifies which button it is. “Yes” submits the pending form using the [submit()] method, which—unlike clicking a button—does not trigger the [submit] event (otherwise, the window would reappear); “No” hides the window.

Without [JavaScript], the form is simply submitted without confirmation: the page remains usable. This is progressive enhancement: [JavaScript] adds convenience, but the application does not depend on it.

docs.title: 7. The Lifecycle of a Request
docs.text:
Between the arrival of a request and the dispatch of its response, [Django] goes through several steps, and the application can intervene at each one. We have already encountered several of these intervention points: the middleware components and their method [__call__] (examples 03, 12, 16, 23), their [process_exception] methods (examples 08 and 12) and [process_view] methods (example 21), and route converters (example 12). This chapter combines them into a single example, which displays a message in the console at each step so that the order can be observed:

    1. the [request_started] signal: the request has just arrived. A signal is a notification, emitted by [Django] at a specific moment, that application functions—the receivers—can receive. They cannot act on the request: they are simply notified;
    1. The [__call__] method of the middleware components, before the call to [get_response]: the middleware components are processed in the order specified by the [MIDDLEWARE] configuration. Routing has not yet taken place: a middleware component does not yet know which view will handle the request. It may also respond on its own, without invoking the rest of the chain: in that case, neither the subsequent middleware components nor the view are called;
    1. Routing: Once all middleware components have been processed, [Django] searches for the route that matches the requested path (example 02); the route parameter converters (example 12) are called at this point. If no route matches, a [Http404] (404) exception is thrown;
  • 3 and 4. The [process_view] method of the middleware components, in the order specified: the view has been selected but not yet called. A middleware component then knows the view and its parameters; it can let the process continue (return [None]), respond on behalf of the view, or throw an exception;
    1. the view, and the template it generates;
  • x. The [process_exception] middleware method, if the view has thrown an exception, in the reverse order of the configuration. The first one to provide a response stops the search. If none provides one, [Django] generates the error response itself: its detailed page in debug mode, or the application’s error page, provided by the views [handler400], [handler403], [handler404], and [handler500] (see below). An exception thrown elsewhere (in the [__call__] or [process_view] of a middleware component, or in routing) does not pass through [process_exception]: [Django] converts it into an error response upon exiting the relevant middleware;
  • 6 and 7. The [__call__] method of the middleware components, following the call to [get_response], in the reverse order of the configuration: the response is ready, and each middleware component can modify it (add a header, a cookie);
    1. The [request_finished] signal, sent after the response is sent to the browser. Receivers can no longer modify the response: they are used for processing tasks that can wait (such as closing database connections, which is what [Django] itself does), without making the user wait.

This is equivalent to the filters of [Java] and the interceptors of [Spring MVC], the action filters of [ASP.NET Core MVC], and the functions [before_request] / [after_request] and [Flask] functions, the middleware in [Laravel], and the event listeners in [Symfony]. Compared to these, the difference lies in the structure: a middleware component encapsulates the rest of the processing (it calls [get_response], and thus sees the request before and the response after, within the same code, like the Russian nesting dolls in Example 03), whereas an event listener reacts to an event, and you must listen for two events—one before and one after the action—to take action. The order of the middleware components, meanwhile, follows the list in the [MIDDLEWARE] configuration, rather than a numerical sequence: this is easier to read, but you must be familiar with the ordering constraints for the middleware components in [Django] (the session before authentication, for example; as specified in the [Django] documentation).

# calc/logger.py: a message in the console of the development server

import sys


def log(message):

    print(message, file=sys.stderr)

docs.title: 7.1.2. Before and after everything else: the signals
docs.text:
# calc/signals.py: two Django SIGNALS, emitted at the start and at the end of each request

from django.core.signals import request_finished, request_started
from django.dispatch import receiver

from . import timer
from .logger import log


# @receiver: the function is called at each emission of the request_started signal,
# before all the middlewares
@receiver(request_started)
def start(sender, environ, **kwargs):
    log(f"--- {environ['REQUEST_METHOD']} {environ['PATH_INFO']}")
    log("0. signal request_started")


# request_finished: at the very end, AFTER the response is sent to the browser; we
# can no longer change the response
@receiver(request_finished)
def finish(sender, **kwargs):
    duration = timer.stop()
    # the measurement has not started if the view was not reached
    if duration is not None:
        log(f"8. signal request_finished (end, {duration} ms)")
  • line 3: the two signals from [Django] that frame each request;
  • lines 12–15: the [@receiver] decorator hooks the [start] function onto the [request_started] signal: it will be called every time the signal is emitted. A receiver receives the signal emitter ([sender]), followed by named parameters specific to each signal; [**kwargs] collects those it does not name, as required by the documentation for [Django] (a signal may receive new parameters in a future version). [request_started] provides [environ], the WSGI dictionary for the query (example 01): the [HttpRequest] object does not yet exist. The receiver displays the method and the path, followed by message #0;
  • lines 20–25: message No. 8, when everything is finished, with the duration measured by the timer (see below), if the measurement has started.

[Django] sends other signals: before and after saving a template from ORM ([pre_save], [post_save]), when a user logs in ([user_logged_in])... and the application can define its own. A receiver must be registered when the application starts, before the first request. The designated location for this is the application configuration:

# calc/apps.py: the CONFIGURATION of the calc application

from django.apps import AppConfig


class CalcConfig(AppConfig):
    name = "calc"

    # ready: Django calls it once, at startup, when all the applications
    # are loaded. This is where the signal receivers are connected
    def ready(self):
        from . import signals  # noqa: F401 (the import is enough to connect them)
  • lines 6–7: An application’s configuration is a class that inherits from [AppConfig], conventionally located in the application’s [apps.py] module, and which [Django] locates on its own. [name] is the name of the application package. This is also where you would give the application a human-readable name ([verbose_name]);
  • lines 11–12: [Django] calls the method [ready] once, at startup, when all applications are loaded. Importing the [signals] module there is sufficient: its [@receiver] decorators attach the receivers when they execute. The import is done within the method, rather than at the top of the file, because a module that uses the ORM templates cannot be imported until the applications have been loaded. The comment [# noqa: F401] instructs code-checking tools not to flag an “unused” import.

docs.title: 7.1.3. Before and After the View: The Logger Middleware
docs.text:
# calc/middleware.py: the middlewares of example 24, in the order of the MIDDLEWARE setting

from django.core.exceptions import BadRequest, PermissionDenied
from django.http import Http404
from django.shortcuts import render

from . import timer
from .errors import DomainError
from .logger import log


# the FIRST middleware: it sees each request go by before the others (and before
# the routing), and the response AFTER all the others
class Logger:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        log("1. Logger, before (before the routing)")
        response = self.get_response(request)
        log(f"7. Logger, after (code {response.status_code})")
        return response


# process_view: AFTER the routing: the middleware knows the chosen route
class Block:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        return self.get_response(request)

    def process_view(self, request, view_func, view_args, view_kwargs):
        # resolver_match: the result of the routing (the view, the name of the route...)
        log(f"3. Block, process_view (route: {request.resolver_match.url_name})")
        if "block" in request.GET:
            # an exception: the rest (Timer, the view) is not executed
            raise PermissionDenied("access blocked")
        return None


# a middleware that only acts for the views marked by the @timed decorator:
# BEFORE the view (process_view), AFTER it; the end of the measurement is entrusted to the
# request_finished signal (see calc/signals.py)
class Timer:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        response = self.get_response(request)
        if getattr(request, "timed", False):
            log(f"6. Timer, after the view (code {response.status_code})")
        return response

    def process_view(self, request, view_func, view_args, view_kwargs):
        # getattr(object, name, default): the attribute of the object, or the default if it does not exist
        if getattr(view_func, "timed", False):
            log("4. Timer, process_view (before the view)")
            request.timed = True
            timer.start()
        return None


# process_exception: an exception left the view; this middleware replaces it
# with our error page
class ErrorPage:
    CODES = {BadRequest: 400, PermissionDenied: 403, Http404: 404}

    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        return self.get_response(request)

    def process_exception(self, request, exception):
        for cls, code in self.CODES.items():
            if isinstance(exception, cls):
                log(f"x. ErrorPage, process_exception (HTTP {code})")
                break
        else:
            # the else of a for loop: executed if the loop was not interrupted by break
            if not isinstance(exception, DomainError):
                return None    # the others: Django's error page
            log(f"x. ErrorPage, process_exception (DomainError: {exception})")
            code = 500
        # the response replaces the exception; it then goes back through the middlewares
        # (Timer, then Logger), like an ordinary response
        return render(request, "error.html", {"code": code}, status=code)
  • Lines 14–22: the first middleware in the configuration: it processes the request before all others (message #1) and the response after all others (message #7), along with its code ([status_code]). It does not know the route, since routing has not yet taken place. It is used for processing that applies to all requests: logging, handling a proxy (the case study mentions this in relation to the clients’ address IP)...

docs.title: 7.1.4. Routing: calc/converters.py
docs.text:
# calc/converters.py: a path converter (see example 12): the segment
# turned into an integer, or into None if it is not an integer (it is then the
# view that decides)

from .logger import log


class IntegerConverter:
    # any segment, without a slash
    regex = r"[^/]+"

    def to_python(self, value):
        log(f'2. IntegerConverter, the routing (received value: "{value}")')
        try:
            return int(value)
        except ValueError:
            return None

    def to_url(self, value):
        return str(value)

A route converter (example 12), which writes message No. 2. It accepts any segment (the expression [[^/]+]: one or more characters that are not slashes) and converts it to a whole number, or to [None] if it is not one: unlike the [int] converter (example 02), which would return a 404 page for [/square/abc]; here, the view will determine the outcome. The file [config/urls.py] saves it as [integer]:

# config/urls.py: the main routing table

from django.urls import path, register_converter

from calc import errors, views
from calc.converters import IntegerConverter

# the "integer" converter (see calc/converters.py)
register_converter(IntegerConverter, "integer")

urlpatterns = [
    path("square/<integer:n>", views.square, name="square"),
]

# the views of the application's error pages: Django uses them for the errors
# 400, 403, 404 and 500 (except, in debug mode, for 400, 404 and 500, which it replaces
# with its detailed pages)
handler400 = errors.page_400
handler403 = errors.page_403
handler404 = errors.page_404
handler500 = errors.page_500
  • Lines 18–21: the error page views, described later.

docs.title: 7.1.5. After routing: the "Block" middleware
docs.text:
Let’s return to the [calc/middleware.py] file:

  • Lines 26–39: The second middleware only acts within its method ***[process\_view], after routing. [request.resolver_match] describes the result of the routing (Example 16): the route name ([url_name]***), the view, and its parameters. Message No. 3;
  • Lines 36–38: The parameter [?block] of URL causes a 403 error (Forbidden, access denied): The exception [PermissionDenied] interrupts processing; the subsequent [process_view]s and the view are not called.

docs.title: 7.1.6. Before the view: the Timer middleware and the @timed decorator
docs.text:
We want to time only certain views—those that request it. All we need to do is mark them with a decorator of our own design:

# calc/timer.py: one stopwatch per thread of execution, and the @timed decorator

import threading
import time

# threading.local: an object whose attributes are SPECIFIC to each thread of execution
# (thread); the server handles each request in its own thread
_local = threading.local()


def start():
    # perf_counter_ns: a precise clock, in nanoseconds
    _local.start = time.perf_counter_ns()


# the elapsed time in milliseconds, or None if the stopwatch has not started
def stop():
    start = getattr(_local, "start", None)
    _local.start = None
    if start is None:
        return None
    return round((time.perf_counter_ns() - start) / 1e6)


# a DECORATOR that does not change the view: it MARKS it, with an attribute that the
# Timer middleware can read
def timed(view):
    view.timed = True
    return view
  • lines 27–29: a decorator that does not replace the view; it adds an attribute, [timed], and returns it. In [Python], a function is an object to which attributes can be added. This is how [Django] itself marks certain views: [@csrf_exempt] (Example 18) adds the attribute [csrf_exempt], which [CsrfViewMiddleware] reads in its method [process_view];
  • Line 8: The timestamp must be passed from [process_view] to the signal [request_finished]. However, the server processes multiple requests simultaneously: a regular module variable would be shared by all of them. A [threading.local] object has attributes specific to each thread: each request, processed in its own thread, has its own start time;
  • lines 11–22: starting and stopping the timer. [time.perf_counter_ns()] is a precise clock, in nanoseconds, designed to measure durations. [getattr(object, name, default)] returns an object’s attribute, or the default value if it does not exist: the timer may not have started in this thread. The duration is returned in milliseconds.

The middleware that reads the mark, in the file [calc/middleware.py]:
